places.name: A Place of Pure Love / Peace / Bliss
places.description: A large group of accounts locate themselves not by geography but by affect: the place IS the feeling. 'I was in this place of just pure unconditional love'; 'I was in this state of absolute bliss.' Narrators frequently slide mid-sentence between 'place' and 'state' as though the distinction had stopped mattering, and several say explicitly that the love was the environment rather than something in it — you were inside love the way you are inside a room.

aliases.note: the strongest form: the feeling replaces both place and self

sensory: love as ambient medium rather than emotion
peace with a texture — thick, warm, holding
no object to attach the feeling to
the feeling continuing to be reported as a location after return

quotes.text: And then all of a sudden, I was in this place of just pure unconditional love.
I was in this state of absolute bliss.
quotes.speaker: Ingrid Honkala

quotes.text: And then when I am in this state of bliss in just a flash like that, I appear in the maid's room
quotes.speaker: Ingrid

quotes.text: But it wasn't a place like here. It was an environment, an atmosphere. And it was love.
quotes.speaker: Ellyn

places.notes: Lowest precision of the entries kept: modern therapeutic idiom ('acting from a place of love', 'coming from a place of knowing') accounts for around half of raw hits and is post-NDE commentary, not a location during the experience — the negative_regex targets exactly that construction. Declines with evidential strength (7.64% -> 4.42% at cv>=23), consistent with the false-positive idiom being commoner in the more discursive, less evidentially rated accounts. Audit found false positives of the form: Present-tense spiritual teaching and after-effect talk: 'create from a space of love', 'find that place of love and acceptance that we all hunger for' (5 passages); Meditation, mystical practice or post-NDE re-entry into the state rather than the NDE itself ('energetically transform myself back into that space of love'); Third-party speculation about where the dead are: a reverend at a funeral, a father assumed to be 'in a place of peace'; A researcher/host generalising about what NDErs long for after they return; 'place of knowing' during an unrelated psychic episode about a drowning child — same construction, different place.

places.name: Coming Out of the Body
places.description: The moment of separation. People describe it less as dying than as being detached — popped, sucked, lifted, whisked or squeezed out of a body that is suddenly not theirs. Some feel a distinct exit point (the crown of the head, the chest, the feet); many feel nothing at all until they notice they are somewhere else looking at themselves. Almost nobody reports pain in this moment; the pain stops first, and then they are out.

aliases.note: the corpus's default phrasing; 41% of docs contain some form of 'left/out of the body'
sudden, effortless separation
the most common forceful image; also 'like a piece of dust in the vacuum hose'

aliases.term: lifted right out of the body
my soul injected from my body
aliases.note: one experiencer's word for the shake-then-pop

aliases.term: astral projection / my astral body left
aliases.note: used by experiencers who already had a metaphysical vocabulary

aliases.term: my point of perception was whisked out
aliases.note: phrasing preferred by clinician-experiencers

sensory: the pain stops a beat before the separation
a shake, a pop, a click or a jolt at the instant of exit
a felt exit point — crown of the head, chest, or 'it left through my feet'
sensation of suction, like a vacuum hose
weightlessness immediately afterwards

quotes.text: I felt this shake and this pop, and I was ejected from my body. So now I'm in this dark void.
quotes.speaker: Brian Hoyland

quotes.text: It was as if I were being vacuum-sucked out of my own body.
quotes.speaker: Anne Archer

quotes.text: I felt the shake and this pop and my soul injected from my body.
quotes.speaker: Brian Hoyland

quotes.text: And it was like I was whisked out of my body.
quotes.speaker: Yvonne Kason

quotes.text: two arms grabbed me and pulled me out of my body, catapulted me through the ceiling, and I was flying
quotes.speaker: Gareth Duignam

places.notes: MORE common among the best-evidenced accounts: 26.59% of all accounts vs 35.36% at cvNDE>=23. That is expected — cvNDE rewards veridical perception, which requires the experiencer to have been out and observing. The regex is deliberately restricted to first-person separation verbs; the looser phrase 'out of the body' alone hits 28.47% but includes interviewer questions and third-party discussion. Audit found false positives of the form: Literal bodily discharge: 'the water that came out of my body' after paralysis — the phrase matched, the meaning is plumbing; Recurring post-NDE out-of-body practice at night ('I started having out-of-body experiences again... I'd start leaving my body and be taken to other realms') — aftereffect, not the separation moment; Note on strictness: several true positives are separations that were not medically near-death (a traumatic dissociation, a kundalini-style exit in an auditorium, a spontaneous exit on a friend's couch). I counted these as true because the passage describes the exit itself; a stricter map that requires a clinical near-death event would score this packet lower..

places.name: the choice
places.description: The moment the decision is handed to the experiencer. It is usually put as a plain question — 'do you want to stay or return?', 'you can stay or you can go back' — and often paired with information intended to inform it: what will happen to the children, what work remains, what the return will cost in pain. Almost nobody wants to go back. Many report that the offer is genuinely free and that the beings will not argue.

aliases.term: do you wish to stay or return?
do you want to go back?
you can stay or you can go back

sensory: posed as a question, never as pressure
asked telepathically in most accounts
sometimes accompanied by a preview of the life that would follow each answer
several report the offer being withdrawn the instant the decision forms

quotes.text: they did let me know the choice was mine and I could decide what I wanted to do.
And he said, "Do you wish to stay or return?"
'You can stay if you want, or you can go back. But if you go back, you have to do something.'
quotes.speaker: Bill

quotes.text: You can stay or you can go back.
quotes.speaker: Ellyn Dye

quotes.text: I felt I could stay there, then glanced around at my Son, my Wife, and finally, my baby girl, and something told me I need to be there for them.
quotes.speaker: Lorraine

places.notes: The structured coding puts 'choice_to_return' at 78.3% of all accounts and 85.1% at cv>=23, at mean journey position 0.867 — so the choice is nearly universal even though only 6.72% phrase it in these particular words. My lexical measure declines at cv>=23 (5.52%) while the coded element does not, which suggests the well-evidenced accounts describe the decision without the stock question-and-answer framing. Audit found false positives of the form: Negations that the regex reads as hits — the forced-return cases: 'I was not given a choice to stay or go back, I was just pushed back into my body', 'I didn't make the choice to come back' (P5, P10).; General metaphysical teaching about how transitions work for everyone — 'we always have the choice to come back', 'around this age you can get a choice to leave' (P1, P17).; Interviewer questions containing the words ('did you want to go back to it?', 'did you want to return?') where the answer describes attachment, not an offer (P8, P23)..

places.name: The Other Side
places.description: The corpus's own umbrella name for the unnamed destination — a name that is purely relational, saying only that it is not here and that there is a boundary. It absorbs everything: the garden, the city, the light, the dead, the darkness. Its great advantage for narrators is theological neutrality — Christians, secular experiencers and interviewers all use it without committing to any doctrine — and it is used both spatially ('on the other side') and as a direction of travel ('crossed over').

aliases.note: the default neutral name
the verb form
the named alternative; many narrators use both, 'the other side' when hedging
used when the speaker will not commit to arrival

sensory: a there implied by a here
a crossing implied without a described crossing-place
used for both the landscape and the population
described more by relation than by appearance - it is where the dead are
the boundary itself is what is felt, not the landscape

quotes.text: I got to see it in action, in real-life application on the other side of death. Trust me, there is no such thing as death.
these other beings were here to help me and to welcome me and to comfort me on the other side.
quotes.speaker: Anita Moorjani

quotes.text: there is no comparison here for what you experience on the other side. Just, just none.
they were going to share more about not only their experiences on the other side
It's the instant that I was conscious in this body again, I was where I died. I just went to the other side.
quotes.speaker: Anna

places.notes: The most widely used name for the destination in the entire corpus — more common than 'heaven' phrasings — and it rises steadily with evidential strength (52.66% all, 57.73% at cv>=18, 61.33% at cv>=23). Important caveat: the phrase is heavily used by INTERVIEWERS and hosts as well as experiencers, so doc-frequency overstates first-person usage. The lookahead in the regex strips the common literal senses (other side of the road/room/bed); the residual false positives are contrastive rhetoric ('on the other side, we can enslave ourselves to the news'). Audit found false positives of the form: Channel and organisation boilerplate — 'Spirit Travels, where we narrate the experiences of people who have glimpsed the other side of death', the IANDS NDE Radio show open, an IANDS event promo (3 of 24); Interviewer speech: questions and study citations ('20% of cardiac arrest patients remember something from the other side') (3 of 24); General teaching or speculation about what happens to everyone when they cross over (3 of 24), including one flat denial: 'there is no other side'; Post-NDE mediumship — 'I do get communication from the other side' — and aftermath scenes where a relative doubts the speaker went there; Purely spatial ordinary usage: walking to the other side of an island; a war/dream scene 'when I went to the other side and stepped on a grenade'; The phrase is so tradition-neutral that it is also the corpus's most common HOST vocabulary, which is what drives the 998-account match count.

places.name: The Light
places.description: The destination almost everyone arrives at: not a lamp shining on a place but a place made of light, which people enter, stand in, are held by. Experiencers describe going into it, being in it, being part of it. It is spoken of as somewhere you ARE, not something you look at — 'I was in a sea of light', 'I found myself in a world of light'. Many say plainly that the light was itself the loving being; the distinction between the place and the person in it collapses.

aliases.note: the corpus's own default name; usually capitalised in written accounts

aliases.term: the light at the end of the tunnel
aliases.note: the phrase experiencers themselves flag as 'the cliche' before insisting theirs was different
many name arrival in the light as 'I'm home' rather than by a place-name

sensory: white, but a white unlike earthly white — 'pure white, not yellow'
no discernible source and no direction; the light is the medium, not a beam
tactile — 'palpable', 'like velvet and honey', 'thick like a fog you couldn't see through'
carries emotion the way air carries sound: 'you could feel emotion in the light'
expands: starts small and grows until it fills the whole visual field
accompanied by a hum or vibration that rises as the brightness rises

quotes.text: I saw the light. I was in it. This light is not something you just see and look at. It's like your whole self becomes your vision.
When I reached the point of light, I found myself in a world of light. Everything in this place was made of, and radiated, light.
quotes.speaker: Lisa

quotes.text: let me first say and get out of the way that very bluntly the light is God
quotes.speaker: Tom

quotes.text: the light, it was alive, and it was pulsating and vibrating with energy, blinding light
quotes.speaker: Randy

places.notes: MORE common among better-evidenced accounts (35.95% all vs 38.67% at cv>=18). The regex's weakest arm is the bare 'the light was...' clause, which occasionally catches ordinary room light or metaphor ('walk out of this life in the light'). Note the strong internal disagreement in the corpus about whether the Light is a place, a being, or the experiencer's own self — many say all three at once ('This light is me'). Audit found false positives of the form: Literal light sources in the room: an operating-theatre lamp seen during an OBE, ceiling 'light fixtures' noticed while floating; TV host / book-promo framing ('Betty says that when she died, she went to the light and met Jesus'); Sermon-style speculation using the light rhetorically ('Are we going to the light? Or are we going to the darkness?').

places.name: Speaking without speaking
places.description: How the inhabitants communicate. Experiencers are near-unanimous that no mouths moved and no sound travelled, yet the exchange was complete and instant. Many stress it is faster and more complete than words — whole understandings arrive at once, and questions are answered before they are finished. Several bilingual experiencers note that language ceased to be a barrier. A minority report an additional audible voice that 'went through my bones' alongside the silent exchange.
sensory: no mouths move; some beings have no mouths at all
the answer arrives simultaneously with the question
thoughts are transparent in both directions — they laugh at what you have not said
one account describes it as communication in mathematics and music
an audible voice, when it occurs, is felt in the bones rather than the ears

quotes.text: I heard everything telepathically. No words were heard as sound. They were just put directly in my mind
quotes.speaker: Mindy Speranza

quotes.text: I remember having a quick thought about we just talked without talking
she telepathically said to me to calm myself down she did not speak but I was listening to her
quotes.speaker: Penny Wittbrodt

quotes.text: there was no speech, it was all telepathic, I recognized instantly as my ICU patient
quotes.speaker: Maria

places.notes: Monotone increase across every stratum (26.88% -> 34.81%), matching the corpus's own structured coding (telepathy 60.0% all vs 70.2% cv>=23) at a stricter threshold. Interesting tension: the corpus entity census records 'verbal' (3,900) MORE often than 'telepathy' (2,942) as the communication method, so silent exchange is dominant but not universal — a substantial minority of experiencers insist they heard an actual voice. Audit found false positives of the form: Telepathy in a practice rather than in the NDE: hospice/death-doula work coaching a dying man telepathically, mediumship and Ouija-board sessions, dragons contacted telepathically during a volcano ritual (4 passages); Researcher summaries of other people's data — a pre-birth-experience study across 10 countries reporting telepathy; Podcast boilerplate: a four-part afterlife-communication series intro promising to relay what was 'received telepathically'; Deathbed-vision speculation about what dying people generally hear from the other side.

places.name: the knowing
places.description: The state, usually adjacent to or immediately following the review, in which everything is understood at once. Experiencers describe it as knowledge arriving without being sought - a download, a flooding, a lid coming off - and as the disappearance of questions rather than the receipt of answers. Several say they had nothing to ask because there was nothing left unknown; one describes knowing everything the light knew, about flowers, plants, asteroids, suns and novas. The corpus's own preferred word for this is 'download'.

aliases.note: the corpus's dominant idiom - 'a download of information', 'a knowledge download'

sensory: arriving all at once rather than sequentially
questions dissolving rather than being answered
knowledge experienced as available on demand - 'you think of it, it comes to you'
described as flooding, pouring, a funnel, a lid coming off

quotes.text: all the questions I'd ever had in my life were answered in sort of this instant of this information. And that one point was love.
quotes.speaker: Krista Gorman

quotes.text: all knowledge was downloaded instantly. I knew where I was. I knew who I was
quotes.speaker: Crystal McVea

quotes.text: once I was in the light, I knew everything the light knew. I knew all about the universe. I knew everything about flowers, about plants, about asteroids, about suns, about novas, everything.
quotes.speaker: David Sunfellow

quotes.text: which by the way, is quite a download of information all at once. I saw everything in the eternal now, all at once, every possibility
quotes.speaker: Chrystal Rae

places.notes: The structured coder marks knowledge_download present in 61.4% of accounts, so this lexical regex is capturing perhaps a seventh of the phenomenon - the state is usually described without these fixed phrases. life_review > knowledge_download is the second most common transition in the whole corpus (1072 occurrences, 19.7% of sequenced accounts), which is why this sits immediately downstream of the review. Audit found false positives of the form: 'Download' in ongoing post-NDE practice - waking at 1-3am to download information for transcripts, general theory that 'sometimes you get a great download' (docs ZqE188Qmp5o, 5zN52hVfIR4); Post-NDE psychic ability in daily work: 'I knew everything about everybody that walked in the door' at her aesthetics business (doc=f8v2EN-_cXk); 'I knew everything that was happening to me' meaning veridical awareness of the ambulance/hospital events, not the state of total understanding (doc=zePilVOXHLc); Ordinary-life knowing: guides warning about a real estate crash, childhood classes where 'I understood everything' (docs unClNFOH7Jo, rlMfY_l8aC4); General spiritual musing about whether we should know all the answers, and present-day practice with a 'What would love do?' necklace (docs zwa02Vo8S08, P2bz4Q9uIaQ).

places.name: The Source, the Universe, Oneness
places.description: The secular and New Age naming of the same destination and the same presence: an origin you dissolve back into rather than a kingdom you are admitted to. Described as consciousness, energy, intelligence, the field of everything. Experiencers who use it often say explicitly that they chose it to avoid the word God.

aliases.note: 10.95% of documents
used as a personal agent - the Universe told me, the Universe wants
12.61% of documents; peaks at cv>=18 (13.26%)
the diplomatic option
the seam where the two vocabularies are stitched together

sensory: absorption rather than arrival - being pulled or drawn in
loss of the sense of a separate self
described as energy or vibration rather than as scenery
no figure, no face, no location

quotes.text: it was just this sense of this huge enormous oneness of everything that ever has been and ever will be and and anywhere in the universe
quotes.speaker: Colin Perry

quotes.text: I think source is more appropriate to use because God is such a loaded term, but the source of energy was absorbing this universe, including myself, into it.
quotes.speaker: Andrew Petro

quotes.text: And I made it to what they call, or I call it, Source. So I didn't see God. I didn't, you know, Jesus didn't pay me a visit.
quotes.speaker: Laura Catchlich

quotes.text: I was just, I was home. I was in such joy. I was being completely loved by the source.
quotes.speaker: Yvonne Kason

quotes.text: I feel as though I'm having this conversation with a higher entity, a loving judge. Then she writes, "The Source."

places.notes: This is the only major naming cluster that runs DOWNWARD with evidential strength: 30.12% overall falling to 23.20% at cv>=23. The same inversion shows in the structured element table (cosmic_unity 60.9% overall, 49.2% at cv>=23). Two readings are available and the data does not decide between them: either Source/oneness language attaches to more interpretive, less veridically-anchored accounts, or the veridical-perception score rewards the concrete hospital-room detail that dissolution accounts by definition lack. Precision is the weakest of my entries (~0.6) because 'the source' has heavy ordinary usage; the tighter subset 'the Source' alone gives 10.95%. Audit found false positives of the form: 'The universe' as everyday idiom for fate or providence: 'trust the universe is going to bring you helpers', 'the universe was like, okay, you said yes' (3 passages); 'Source' as an ordinary noun: 'that's really the source of my work and my life now'; 'a source of water and the source of light' as scenery; Popular-science talk: Niels Bohr, the universe as a symphony, NASA frequencies — no experience content at all; Host monologue generalising about what everyone becomes ('We enter a state of bright brilliant light... We become Oneness') before introducing a guest; Researcher quoting aggregated statements from other people's accounts; Post-hoc philosophy about consciousness and ascension written years after the event.

places.name: The Presence
places.description: The being in the light, encountered before and often instead of any name. People report a presence behind them, beside them, in front of them — usually unseen, sometimes explicitly faceless — that is immense, loving, and instantly familiar. A recurring and striking pattern: they cannot see it, do not have a name for it, and are nevertheless certain of who it is. Naming happens afterwards, in the retelling, and is drawn from whatever vocabulary the experiencer has.

aliases.note: the plainest and most common formulation
in the corpus's entity census, 'being of light' is 7.7% of encounters and 'unknown' 27.5%
the single most common unnamed identity in the corpus's entity census (286 encounters)

aliases.term: I didn't have a name for the presence

aliases.note: many simply address the being AS the light

sensory: positional: overwhelmingly reported as BEHIND or beside, rarely face-on
unseen but unmistakably located — 'right here, right next to me'
no face; several say they did not dare turn around
immense scale: 'so powerful and so cosmic and so wise'
communication by thought, or by nothing at all — 'presence_only' is the third most common communication method in the corpus

quotes.text: And I felt the presence of someone. Someone was with me. Could not see them. Couldn't tell you what they looked like, but I knew somebody was standing next to me.
quotes.speaker: Randy Schiefer

quotes.text: But this presence was always at my side. I knew it had always been there.
quotes.speaker: Heidi Prislin

quotes.text: I somehow instinctively knew that we knew each other but I didn't have a name for the presence
quotes.speaker: Wayne Morrison

quotes.text: there was the presence next to me of what I felt was God
quotes.speaker: Barbara Bartolome

places.notes: Clearly MORE common among better-evidenced accounts: 10.82% all, 13.40% at cv>=18, 14.36% at cv>=23. This is the key finding for the brief's naming question: the UNNAMED presence gets commoner as evidential strength rises, while the named identities (Jesus 19.40% -> 14.92%; Source 7.59% -> 4.97%) get rarer. About a third of matches are outside the NDE proper (felt presences at home, in hospital, in later life). Audit found false positives of the form: Post-NDE encounters in ordinary life: a presence felt on an aeroplane, in sleep paralysis two weeks later, in a dark hospital room while a son was in surgery (docs CmY-Oa1kOHU, lXO5hctRdN0, FFOPXWsQYPo); A visitation dream about a dying baby, reported by a nurse (doc=3hf2cKJbecQ); Interviewer supplying the word - 'You did talk about this presence that was there' - plus channel plug (doc=e8qfghtJySI); The interviewer paraphrasing a waking event in which the experiencer's father spoke (doc=aN2i_ErIF2w); Heavy overlap with the-unseen-presence packet; the two regexes appear to be measuring the same passages.

places.name: the life review
places.description: The place in the journey where your life is given back to you to be seen. Experiencers almost never call it 'judgement' - they call it a review, a reliving, a re-experiencing. It is not remembering: people insist they were IN the events again, with the original feelings intact, but now with understanding added. It commonly runs from birth (or from conception, or from the womb) forward to the moment of dying, and it is repeatedly described as more detailed than memory could ever be - 'every single minute detail', things forgotten for decades.

aliases.note: by far the dominant term; many say 'I later learned it's called the life review'
several insist review is the wrong word - 'it's not a review, it's a relive'

aliases.term: my life flashed before my eyes
aliases.note: the folk phrase; many use it then correct it as too shallow
used when the content was future rather than past
a widely repeated framing among experiencers
used by one experiencer-researcher comparing traditions
usually invoked only to be denied: 'there was no judgment day for me'

sensory: runs from birth (sometimes from conception or in the womb) forward to the moment of death
sometimes plays in reverse, from the dying moment backwards
detail far exceeding ordinary memory - 'every single minute detail'
original emotions restored, but with understanding added
no fear or defensiveness while it runs; the fear comes afterwards in the telling

quotes.text: My life review took the form of a large disorganized room, and in that instant, I was able to see how all the parts of my life were connected to one another.
Christ took me through a life review that was filled with compassion and understanding and absolutely absent of judgment.
quotes.speaker: Dr. Mary Neal

quotes.text: It wasn't a review of my entire life in every detail, but only those moments of intense love that I felt in a shared experience with other people.
quotes.speaker: Manuela Fazzi

quotes.text: I was just surrounded by this review of my life. It was like a 360° kind of panoramic movie of my life.
quotes.speaker: Bubba Herrick

places.notes: The structured coder marks life_review present in 49.3% of accounts, but the literal phrase 'life review' occurs in only 24.2% - so roughly half of reviews are described without the term, which is why this regex adds 'my life flashed/passed', 'reliving my life' and 'review of my life'. Prevalence rises modestly with evidential strength (25.9% all vs 29.8% at cv>=23). A minority explicitly report having NO life review and say so ('there's no life review, but in my case there's a life preview'); those docs still match, which is the main precision loss. A small distressing variant exists in which only the harmful acts are shown. Audit found false positives of the form: Explicit denials, which the phrase-match cannot distinguish from reports: 'I didn't have a life review', 'it was not a life review', 'there's no such thing as a life review' for infants (4 passages); Interviewer questions asking whether there was one ('Bill, did you have a life review when you had your first NDE?'); Researcher and study summaries: children's NDE statistics, shared-death companions who 'participate in the life review'; Second-hand accounts — a mother relaying her dead son's life review; Generic teaching in the second person about what everyone undergoes ('you have a life review up there, so revenge is impossible').

places.name: The dead of your own family
places.description: The people met are overwhelmingly your own dead: mother, father, brothers, sisters, uncles, aunts, cousins, spouses. They are recognised instantly, often before being seen clearly — recognition is by 'energy' or by knowing rather than by face. They typically do not explain themselves; they reassure, they say it is not your time, and several accounts note they are noticeably busy and involved, not idle.

aliases.term: family members on the other side

aliases.note: sometimes used interchangeably, sometimes distinguished from blood family

sensory: recognised by energy or knowing rather than by sight
no aging or illness carried over
period clothing from the era each of them lived in
they hug, take your hand, put a hand out
communication is soundless (see telepathic-speech)

quotes.text: I was suddenly before my two deceased grandmothers.
quotes.speaker: Julie Papievis

quotes.text: I was greeted by people I had known in the past. Um, relatives, my, uh, a grandpa was there, um, an aunt that had died just previous to this.
quotes.speaker: Kristle Merzlock

quotes.text: I saw thousands of people there, including my mom, grandmothers, and aunt, and an uncle. Everyone looked 25 to 30 years old.
there was no speech, it was all telepathic, I recognized instantly as my ICU patient
quotes.speaker: Maria

places.notes: This is the strongest evidential gradient in my whole region: 8.73% of all accounts, 19.89% of the best-evidenced (cv>=23) — a 2.3x enrichment, monotone across all four strata. The corpus's own structured coding agrees independently (deceased_relatives present in 39.9% all vs 58.6% cv>=23). Whatever produces high veridical-perception scores also produces encounters with the family dead. My regex is far more conservative than the structured coder's, so treat 8.73% as a floor, not a prevalence. Audit found false positives of the form: The single largest class is NEGATIVE: the phrase is the canonical expectation, so experiencers use it to report that it did NOT happen - 'I didn't see anyone, like any dead relatives', 'I don't see dead relatives, none of that', 'how come I'm not seeing my deceased relatives?', 'I thought they would be there for me... where is everybody?' (docs zecVmC3Mcg8, kQ26a98telc, F-rp6bqfJWQ, zKLqZ525oaA); Third-party and research framing: a salesman's case retold, a hospice researcher's 1400 interviews, a Facebook-page summary of 'what many have noted', an interviewer narrating Carolyn's NDE (docs SO0Oys9Nf8o, HgOId0hWfV4, 7KFeKdJktsg, 4lrCbB9gla8); Waking-life visitations and mediumship: a grandmother who appeared to start a granola business, a psychic instructing prayer to a dead grandmother, hearing clients' dead loved ones as a teenager, a visitation dream three nights after a sister died (docs ZWgQ7SwCgZ8, sC5KsWUIsQw, icRlaN2ned8, 0Vf5tSEYT9E); Deathbed clairvoyance describing what OTHER dying people's relatives do (doc=VbM2nUpZsEU); Frequency-technology marketing: 'say you want to visit your dead relatives, that's a certain blend' (doc=gIp8wWgMDsc); Root cause: 'deceased/dead relatives' is the corpus's meta-vocabulary, not its experiential vocabulary. Real accounts say 'my grandmother', 'my mother', 'my wife'. A kin-term regex (I saw/was met by + mother|father|grandmother|brother|sister|uncle|aunt|wife|husband) would measure this feature; this one measures the discourse about it..

places.name: the point of no return
places.description: The place in the journey where the experiencer understands that one more step forward ends the possibility of coming back. Most people do not name it; they describe arriving somewhere and simply knowing that this is the edge. When they do name it, they call it the point of no return, the border, the boundary, or the line. It is almost always encountered late, after the light, the beings and the life review, and it is where the narrative turns around.

My lexical regex catches only the small fraction who name the boundary explicitly (0.96%). The gap between 37.5% and 0.96% is the single most important fact about this region: the boundary is overwhelmingly reported without a name and often without an object. Note that cv>=18 (0.69%) is LOWER than cv>=13 (1.45%) for the named phrase, while the coded element barely moves across strata — better-evidenced accounts are no less likely to hit a boundary, they are just less likely to reach for the stock phrase. Audit found false positives of the form: the medical 'point of no return' in the OR - the doctors knowing time was running out; life-decision metaphor: a career pivot, leaving a company, 'I'm either going A or B'; hypnotherapists, hosts and commentators describing the threshold as a general NDE feature or in other people's regressions (4 passages); the interviewer supplying the phrase and the experiencer only assenting, with no place described; note: 6 of the 15 true positives are three duplicated accounts re-published on different channels.

places.name: There Are No Words for It
places.description: The most common single feature of the whole corpus after peace: the narrator stopping mid-sentence to say that what they are describing cannot be described. It is not modesty or a figure of speech — experiencers repeatedly say they searched for years for the right words and gave up, that the words they are using are the wrong size, that language was built for a world where things have edges and this had none. Almost half of all 6,176 accounts contain an explicit statement that description has failed. It attaches to everything: the light, the love, the colours, the speed, the knowing, and above all the place itself.

rarer, used by more literary or educated narrators

places.notes: This is the single largest finding of this pass. 42.58% of the corpus contains an explicit statement that language failed; the rate is slightly HIGHER among the best-evidenced accounts (45.58% at cv>=18) than in the corpus as a whole, so ineffability is not a marker of vague or weak testimony — it rises with evidential strength. Loosening the pattern to include bare 'no words' pushes it to 45.19%, but that catches 'no words came out of my mouth' (paralysis during OBE) and 'no words were spoken' (telepathy), which are different phenomena; both are excluded by the negative_regex. Precision on the tight pattern was near-perfect in the sample: every one of ten cv>=18 snippets was a genuine ineffability claim about the experience. Audit found false positives of the form: Ineffability attached to post-NDE aftereffects rather than the experience: 'it's hard to describe' about a changed personality, a restructured body, new intuitive abilities; Ineffability attached to physical medical pain — a hemorrhage described as 'indescribable' and 'can't be described unless you've experienced it'; One case where 'I can't describe it any other way than saying...' is a rhetorical lead-in to a description, not a failure of language.

places.name: The Tunnel
places.description: The famous one, and it is neither universal nor uniform. People are drawn, sucked, thrown or gently shuffled into a long enclosed passage and carried along it, usually feet first or head first at great speed, toward something bright at the far end. Its walls are variously dark and velvet-soft, ribbed like a fuselage, made of light-specks, glass, or covered with scenes from the traveller's own life. Some ride it terrified, some in total peace; a few report other travellers alongside them. Crucially, only about one account in five describes it, and many are emphatic they had nothing of the kind.

This tracks the corpus's own structured coding (tunnel 23.9% all / 33.1% cv>=23) closely, which is reassuring. Beware the bare word: /tunnel/ matches 35.02% of docs, but a large slice of that is interviewers asking about tunnels and experiencers denying them — see the-tunnel-that-wasnt. Residual false positives in my regex are almost entirely sentences of the form 'I didn't go through a tunnel', which doc-level matching cannot exclude; hence precision 0.85 rather than higher. Audit found false positives of the form: Meta-commentary about NDEs in general rather than the speaker's own transit: 'Not everybody goes through the tunnel', 'only 30 percent have tunnel experiences' (2 of 24); Explicit denials that the speaker had a tunnel: 'I did not have the full-blown experience where you go through the tunnel'; Workshop-leader summaries of OTHER people's accounts: 'what they have in common is they go through a tunnel'; Pure metaphor from ordinary life: 'sent me into this like PTSD tunnel'; A narrow gap between crowding souls described in passing as 'this little tunnel between them' — not the transit passage.

places.name: it is not your time — you have to go back
places.description: The judgement that closes the boundary scene. Almost always a single compound utterance: a statement about time ('it's not your time', 'your time has not yet come') joined to a directive ('you have to go back', 'you must return'). It is delivered by God, Jesus, an angel, a dead relative, or an unattributed voice, and it is almost never negotiable — experiencers argue, beg and refuse, and it makes no difference.

The bare phrase 'not your time' alone is 7.25% (448 docs) and also climbs. One strongly-evidenced experiencer (6oDB4BzndCQ, cv=23) explicitly names it as the expected script he did NOT receive — 'I didn't have the classic declaration made to me' — which is good evidence the corpus knows this is a formula and does not always fill it in. Audit found false positives of the form: Idiomatic narrative backtracking: 'I have to go back and say...', 'if I have to go back to one of the ones that shaped me', 'I had to go back to my parents' lives' when writing a memoir (3 passages); Medical usage: 'I had to go back in for emergency programming' of a spinal stimulator; The experiencer's own decision or request to return rather than a verdict delivered to them ('I asked the being if I could go back', 'I knew I had to go back'); Explicit negation: 'my guides didn't tell me what to do. They didn't say, You have to go back or not'; Moralising about God's timing in general ('until it is your time, it's not your time'); Note: this packet is a near-duplicate of 'the-order-to-return' — same claim, same failure profile. They should probably be merged or one dropped..

places.name: The Passage - Tunnel, Stairway, Road, River, Elevator
places.description: The conveyance between the body and the destination. The corpus supplies a menu and each experiencer gets one: a tunnel, a tube, a shaft, a corridor; a stairway or staircase going up into cloud; a road or path to walk; a river or bridge to cross; occasionally an escalator or lift. The reported function is identical - motion toward light, no ability to stop, a sense of being carried - only the vehicle changes.

0.74% in a 'led to' frame

places.notes: The most interesting demographic result in this set. The stairway variant is not merely a Christian ornament on the tunnel: it is roughly 3.7x more common among the best-evidenced accounts (1.81% -> 6.63%), and the ornamented golden/marble/white/crystal stairway is 4.9x more common (0.91% -> 4.42%). The tunnel shows the same direction but a shallower slope. Meanwhile the road, the bridge and the escalator do not enrich at all. Precision caveat: bare 'stairs' is hopeless (house stairs, hospital stairs, falling down stairs) so I excluded it and kept only 'stairway/staircase' plus ornamented 'stairs'; even so about half the cv>=18 staircase matches I read were ordinary architecture. The tunnel arm is much cleaner. Note also the explicit negatives - people who volunteer 'I didn't see a tunnel, I didn't see a stairway' - which is itself a menu-awareness effect worth tracking. Audit found false positives of the form: Literal hallways, stairwells and rivers in this world: a hospital corridor, paramedics carrying stretchers down a stairwell, being sent across a river to South Africa, crossing a river on a rope swing, skipping down the hallway at work (6 passages) — 'hallway', 'river' and 'stairs' are the leaky tokens, 'tunnel' and 'corridor of light' are nearly clean; Interviewer generalising about the menu itself ('some even go through a tunnel, some don't'); Explicit denial: 'I recall arriving in a beautiful, completely strange world, not through a tunnel or a light'; Post-NDE domestic scenes: spirits seen 'down the hallway' at home.

places.name: It is not your time
places.description: The near-formulaic sentence that ends the visit. It is delivered by a relative, a guide, an unseen voice or a religious figure, and is almost always some variant of 'it's not your time' or 'you have to go back'. Frequently it is repeated two or three times against the experiencer's protest. Reasons given are usually a task, a child, or unfinished purpose — rarely anything doctrinal.

aliases.note: the single most reproduced sentence in the whole corpus

sometimes a hand held up 'like a stop sign'

places.notes: Mildly enriched in better-evidenced accounts and then flat. The corpus's own journey coding puts 'forced_return' at mean relative position 0.893 and 'choice_to_return' at 0.867, so this sits right at the hinge of the narrative. A small but striking counter-case exists: at least one experiencer (Venia Hill) was told the opposite — 'it WAS my time' — and returned anyway. Audit found false positives of the form: Hosts and researchers describing the formula in the abstract: 'what normally happens is they're greeted by somebody who tells them, it's not your time', 'mothers with children are told on the other side, it's not your time', channel outro commentary comparing this case to the usual script (4 passages); Someone else's NDE relayed by the host — a colleague whose dead wife told him 'It's not your time, stay for Spencer'; Ordinary-life guidance voices: a voice in a bank saying 'You need to go back and ask someone else'; The experiencer's own reflection that 'it just wasn't my time', or their own begging to be sent back, with no utterance delivered to them; Return described with no verdict at all ('when they sent me back' / 'why would God send me back'), which the phrase-match cannot separate from the spoken order; Note: near-duplicate of 'the-verdict-not-your-time'; the two packets share passages by doc and should be reconciled..

places.name: Not wanting to come back
places.description: The most emotionally loaded thing in this region and, in raw prevalence, one of the largest. Experiencers say plainly that they did not want to return, that they begged and pleaded to stay, that they grabbed hold of the being's legs, that they screamed no. The reason given is almost never fear of pain — it is that the place felt like home in a way earth never had. Many are still visibly upset about it decades later during the interview.

The explicit begging/pleading sub-pattern alone matches 98 docs (1.59% all, 3.31% cv>=23) — doubling in the best-evidenced accounts, the sharpest gradient of any sub-pattern I measured. Note the reciprocal grief: several accounts describe the being apologising, promising to meet again, or sending someone back WITH them. Audit found false positives of the form: Inverted matches — the same vocabulary used for the OPPOSITE wish: 'Please let me go back, I begged... I was the first soul to beg to go back instead of begging to stay'; 'I begged God not to die' (2 of 24); Ordinary-life reluctance: not wanting to leave family when a husband insisted on moving house; devotees who 'didn't ever want to leave' a guru's ashram; Interviewer summarising other guests: 'a lot of our guests have said I did not want to return... but in your case that was not the situation'; Minor nuance, not counted as an error: one true match refuses to return because of remembered PAIN rather than the pull of the place, against the claim's stated reason.

places.name: The Void — the Darkness You Travel In
places.description: Black, boundless, without floor or direction. People fall, drift or race through it; some stay in it a long time. It is not simply an absence of light — many say they could see perfectly well in it, or that it was an 'illuminated darkness', or that it held stars. Reactions split sharply: for most it is peaceful, warm and womb-like; for a substantial minority it is the most frightening place they have ever been, and they call out into it for help. It is the most common environment in the region after the body itself, and it frequently precedes the tunnel or replaces it entirely.

one experiencer reads it as 'before let there be light'

The corpus's own journey coding makes the void far more central than the tunnel: void_darkness appears in 57.1% of sequenced accounts against 18.1% for tunnel, and its mean journey position (0.056) is earlier than the tunnel's (0.222) — i.e. the darkness usually comes FIRST, and the tunnel, if it comes at all, forms inside or after it. The commonest transitions in the corpus are void_darkness>peace_calm (14.3%) and void_darkness>bright_light (10.0%). Audit found false positives of the form: Interviewer speech and book plugs that name the void without describing it ('explaining the different levels of consciousness and where you went into the void') (2 of 24); Second-person teaching about what happens to the dead generally: 'You may go into the void. After death you may end up quite stuck in this void'; Aftermath reflection that references the void only to say it removed the speaker's fear of death — no description of the place; Ordinary-life darkness: a man walking off into the dark outside a hotel bar.

Audit found false positives of the form: 'Unconditional love' used as doctrine or cosmology rather than perceived substance: 'the active ingredient in any religion is the unconditional love of God', 'the Devan is the density closest to pure love' (4 of 24); Recurring podcast intro montage — the identical 'Round Trip Death' cold-open clip ('absolute love and peace... places.name: A Place — Just 'A Place'
places.description: The commonest way the otherworld is introduced is with no name at all: 'I found myself in a place.' The indefinite article does the work — it is a place, not the place, not heaven, not anywhere the narrator can situate. What follows the phrase varies enormously (a meadow, a whiteness, a butchery, a cloud, pure unconditional love), which is the point: 'a place' is the empty container people reach for before they have decided what to call what they saw. Many narrators use it repeatedly and never upgrade it to a name.

In eight of ten sampled snippets the phrase introduced the otherworld directly; the false positives were mundane ('I was in a place of awe' about a walk on Earth). Note that 'a place' is often used ALONGSIDE a name later in the same account — people say 'a place' first and 'heaven' second, which suggests the indefinite phrase is closer to the raw memory. Audit found false positives of the form: 'A place where' as pure metaphor for an emotional or mental state: 'it put me in a place where I had a hard time trusting', 'I've got into a place where I love the word God', 'how she came to a place where she felt the need to kill herself' (3 passages) — this is the dominant junk class; Ordinary geography: relocating 800 miles 'to a place where I didn't know anyone', Hawaiian ghost-lore about going 'to a place' to see night marchers; General theological speculation in the second person ('when you die it is forever in a place of beauty', 'you're in a place where now you got to figure out if you want to reincarnate'); Someone else's NDE quoted by the narrator ('my client said, I went to a place where I could look up everything'); Interviewer echoing the phrase back as a question; one third-person spirit-world narration that is not a first-person report.

places.name: For Lack of a Better Word
places.description: The naming hedge: a narrator uses a word while explicitly disowning it. 'A being, for lack of a better word.' 'The source of all love, that's, for lack of a better word, God — but I don't mean that in a religious sense at all.' 'I call it a lobby.' This is the corpus's characteristic move when the thing encountered has no available name: borrow the nearest word, flag the borrowing, and keep going. It is applied to places, beings and God alike, and it is one of the clearest signals that the imported theological vocabulary in these accounts is often provisional rather than doctrinal.

places.notes: Rises with evidential strength (13.37% -> 16.02% at cv>=23). The bare hedge 'for lack of a better word' alone is 2.19% of docs; most of the mass comes from 'the best way I can describe it', which at 6.36% is one of the corpus's most characteristic verbal tics. Note that the hedge attaches to BEINGS at least as often as to places — the same linguistic mechanism covers both, which is why it is filed as a state rather than a place. Audit found false positives of the form: The hedge attached to ordinary-life content instead of to something encountered: 'I'll call it a traumatic childhood', 'my little Johnny Appleseed ways', 'the best way to describe it is my throat closing up' (a drug reaction), 'I would call it going into the void' applied to mountaineering (4 of 24); The hedge used inside general teaching about who greets you, not about a perceived thing; The hedge attached to non-NDE spiritual events: a kundalini awakening during recovery, a wave of love felt while walking down a sidewalk; Note on scope: the hedge also fires often on the vacated body seen from outside ('like a rag doll', 'a sack of meat'), which I counted as true since it is perceived during the experience — if the map means the hedge only for unnameable places and beings, those two would drop precision to about 0.63.

places.name: Home
places.description: Not a location so much as a recognition: on arriving, experiencers say the place is home and that earth was the trip away. It is stated flatly and often as the first thought - 'I'm home' - before any being, landscape or light is described, and it is frequently the reason they did not want to return. Several are greeted with the words 'welcome home'.

places.notes: Mildly MORE common in the best-evidenced accounts (19.67% -> 23.76%). This is the largest gap in the catalogued map: 'home' is how experiencers name the destination more often than they name heaven, and no themed brief covered it. Precision is the weak point - the word is unavoidably biographical ('I was home when it happened'), so treat ~20% as an upper bound and the direction of the cvNDE gradient as the reliable part. Audit found false positives of the form: Ordinary earthly home: 'I feel like I'm home when I'm in nature', 'that's why home feels like home' (colours we wear), 'I didn't feel unsafe in my home, I grew up with loving parents' (4 of 24); The recurring 'Round Trip Death' channel intro montage, identical text in three separate docs ('I'm back home again... places.name: The presence you cannot see
places.description: Someone is there, usually behind or beside the experiencer, never looked at directly and often never seen at all — yet its identity is felt with certainty and its emotional quality (gentle, non-judging, patient) is the strongest thing about it. The corpus's own entity coder records 'presence_only' as a communication method 2,149 times. Several experiencers say they deliberately did not turn around.

places.name: Up at the Ceiling, Looking Down
places.description: The first place people find themselves after leaving: hovering at ceiling height in the corner of the room, looking down on their own body and on the people working over it. The vantage is described with unusual precision — a specific corner, a specific height ('20 or 25, 30 feet above my body'), sometimes the sensation of the back of the head pressing against the ceiling as though it were a barrier. Several note there was no ceiling as such, only 'about ceiling height'. Emotion here is flat and curious rather than frightened; the body below is regarded as an object, often unrecognised at first.

places.notes: The strongest cvNDE gradient anywhere in this region: 12.21% of all accounts, 23.76% at cv>=18, 31.49% at cv>=23 — nearly a 2.6x enrichment. This is the veridical-perception engine of the whole corpus: the room seen from above is the claim that can be checked, so accounts containing it score higher by construction. The bare word 'ceiling' alone appears in 8.68% of docs but includes dying relatives staring at ceilings and metaphors; the constrained form above is far cleaner. Audit found false positives of the form: Ordinary-life ceilings: 'I lift him up to the ceiling' in a post-healing story (doc=cOSSHHeZ_js); A ceiling belonging to a different place - the high, angled ceilings of a hell-realm room (doc=Dh4Fep5og1U); Interviewer generalising about what 'some people' report, with only a bare 'I did' from the experiencer (doc=ZOZ8Wugh438); Theory rather than experience: a nightly-sleep model in which the spirit body rises near the ceiling every night (doc=WagtZ82vLgk); A light in the corner of the room (Archangel Michael appearing) rather than the experiencer's own vantage looking down (doc=cofs12aN6iQ).

places.name: Guides, guardians and the one who comes to fetch you
places.description: A being whose role is transit and instruction rather than reunion. It introduces itself ('I'm Allan, I'm your spirit guide'; 'my name is Elizabeth, I am your guardian angel and I'm here to help you'), takes the experiencer by the hand, and leads them into the light, along a path, up a staircase or into a building. Guides are far more often described as functionally helpful than as adored. Many experiencers report the same guide continuing to speak to them for decades afterwards.

places.notes: The broadest place in my region and the one whose precision I trust least. Roughly 40% of matches are post-NDE ongoing guide relationships, general belief statements about guides, or interviewers using the term — not a guide encountered during the experience. The 'took my hand and led me' and 'led me to the light' sub-patterns are far cleaner (1.17% and 4.63% respectively, ~90% precision) and could be split out downstream if a tighter measure is wanted. Audit found false positives of the form: Post-NDE guide contact in ordinary life — found through a YouTube guided meditation, spoken to 'not so long ago', heard during a phone call in 2013, visiting in dreams for three years afterwards (6 passages). This is the single largest junk class.; 'Guardian angel' as metaphor for a helpful stranger — the slow driver who kept you out of a crash 'was your guardian angel'; Ordinary-life guides and teachers: a first-grade teacher, a yoga teacher, a meditation guide, a schoolteacher at an accident scene; Interviewer/host framing: a researcher recounting two other experiencers' guides; NDE Radio host describing childhood belief in guardian angels; Post-hoc speculation about what guides are ('I have since come to understand that we have, call it spirit guides').

places.name: The Green Country
places.description: An open, living countryside that people arrive in after the dark passage or the light: meadows, rolling fields, grassy hillsides, pastures running to the horizon. Experiencers almost always say it is earth-LIKE but not earth — the same kinds of things (grass, flowers, trees, water) rendered at an intensity earth cannot hold. It is usually described as vast, unspoiled, and with 'no sign of death or decay' anywhere in it. Most say the ground under their feet felt solid and that they walked or glided across it.

places.notes: This is the parent region for everything else in this file — the other entries are features found inside it. Sharply enriched among the best-evidenced accounts: 13.80% of all accounts but 24.31% at cv>=18 and cv>=23. False positives come from earthly biography (lawn mowing, farm work, hiking) and from after-effect passages where returnees describe seeing earthly grass more vividly. A substantial minority who reach an otherworld see a CITY or structures instead of, or beyond, this countryside — that belongs to another region. Audit found false positives of the form: 'Green' as the colour of a being, a light or an energy rather than a landscape: an emerald-green light being, Archangel Raphael's green healing energy, Jesus radiating emerald green in a therapy room (3 of 24); A person named Meadow Walker matched on the landscape vocabulary — pure word collision; Ordinary earthly fields: a police officer parked beside an open field of tall grass before the incident; enhanced-but-explicitly-alive perception of 'a simple coconut tree and green grass' where the narrator says 'so I wasn't dead'; A vision of Earth's restored FUTURE with lush green forests, narrated in the third person; A lush green garden seen in a dream after hospital discharge, which the narrator labels a dream; Other planets and biospheres remembered from past lives ('the sky was greenish, the grass was sort of blue').

places.name: Beings of light without form
places.description: Beings that have no body at all — orbs, spheres, balls of light, energy fields, 'light fragments', figures shining in different colours. Experiencers stress that they had no faces and yet were unmistakably individual and unmistakably known. Some accounts say the experiencer was one of these too: 'we're beings of light, really, is what we are'. This category shades into and often merges with angels, guides and the crowd of souls; the corpus does not police the boundary.

Overlaps heavily with whatever the singular 'being of light' place captures elsewhere in the map — my interest here is the PLURAL, formless, non-divine population, which is what the plural aliases pick up. The main false-positive source is post-NDE philosophising ('we're all beings of light trapped inside these meat sacks'). Audit found false positives of the form: Researcher / host summaries of the NDE model: 'The research said that you go down a tunnel, you meet a being of light'; a Moody-style 'they tell us they may meet a being of light' (2 of 24); 'We are light beings' as philosophy about humans in general, answered to an interview question — no being perceived; Experiences outside the NDE: a DMT trip, an Egypt temple tour 'connecting with light beings', a medium telling the speaker they are 'a strong light being', light beings visiting years later during a divorce (4 of 24); A film plot (The Astral City) in which 'beings of light would show up'; Explicit negation: 'It was neither Jesus, nor an angel, nor a luminous being, but a simple man in a tunic'; Channel/website plug about 'advanced light beings' and ET civilisations.

places.notes: Heaven is the strongest single naming in the corpus and it gets STRONGER with evidential quality: 34.36% overall, 43.65% among cv>=23 accounts. Contrast with 'Summerland' (0.05%) and 'nirvana' (1.33%): the alias set is not evenly stocked. The corpus's population is Anglophone and Christian-adjacent, so this is a demographic fact about the tellers before it is a fact about the place. Note that Christian namings and secular namings frequently coexist in the same document - 'heaven' and 'the Source' are not mutually exclusive vocabularies here. Audit found false positives of the form: Scripture and liturgy: the Lord's Prayer ('Our Father which art in heaven'), 'the kingdom of heaven is within you', 'angels in heaven rejoice', catechism answers — 5 passages; Idiom: 'What in heaven's name was I doing...', 'I reached up to heaven' as a physical gesture; Host/interviewer boilerplate summarising a guest's NDE ('On the way to heaven, he saw all the prayers...') and book-show framing; Ordinary biography: a dying patient shouting 'I'm going to heaven tomorrow!' in a hospital hallway; a six-year-old son's pre-birth memories; Explicit denials that heaven is a place: 'it wasn't a place like going to heaven is a place', 'I haven't been to heaven, I haven't been to hell', 'Heaven is not a place, it is an awareness'; General theology about who gets in ('in heaven, you're all connected').

places.name: Total Acceptance, No Judgment
places.description: Almost nobody in this corpus reports being judged by the light. The formula 'there was no judgment' recurs constantly, usually alongside a life review in which the experiencer sees their worst acts and is met only with a question — 'what did you learn?' — and more love. Many add that the only judgment present was their own, turned on themselves. Christians and non-Christians report this identically, and several say it directly contradicted what they had been taught.

Audit found false positives of the form: 'No judgment' as modern conversational filler about ordinary life - eating meat vs veganism, playing with animals, healing clients (docs xyS1Y21QmN8, lDV_EYhPqZc, vZ9IvPuCBug); Describing a living person as non-judging ('my teacher has no judgment') (doc=Sq5O8jdrRfk); Doctrinal generalisation about a pre-earth realm or 'the other side' stated as belief, not as something perceived (docs 28dqyrFMD9A, _a0xoFLbo3E); A different sense of the word: 'no judgment about it, just pure observation' = emotional flatness at the ceiling, not absence of condemnation (doc=QN6UdytCcFg); 'No condemnation' about an invitation to a healing conference in ordinary life (doc=5BI5pex8qeI).

places.name: Angels
places.description: The most-named non-human category in the corpus after God and Jesus. Wings are the contested detail: roughly as many experiencers say the angels had no wings as say they did, and several explicitly correct the expectation ('they didn't have wings — they were dressed in ornate gowns', 'they really were these orbs of light'). Where wings are reported they are large, soft, feather-bed-like, and used to enfold rather than to fly. Angels are frequently taller and more luminous than the human dead, and are described as escorts and protectors rather than as conversationalists.

The corpus entity census logs 1,068 angel encounters plus 191 'angel' and 83 'guardian angel' raw identities, so this is a genuinely large category, not an artefact. places.name: Karma, Past Lives and Coming Back
places.description: The same review-and-return sequence, narrated in Eastern rather than Christian vocabulary. What one account calls judgment another calls karma; what one calls heaven another calls a stop between incarnations; what one calls 'it is not your time' another calls unfinished karmic work. Experiencers report being shown previous lives inside the review, being told they chose this life before birth, and in a few cases being shown the life they would return to next.

places.notes: Runs downward with evidential strength on every step (24.89% -> 23.28% -> 20.72% -> 19.34%), the same direction as the Source/oneness cluster and the opposite of heaven and the stairway. Worth flagging honestly: this pattern catches a great deal of post-hoc interpretive talk in interviews, not only in-experience content, so the decline may reflect that the best-evidenced accounts are more tightly focused on the event itself. The alias-mapping value is nonetheless clear - the council reappears as the Lords of Karma, the hall of records as the Akashic records, the life review as past lives, and 'it is not your time' as unfinished karmic work. Audit found false positives of the form: Past-life work as a profession or therapy: a past-life regression hypnotherapist, a stage healer 'clearing your past life', clients asking not to be told about bad past lives (3 passages); Post-NDE psychic aftereffects in ordinary life — seeing other people's past lives in their auras, recognising a stranger as a past-life soul contract; Book and website plugs that happen to use the vocabulary ('DharmaTalks.com', 'my karma... more about the dharma'); Interviewer theology questions ('what's your thoughts on reincarnation?') and the guest's non-answer; Free-floating philosophy about karma, ego and reincarnation with no experience attached; Explicit negation ('Was there a life review where you saw your past life? No, I didn't see it there') and one contrast case ('some people say they have past life reviews. For me it was more like...').

places.name: The Named One - Jesus, Christ, Buddha, Krishna, Allah, the Great Spirit
places.description: The central figure encountered in or beside the light, given a proper name drawn from the arriver's own tradition. The behaviour described is near-identical across names: the figure is already waiting, radiates unbearable love, communicates without speech, holds or embraces the person, and delivers the verdict about returning. Only the name and the clothing change.

places.notes: The naming is overwhelmingly lopsided: this is an Anglophone, mostly North American YouTube corpus, so Christian namings outnumber all others by roughly 20:1 in encounter frames. That skew is a property of WHO IS SPEAKING, not of the destination. Non-Christian names appear far more often inside rhetorical lists ('God, Jesus, Buddha, or any other entity') than in first-person encounter frames - the gap between 6.98% for the bare word Buddha and 0.26% for 'saw/met Buddha' is the clearest demonstration of this in the corpus. Denominational base rates of the speakers: Catholic 18.62%, Jewish 5.73%, Buddhist 5.39%, Muslim/Islam 4.18%, Hindu 3.89%, Mormon/LDS 1.49%, Jehovah's Witness 0.42%, Sikh 0.16%. Precision caveat: 'Jesus' is also a common given name and an expletive; roughly a third of raw matches are biographical or conversion narrative rather than NDE encounter. Audit found false positives of the form: Interviewer speech that names Jesus while framing a question ('Over and over, you talked about this was Jesus that saved you') (2 of 24); Retellings of other people's famous NDEs: Howard Storm, the 'Heaven Is for Real' boy, a host narrating a guest's account in the third person ('she said, there was Jesus floating up 30 feet in the air') (3 of 24); Scriptural and theological exposition with no encounter described: 'Moses gave us 613 laws, Jesus said I am the fulfillment of the law'; Explicit non-identification, which is the exact opposite of the claim: 'I truly can't say it was God. I truly can't say it was Jesus'; 'people ask me if that white light was Jesus — I don't know' (2 of 24); The ABSENCE of the figure, in hell accounts: 'I was without the presence of Jesus Christ. I felt he was absent'; An ordinary-life church visit where the speaker felt 'the presence of Jesus' in a pew weeks after the accident.

places.name: no judgement here
places.description: The most consistently reported quality of the review: the total absence of condemnation. Experiencers repeatedly say nobody was judging them - not God, not the being holding them, not the beings watching. Where they had been raised to expect a throne, a scepter, a gavel and a verdict, they found instead compassion, interest and even amusement. Many report the being explicitly refusing the frame: 'that's your judgment of it, not ours'. Remorse is still present and can be agonising - but it is remorse without condemnation, and several call this the single fact that changed their lives.

aliases.note: the near-universal phrasing

aliases.note: used to negate the expected theology

places.notes: This is the single most contested item in the region. A minority of accounts - particularly the distressing and the explicitly evangelical ones - report the opposite: being questioned by God, shown only their harms, or feeling accountable and afraid. The phrase also drifts into general post-NDE philosophy ('there is no hell, there is no judgment'), which is the main precision loss. Slightly less frequent in the best-evidenced stratum. Audit found false positives of the form: Self-help and audience-directed teaching: 'love yourself with no judgment, no attachment', 'there's no judgment on you in any way, shape or form' (docs LNz2TlZMn7M, 9NXyfhw-lb0); 'No judgments' about spiritual seekers' paths and growth levels (doc=CAd-JbQI5q8); A researcher analysing what other experiencers say and warning against their interpretation (doc=_TsOqTRUL3c); Generalisation about the whole population of NDErs rather than the speaker's own review (doc=MkARlQQYFFY); Scriptural exegesis - the prodigal son parable, where God 'isn't judging you' (doc=AD5MIrb5Z7A); A separate meditation experience, explicitly not the NDE (doc=Bzh2puwUODw); Different sense: 'no judgment' meaning non-assessing, emotionally flat observation of the ambulance/accident scene (docs osXjHPbUmcY, K7TK10YfTWw); Ordinary life: 'there's no judgment for me' about old friends who think he's crazy (doc=-8JjYWmWVMQ).

places.name: The Pinpoint of Light in the Distance
places.description: Far off in the black — at the end of the tunnel, or simply out there in the void — a single tiny light. People reach for the smallest possible words for it: a pinprick, a pinpoint, a speck, a dot, a flashlight held by someone far away, a single star in an otherwise empty sky. It grows, or it rushes toward them, and the closing of that distance is the pivot of the whole journey. Several stress that they moved toward it without willing it, and one insists the light came to her rather than she to it.

Precision is limited by metaphorical 'points of light' and by the idiom 'light at the end of the tunnel' used about recovery or hardship; roughly four in fourteen sampled snippets were of that kind. The corpus's transition data supports this as a real waypoint: tunnel>bright_light is one of the top transitions (5.5% of sequenced accounts) and void_darkness>bright_light is higher still (10.0%). Audit found false positives of the form: Explicit negations: 'no tunnels, no light at the end of the tunnel, no spirits, nothing'; a spiritist describing the expected script then confirming 'none of this happened'; a tunnel with no light at the end (P6, P13, P15).; 'Light at the end of the tunnel' as the ordinary English idiom for hope, used in a prediction about humanity's future (P7).; 'Speck of light' used inside a simile spoken by a being rather than as a perceived distant light (P16)..

People report watching their own legs dissolve, or reaching for something and realising there is nothing to reach with, and are frequently more struck by this than by the surroundings.

The catalogued map covers how the DEAD appear (restored bodies) but never what the experiencer themself is made of, which is a separate and frequently-volunteered observation. Main false positive: 'there was no body in the bed' and clinicians saying 'no body reflexes'. Audit found false positives of the form: one biography match on the same 'had no / didn't have any' construction applied to something else entirely — 'I didn't have any regular religious training as a child' (yaWiPiE5jQs).

Reported as neither male nor female, sometimes without a face, sometimes as a shape made only of light. Experiencers frequently say explicitly that they do not know who or what it was and are unwilling to guess.

places.notes: Runs the OPPOSITE way to evidential strength: 8.57% overall but only 4.42% among cv>=23 accounts, while the named-figure pattern holds at 11-14% across strata. The unnamed vocabulary is commonest in the more discursive, spiritually-eclectic accounts. A separate marker of naming refusal - 'I don't know what/who it was' - runs 8.10% overall and RISES to 11.05% at cv>=23, so it is not that the best-evidenced accounts are more certain of identity; they are more willing to say they cannot identify it while still not reaching for the phrase 'being of light'. Audit found false positives of the form: Ongoing post-NDE visitations and channelling: 'since then I see beings that visit me', 'that's how I was trained by Jesus and other beings of light' (docs TEdeJcMC_EA, gr2Lksx6lJ4); A dream at age 14 in which a light being appeared, explicitly framed as a dream (doc=cTiQrBB_sxI); Researchers and hosts describing other people's cases or theorising about how the being is interpreted (docs QQWoQFtxYsM, l3knFDM9vLE, zd3_JCoz-kA); Religious belief and upbringing: 'I believed I had angels and saints and all of these beings of light' (doc=LndPnnVfPw0); A living human described as 'a light being' because he had a glow about him (doc=Oj-n3kP4tbE); A token accident - 'the light being light, which is everything created from unconditional love' is not a being at all (doc=VhvGoA2oSE8); Interviewer asking 'And what about the being of light?' with a one-word answer (doc=kiww4X_lSQM).

The corpus's own phrasing: 'a warmth, uh, not a temperature warmth. some have described it like just being hugged by the universe.' Several report the warmth first and only then realise the warmth IS the love. It is described as coming from inside as much as outside — 'in me, through me'.

Audit found false positives of the form: post-NDE ordinary life: feeling 'a slight warmth' running fingers over oracle cards (W-y1sD7Kjt4); pre-birth 'home' memory recalled years later while watching a movie, not perceived during the NDE (boVaPw6N3Sw); generic channelled spirit-world teaching about conditions there ('the great central source of light... always delightfully warm'), no first-person perception (kdYRNYSQOl4); an angelic comfort presence felt in the hospital bed rather than in the other world (iqJjlKwCVRY).

places.name: More Real Than Real
places.description: Experiencers insist, almost defensively, that the other place was not dreamlike but the reverse: more solid, more detailed, more present than waking life. The comparison is volunteered without prompting and is usually offered as the reason they cannot accept a hallucination explanation. The phrasing collapses into a small set of near-identical formulas across thousands of unrelated accounts.

Frequently co-occurs with the-home in the same sentence; several accounts explicitly link them ('it feels more real, and so that gives you that feeling of being home'). Audit found false positives of the form: the interviewer/host saying it, not the experiencer — 'what I hear from people that have had NDEs is that it feels more real than reality' (CzdQVZhLVQw, 8Ptwu4Mar_E, GBlrSg8GWV8, 3ogvhI-tcdk); researchers and advocates generalising about NDErs as a class — 'they will tell you it was more real than reality' (0mM3ut9pBvA); channel bio boilerplate about a famous experiencer in the third person (o-U0ygvKvw0); a spouse describing her husband's experience, having had none herself (C37LjuBwg24); religious assertions with no perceptual content — the supernatural world / hell 'is realer than this world' offered as doctrine against skeptics (BHggP2VgfS4, h1uEl6Fi9sQ).

places.name: The Tunnel That Wasn't
places.description: A substantial group say, often unprompted and often with a note of apology or defiance, that they had no tunnel. They know the cliché — several name Moody or Kübler-Ross or 'the Hollywood version' — and they report its absence as a fact about their experience. In its place they describe going straight into the light, waking up already in a garden, stepping down into a meadow, or an instantaneous shift with nothing in between. One was told by a self-proclaimed expert that his was therefore not a near-death experience at all.

Combined with the corpus's own coding (tunnel present in only 23.9% of accounts and only 18.1% of sequenced journeys) the picture is clear: the tunnel is a minority route, not the standard one, and its cultural centrality is not matched by its prevalence. Note also that these denials sit INSIDE the tunnel regex's matches at doc level, which is the main cap on that item's precision.

places.name: The Recognition — I Had Been Here Before

People say it felt familiar, that they recognised the place, that they had been there before — often while simultaneously acknowledging they had never seen it in this life. The familiarity extends to the beings ('I know these people'), the light ('it had always been there and I just forgot'), and the knowledge itself. Several describe the total absence of the astonishment they would have expected.

places.notes: Rises gently with evidential quality (7.14% -> 8.15% -> 8.29%). Precision was measured across two samples: 12/12 clean at cvNDE>=18, roughly 9/14 in the mixed-quality sample, giving ~0.85 overall. The dominant false positive removed by the negative lookahead is 'familiar with' meaning merely acquainted. This is the same underlying report as the-home seen from a different angle — home is what the place IS, recognition is how it is known — and they co-occur heavily. Audit found false positives of the form: 'I have been there before' meaning 'I have visited it (in my NDE)' rather than 'it felt already known' — the one systematic semantic slip; Familiarity in ordinary life: Reconnective Healing frequencies, a dream about riding in grandparents' Buick; Post-NDE amnesia where nothing felt familiar (a polarity flip the regex cannot see); Familiarity of unpleasant earthly sensation on re-entering the body; Past-life confusion ('they were familiar to me, but not as they thought they were').

places.name: Another Dimension

It is used to mean roughly 'a reality overlapping this one that you look into rather than travel to' — several describe looking through the light 'as if into another dimension', or being at the hospital and in another dimension simultaneously. A minority give it a number (the fifth dimension, the fourth), usually those with prior metaphysical reading; most leave it unnumbered.

Roughly four in ten hits are metaphorical or belong to post-NDE interpretation rather than the experience itself. Also inflated by interviewer prompts: in several translated Brazilian interviews the interviewer supplies the word ('Would you say you went to another dimension?') and the experiencer resists it. Audit found false positives of the form: The interviewer supplies the word in a question and the experiencer only assents - this is the single biggest class (docs i6iCjDieaLc, MbNVvz0DzMw, XTqs-n7aniY, pgDyFqCpulU); Numbered-dimension cosmology from prior metaphysical reading, describing a schema rather than a perceived place - 'we're in a construct of 12 dimensions', third/fourth/fifth dimension remote-viewing theory (docs yXfPyJSU2Z0, cXKJpmRm6iQ, FvajKZf1u5Q); Metaphor for shock: 'I completely went into another dimension and was absolutely 100% useless' at an accident scene (doc=MlD3102w8Rw); Other people's experiences - Strassman's DMT volunteers, general audience speculation that dreams are another dimension (docs mSotnAe7rsM, W1gU_uikYuo); Astral-projection practice sessions rather than an NDE (doc=KXvXjjHsXkQ); Book-plug generalisation about where loved ones go (doc=d3FfvNmOi6g).

places.name: Wherever I Was
places.description: A distinct construction from 'a place': here the narrator explicitly flags that they do not know, and cannot find out, where they were. They are certain of the experience and uncertain of its address. It is often used as an aside in the middle of a confident sentence — 'a tremendous sense of peace wherever I was' — and sometimes hedges a religious name the narrator is not willing to commit to ('heaven, or wherever I was at'). Some go further and say there is no name for it at all.
