places.notes: Rises monotonically with evidential strength: 6.38% overall, 7.46% at cv>=18, 8.84% at cv>=23. Better-evidenced narrators are MORE likely to admit they do not know where they were — the opposite of what you would expect if confident naming were a sign of a stronger account. Precision is only moderate (5/8 in sample): 'wherever I was' also appears biographically ('uninvite me wherever I was invited to speak', 'wherever I was, I'd fall asleep'), which the negative_regex partly catches. Audit found false positives of the form: The near-identical phrase 'I didn't know what to call it' applied to something else entirely — the NDE label, remote viewing, music therapy, the feeling of God (5 of the 8 false positives); Ordinary-life disorientation: waking drugged in a foreign country, being trapped under lake ice, walking through your own house during a panic attack; Otherwise clean; the surviving matches are genuine in-experience hedges about location.

places.name: The Portal / Archway
places.description: An opening that is not a door and not a tunnel: an aperture that appears in the air, spins open, or simply is, and through which another world is directly visible. People reach for 'portal' when the thing has no frame, no hinges and no length. Some see a forest or a green field through it as though through a window; others go through it and arrive somewhere instantly. The archway variant has a definite arch shape and colours the speaker cannot name.

aliases.note: the corpus's own preferred word for a frameless opening
'a huge doorway without a door, because it's just this huge archway'
one speaker's name for a simple, unornamented arch that opened to show the meaning of life

sensory: round, and moving, and gold at the rim

quotes.speaker: Maria Aparecida Wolf Cardoso Weber

places.notes: Flat across cvNDE strata. Speakers are unusually explicit that a portal is NOT a tunnel ('it wasn't a tunnel per se but it was like a portal of energy'), which makes this a genuinely separate structure from the tunnel region rather than a synonym. Precision loss is overwhelmingly the modern web sense of 'portal'. Audit found false positives of the form: The modern web/tech sense: 'I'm building a real estate portal', 'that's the portal to be able to find that as well' pointing at a website (docs PkTRAmJVVf8, Cl4hMnKYPlU); Energy-work and protection idiom in ordinary life: closing the portal after meditation, a psychic who 'opened a portal' in a client's house, 'you opened up the portal' between podcast guests (docs 1dgpAk3nQh8, OkLjOKU2N9c, ZWgQ7SwCgZ8); Metaphor: 'Love is the portal', a magical sofa that acts as 'a portal of some kind' during channelling (docs zd3_JCoz-kA, ZbudzG3uKrU); Post-NDE clairvoyance at other people's deathbeds, where a portal appears in the room (doc=ZTWpoIeJovE); Interviewer supplying the word ('something opened up like a portal?') or a host retelling someone else's NDE (docs 2vG48fuOmNs, VI7W6QCUrTI); Explicit refusal: 'I don't want to say it's a portal, but just into nothingness' (doc=ZKrfHYllw6k); Cosmology lecture about 'portal gateways' between dimensional constructs (doc=ncpOTGWRxSA).

places.name: The Vastness
places.description: Where the unnamed place is given any dimension at all, the dimension is size without limit. Narrators describe an expanse that keeps opening, an emptiness with no far wall, a vastness they perceive rather than see. Frequently the vastness is not empty but full of something they cannot count — stars, gases, beings, knowledge — and several describe looking INTO the light and finding the vastness inside it, so that the expanse is a property of the light rather than a landscape around it.

aliases.note: commonest single collocation

sensory: size felt rather than seen
no far edge however long you look
vastness perceived as knowledge, not distance
the expanse found inside the light rather than around it

quotes.text: Endless space, endless brightness, no horizon, no depth, no structure as such. It was a nothingness and something at the same time.
I really saw a vastness in this light.
quotes.speaker: Tasso Sou

quotes.text: I felt a vastness and a knowledge that I describe as omniscient.

quotes.text: I cried out into that infinite expanse that I never want to leave this place.

quotes.text: toward this vast emptiness beyond

places.notes: About a third of hits are 'the vastness of the universe' shown to the experiencer as a cosmological display (stars, planets, gases) rather than the unnamed realm itself; whether these are the same place is genuinely unclear from the accounts. Two narrators (Sharon Milliman, twice recorded) supply near-identical wording in different interviews, so the doc count slightly overstates the number of distinct witnesses. Audit found false positives of the form: sermon/scripture commentary — God answering Job about 'the vastness of the universe'; an altar call about 'the vastness of eternity and the finality of God's judgment' (sEVVlRKInQs, OjSv_natOLU); third-person dramatised narration of someone else's NDE ('suddenly, he was weightless, suspended in an infinite velvety blackness') (SBnosgV4QIo); a meditation-induced expansion the narrator herself distinguishes from her out-of-body experiences (GmMvszHb1Ww).

places.name: The Buildings
places.description: Constructed edifices in the otherworld, described generically before the speaker knows what any of them is for. People repeatedly say they 'noticed a building' and then somehow knew, without signage or being told, what it was: a university, a library, a nursery, a place of healing. Buildings are often walked through rather than into - one experiencer says each building he entered opened into a different realm. Several note that the buildings shape-shift or reconfigure themselves to the needs of whoever is inside.

aliases.note: by far the commonest word
where souls prepare for a lifetime

sensory: buildings that get higher and higher until they disappear into the clouds
shape-shifting: buildings that change size and form for their inhabitants
no doors or windows - entry by a 'special way'

places.notes: The clearest cvNDE gradient in this region: 11.32% overall rising monotonically to 21.55% at cv>=23. Precision losses are almost entirely earthly buildings seen during the out-of-body phase (hospital, apartment block, city skyline seen while floating), which is itself an interesting confound because those OBE sightings are what earn the high cvNDE scores. Audit found false positives of the form: 'building' as gerund or compound: 'a building sense of urgency', 'love is the building block of all existence', 'an architect building a building' (docs dMKQYbnqZIg, pnPL-mdtouM, NeuLw8pV_0Q, zDQ1SN3fS9M); The hospital: leaving 'the room and the building', looking for a phone 'somewhere in the building' (docs iEJ2nssxMTo, zLZVh4ND4tY); Ordinary-life buildings: a car thrown into a building, the back of the Salvation Army, a church in Moscow, a past-life office in China (docs 2bHZx78NBsU, krbWhvF-Elg, Xd5-oL3al-c, 0NsLVjC6rd8); Earthly buildings seen during an OBE or life review - a Brazilian city skyline, Vietnam-era rooftops - rather than otherworld edifices (docs vGOOU_7ZrLE, g54-az9lP5w); Idiom: 'we really haven't left the building yet' (doc=7tXaHezdHTw); A meditation-hall building experienced during Vipassana, not an NDE (doc=iWG_rLdW4Ng).

places.name: The Speck of Light in the Distance
places.description: The Light almost always begins as something very small and very far away, seen from inside darkness: a pinprick, a speck, a spark. It oscillates or expands, or the experiencer is drawn toward it 'like a magnet', and it grows until it fills everything. Several are unsure whether they moved toward it or it came toward them.

aliases.term: point of brilliant light in the distance
a little tiny speck of light
light way off in the distance

aliases.note: several use the Star Trek image for the pull

magnetic pull — desire to reach it grows as it nears
ambiguity of motion: 'I don't know if I was going to it or it was coming to me'

quotes.speaker: Peter Panagore

quotes.text: I could see far ahead this pinpoint of light
quotes.speaker: Tom Sawyer

places.notes: Strongly MORE common among better-evidenced accounts: 6.61% all, 8.70% at cv>=18, 10.50% at cv>=23. Usually but not always inside a tunnel — many report the distant light in open darkness with no tunnel at all. Audit found false positives of the form: 'Point/spark of light' used as an analogy or theory rather than a perception — consciousness singularity as 'a light on a lamppost 30, 40 feet away', a pinprick of light used to explain what a SOUND was like, 'your soul is that spark of light of the creator' (P22, P19, P13).; Third-party generalisation and book-plug context — a researcher summarising 'they see a little pinpoint of light and get drawn to it like a magnet', 'other people have said... I saw this light in the distance' (P7, P12).; A large light already arrived at, or a light source seen from inside heaven, rather than a distant speck in darkness (P3, P9).; A post-NDE confirmation event in ordinary physical reality ('a spark of light bloated in front of me... it made a popping sound') and an ego-stripping process ending in a pinprick of light that is the SELF, not a place (P17, P24)..

places.name: Colours That Do Not Exist Here
places.description: The most-reported perceptual quality of the whole landscape: colours outside the earthly range. Experiencers say the palette is not just brighter but larger — millions or billions of distinguishable shades where earth has a handful, colours with no names, colours the human eye has no receptor for. Many reach for the same analogies: black-and-white television to high definition, an undeveloped film finally developed, a veil removed.

aliases.term: colors I had never seen before
aliases.note: the single commonest phrasing

aliases.term: colors that don't exist on Earth
we don't have the color palette here
aliases.note: used by an artist experiencer

aliases.term: greener than green / bluer than blue
the colors were their own sovereign beings

each colour with its own sound or vibration

no muted or dull tones anywhere

quotes.speaker: Russell Ricks

quotes.speaker: Vinney Tolman

quotes.text: the grass is so different than anything on Earth, just millions of shades of green
quotes.speaker: Vinney Tolman

quotes.speaker: Graça Aranha

quotes.text: The green was greener than green. The blue was bluer than any blue I have ever seen.
quotes.speaker: Zachary

places.notes: The highest-precision pattern in this region and one of the most strongly cvNDE-enriched features anywhere: 5.78% of all accounts, 14.92% of accounts scoring cv>=23 — a 2.6x enrichment. Tagged 'state' rather than 'landscape' because it is a quality of the whole otherworld (beings, cities, water) rather than a place you stand in, and left parentless for that reason. Audit found false positives of the form: Colours merely brighter or more vibrant than earth's rather than outside its range ('the colors were more intense', 'a white that dazzled') — 3 passages; these support a weaker claim than the one made; Neuroscience philosophising that colour does not exist in nature at all; An earthly analogy used as the descriptor (Aurora Borealis) with no beyond-range claim; Generalised comparison of 'the other realms' to earth in an after-effects reflection rather than a described perception; Synaesthesia ('the colors were alive', sound bringing colours) rather than impossible hues.

places.name: The snap back
places.description: Re-entry is overwhelmingly violent and instantaneous, not gradual. The verbs are consistent across hundreds of accounts: slammed, snapped, sucked, shot, yanked, thrown, catapulted, whooshed, shoved, kicked. Several describe being drawn back down the tunnel the way they came; one describes it as 'the opposite of a cork getting pulled out of a bottle of wine'. Entry is usually through the top of the head, occasionally feet-first. Gentle descents exist but are rare (33 docs, 0.53%).
sensory: entry through the top of the head; sometimes feet first
an audible ringing or a loud crack at the moment of impact
the opposite of a cork leaving a bottle
a hard 'thud' — one experiencer got 'the biggest headache you can imagine'
the trigger is often a single thought (concern for a child, a partner, the body)

quotes.text: I felt myself suddenly and violently yanked back into my body, which was still about 40 feet away, in the back bedroom - WHOOSH!
And then I just slammed back into my body, and I woke up, and I was crying, and everything hurt.
quotes.speaker: Andrea Courey

quotes.text: the next thing I know, I'm shoved back in my body, and my body feels so heavy and so dense
quotes.speaker: Michelle Claire

quotes.text: And as I was getting sucked back into my body, it's like, um, the opposite of a cork getting pulled out of a bottle of wine.
quotes.speaker: Lura Ketchledge

quotes.text: slammed back into my body, like a jolt right.
quotes.speaker: Hillary

places.notes: Precision is essentially perfect — this idiom has no other use. Flat to cv>=18, then drops sharply at cv>=23 (2 of 181 docs). I would not over-read that: the cv>=23 stratum is small and skews toward accounts whose evidential weight comes from out-of-body veridical detail near the body, where the return is often described as gentle re-merging rather than a snap. The corpus's own coding puts 'sudden_return' at 56.4% of sequenced accounts with a mean journey position of 0.978, so the underlying phenomenon is far more common than my strict lexical measure. Audit found false positives of the form: One passage is a researcher/host generalising about what OTHER experiencers report ('The description I hear the most on people coming back... being slammed back into my body'); One passage is a repeatable self-induced out-of-body experience during a nap, not the NDE re-entry.

places.name: The Levels
places.description: The other world is repeatedly described as tiered rather than flat: levels, planes, layers or spheres stacked above and below, with beings and places belonging to particular ones and movement between them being upward or downward. People describe knowing there were floors above and below them the way you know it in a building, and some ascend through several before being stopped.

aliases.note: the commonest phrasing
ascent through several
less common, older vocabulary

sensory: an awareness of things above you and things below you, like floors in a building

quotes.speaker: Jim Woodford

quotes.text: I could see that there were different levels to things where people were coming and going from and such.
quotes.speaker: Ryan

places.notes: Essentially FLAT across cvNDE strata (15.27% -> 14.92%), i.e. no evidential gradient. The catalogued map treats the other world as a set of named places but never as a vertical stack, which is how a sixth of the corpus describes it. Precision is limited by 'levels' used medically (blood levels, levels of care); the negative regex removes the commonest of those. Audit found false positives of the form: 'Levels/layers' in senses that have nothing to do with a tiered afterlife: levels of consciousness, levels of meditation and belief, layers of brain processing, layers of meaning in the Bible, 'higher levels of degrees', 'it amazes me on so many levels', 'so many different layers and depths' to my story (10 of 24 — the dominant failure); Belief and speculation rather than perception: 'I do believe there are different levels, different spots you can go to', 'I still believe there is different levels over there' (3 of 24); Doctrine delivered as a message about souls progressing to higher dimensions over lifetimes, not a structure the narrator saw; 'Levels' meaning generations of family in a life review; Tiered structure reported from nightly spirit travel rather than from the near-death event.

places.name: The Music
places.description: Sound arrives before or alongside the light: singing, choirs, chords, a symphony with no instruments and no source. Experiencers insist it is unlike any earthly music and that they have never been able to reproduce it since; several describe being inside the sound rather than listening to it. It is often the last thing to fade as they are pulled back.

aliases.note: often described as many voices in unison
angelic chorus, seraphim singing

aliases.term: the most beautiful music you've ever heard
aliases.note: the commonest phrasing

aliases.term: cosmic music / an ocean of sound
harmonies / a tune no human being could write

getting louder and louder as you approach the light
a symphony with no instruments; every note a colour
the experiencer is inside the sound, not in front of it
unreproducible afterwards - people try synthesisers and fail

quotes.text: There was this music that I never heard and never have again that was otherworldly, other instruments, beautiful, all pervasive like this place was music.
quotes.speaker: Ellen Wier

And I hear this glorious music.
None of it was as beautiful as what I call the sounds of the universe or angelic chorus.
quotes.speaker: Kimberly Sharp

quotes.speaker: Hilary Leehane

places.notes: MORE common among the best-evidenced accounts: 5.55% overall rising monotonically to 9.39% at cvNDE>=23. The catalogued map has 'the-singing-landscape' (the landscape itself sings) but not the music as a heard event on arrival - which is far commoner. False positives come from interviewers discussing music research and from post-NDE musical gifts; roughly a third of sampled hits were not in-NDE hearing. Audit found false positives of the form: Earthly singing at the bedside — a sister singing a hope song to the patient in hospital; Explicit denials that inherit the vocabulary ('It was nothing like I've read about other people saying, or angels singing'); Other people's experiences (a niece and father who 'described hearing the most beautiful music ever'); A book plug — Don Piper's 90 Minutes in Heaven quoted as the best description of heaven's music; Musical metaphor for non-auditory experience ('like a beautiful harmonic progression' describing weaving vibrations); Commentary on the purpose of the heavenly choir rather than a description of hearing it.

places.name: Jesus / Christ
places.description: The second most common named identity, and the one most often recognised without being told: 'when the savior of the world stands in front of you, you'll know.' Jesus appears either as a robed human figure with a beard, or purely as light. Recognition is frequently reported by people with no Christian formation, and occasionally by people from other faiths entirely. In several accounts Jesus is the escort who takes the experiencer INTO the light, distinct from the light itself.

aliases.note: 923 raw identities in the entity census, second only to God
used by those who reject a personal Jesus but keep the name

aliases.term: a Man of Light with holes in his hands
aliases.note: reported by an imam who recognised him

sensory: eyes are the most-reported feature — 'eyes of lightning', violet, blue, holding an intense gaze
white robe, sometimes a golden sash; sometimes no body at all, only light
shows the wounds in his hands or side
smiles; the smile is repeatedly what triggers recognition
communicates without speaking: 'we weren't using words'

Jesus embraced me. He was not in a body but was a being of light in the brightest white, golden light.
quotes.speaker: Lee

places.notes: LESS common among the best-evidenced accounts: 19.40% all, 18.65% at cv>=18, 14.92% at cv>=23. Together with the Presence trend (which rises), this is the clearest naming signal in the region — as evidential strength rises, the being is less often given a tradition-specific name and more often left as an unnamed presence. Some matches are the interviewer or host discussing Jesus rather than the experiencer's own encounter. Audit found false positives of the form: Scripture quotation and Bible discussion — 'Blessed are the meek', 'what Jesus said', sermon-style recall from childhood church (P1, P10, P13, P20).; Host and channel intros that name the encounter before the account begins ('he met jesus face to face', 'his favourite vision was when he met Jesus twice', a rhetorical list of what matters most about NDEs) (P3, P7, P9).; A large recurring class of NEGATIONS the regex reads as hits: 'I can't say I saw Jesus', 'I truly can't say it was Jesus', 'Nothing inside me thought it was Jesus, God, Peter, Paul. He was nameless' (P6, P11, P22).; Third-party identification of an unnamed figure — a father telling the experiencer 'you probably met Jesus or God himself' when she never looked at him (P14); an ambiguous waking-room voice the experiencer cannot attribute (P15)..

places.name: being sent back
places.description: The other outcome: no choice at all. The experiencer is sent, pushed, put or simply removed, sometimes mid-sentence and sometimes before they have even reached the boundary they were walking toward. Several describe it as being catapulted, shot, or falling backwards. The consistent emotional report is not fear but grief and protest — people describe arriving back in the body devastated, and in pain.

aliases.term: I was catapulted back into my body
it wasn't my decision to come back

sensory: sudden and instantaneous — 'in one second I was back in my body'
described as a whoosh, a slide backwards, a fall, a catapult
the return into the body is painful where the journey out was not
no farewell; the scene simply ends

quotes.text: I felt two invisible hands on my chest, thrust me backwards and I never got through the door.
quotes.speaker: Claire Daugherty

quotes.text: But I was cut, put back into my ICU before I could, uh, go through that fence. So it wasn't my decision to come back.
quotes.speaker: Alba Monn

quotes.speaker: Israel Shalom

quotes.text: The angel sent me back over the meadow and into my body.
he starts to go through, walk through the archway into the city when the angel stopped him and and sent him back.
quotes.speaker: Santosh Acci

places.notes: This is the only major process in the region that DECLINES with evidential strength: 8.35% overall down to 5.52% at cv>=23. The structured journey coding shows the same shape in reverse — 'forced_return' is coded in 27.1% of sequenced accounts at mean position 0.893, versus 'choice_to_return' at 80.8%. Precision is limited by medical 'the doctor sent me back home' constructions, which the negative_regex only partly removes. Audit found false positives of the form: Ordinary-life uses of 'send/sent back': sent back home as a child, transferred back to another hospital, fear of not being sent back home from the psych ward (P2, P12, P22).; Passages that describe the OPPOSITE — an explicit choice to return ('I was given my way', 'I was given a choice whether to come back or to stay in heaven') (P3, P14).; Third-party and generic speculation: 'people say I chose to stay and they still sent me back', a medium saying a mother 'sent him back', general theorising that being told to go back is still a soul choice (P6, P7, P15, P21).; Physical propulsion at the START of the event rather than the return — lightning throwing the body backwards like a ragdoll (P5).; Involuntary movement INSIDE the afterlife (pushed away from beings, refused passage over a boundary) rather than return to the body (P10, P16); a sleep-paralysis episode where the experiencer asked to be returned (P20)..

places.name: The Space
places.description: Many experiencers reach not for 'place' but for 'space' — a word that carries volume without ground, scenery or edges. The space is usually described by its light behaviour rather than its contents: it is lit from within, it is bright white, it has no visible source of illumination. Where 'a place' implies somewhere you stand, 'this space' implies something you are suspended inside. Several narrators use the two words in the same breath and then correct themselves toward 'space'.

aliases.note: used interchangeably with the void by some

sensory: light with no source
everything glowing from inside itself
no floor, no ceiling, no walls
brightness without glare

quotes.text: I ended up in more of a space space. I'm not standing on grass and I'm not out into the woods and there aren't uh streets paved with gold. But where I'm at is in a space
Drake led me to know that this this space was lit from within.
quotes.speaker: Vinnie Todd Tolman

quotes.text: And I came to this space that was bright white light.
quotes.speaker: Deborah Martin

quotes.text: And this space, this space, it was very bright, as bright as you could imagine heaven to be
quotes.speaker: Thomas Zemke

places.notes: Precision is the weakest of the core entries: 'this space' has drifted into New Age therapeutic idiom ('holding space', 'coming from that space of love'), and roughly four in ten sampled hits were post-NDE metaphor rather than a location during the experience. The negative_regex catches the literal astronomical and architectural senses but not the therapeutic one. Slightly below-average in the best-evidenced stratum. Audit found false positives of the form: 'Space' as emotional or mental state — 'it's okay to stay in that space and be honest with spirit', 'my kids were in the space I was in when my mother passed away' (P1, P18).; Ordinary physical rooms and buildings — 'walking into a space and feeling a strong energy', journaling 'getting that into a space where it's in print' (P6, P12).; Cosmology and perception theory using 'space' in the physics sense — the edge of the universe, convergent focus, light appearing as the space between your hands (P7, P11, P17).; Metaphysical teaching about pre-incarnation ('that is the space... before we individuated from the Godhead') and about reconnecting to 'that space we come in with' (P10, P20).; OBE descriptions of the PHYSICAL setting rather than the other world — the hospital corner feeling bigger, 'the space was the same as what I saw in the physical body' (P22, P23); and a breathwork session describing a 'cube-like space' representing the lungs (P9)..

places.name: The Flowers
places.description: Flowers cover the meadow and garden and are treated as the second wonder after the grass. They are described as radiating light from inside rather than reflecting it, as having colours with no earthly name, and — repeatedly — as responsive: they turn toward the experiencer, speak, sing, ask to be picked, or flow along beside them as they move. Several people report being able to zoom their attention into a single petal and find a whole world in it.

aliases.note: Rajiv Parti's meadow of roses with the Om chant

aliases.term: flowers that glowed from the inside out

places.notes: Unlike the grass, flowers do NOT rise further at cv>=23 (6.63% vs 7.04% at cv>=18) — the enrichment plateaus. False positives are earthly: gardening, flower nurseries, funeral flowers, and a recurring sponsor advertisement for a garden hose. Audit found false positives of the form: present-day earthly flowers — 'look out the window, see where I live now... there are flowers everywhere' (YAXBFbelu74); a guided meditation script the host reads to the audience ('please envision that you are in a space with emerald green grass... hundreds of beautiful flowers') (pbkgMnyqnEE); metaphor — 'everybody else sees a field of flowers' while she alone sees the oncoming catastrophe (2GqJWMn5kGs); a hypothetical someone else's experience — 'maybe you're in a beautiful garden... removing weeds' (PRWLJUCq0iI); generalisation about dying patients' deathbed visions of 'beautiful flowers' (YyQYfCiQV6k); an after-death communication in which a deceased aunt shows a garden, plus flower-related biography (IkISinlMwIs).

places.name: The Ball / Orb / Column of Light
places.description: When the light takes a bounded shape rather than filling everything, it is nearly always one of a small set of forms: a ball or orb or sphere hanging in space, a column or pillar rising further than can be seen, a sea or ocean or pool the experiencer stands in. Several describe a human shape faintly discernible inside the column, 'the way we can see the form of a person in a doorway'.

aliases.note: most common form
used by experiencers from Latter-day Saint backgrounds

sensory: expanding — grows larger and brighter as you approach or as it approaches you
sometimes 'musical light', with a melody or gong-like vibration inside it
a faint human silhouette occasionally visible within
the orb pulses, and each pulse throws off individual points of light described as souls

quotes.text: And then swoosh, I'm sucked up the column of light like an envelope in a pneumatic mail tube.
There arose just an amazing, incredibly beautiful, loving ball of brilliant, loving light.
quotes.speaker: Bill Lawson

quotes.text: It was as if we were in the middle of a radiant pool of white light.
quotes.speaker: Dr. Fabio

places.notes: Clearly MORE common among the best-evidenced accounts — 4.73% all, 5.52% at cv>=18, 7.18% at cv>=23. Adding 'wall|tunnel|river|beam|shaft|cloud|mass|source of light' to the regex raises coverage to 11.16% but mixes in the tunnel, which belongs to another region. Audit found false positives of the form: third-person narration of other people's experiences — a man seeing his dead dog's soul as a ball of light; 'he sees a levitating ball of bright light' (CPcDzI8KK5o, ThvrdY4SDEI); generic instruction about deathbed visions — 'you might see an orb of light leave their body' (vrvk1fYgZfU); a nurse's ongoing clairvoyance at hospital code blues, years after her own NDE (MkARlQQYFFY); metaphor — 'I'm like a pillar of light for this region' (OUGS5aNm9R8); doctrinal cosmology, not perception — the God worlds as an 'ocean of love and mercy... vast ocean of light and sound' (RWgSwYCbhuU); the interviewer describing the image back to the guest (7T3O_y3l1KE); a light apparition floating in a room, not the other world (3n5zyeOaAf0); NOTE FOR THE MAP: roughly a third of the true hits are the experiencer's OWN form ('I was a ball of light'), which is the same evidence as the-form-you-wear; consider splitting encountered orb/column from self-as-orb before quoting counts.

places.name: Calling out, and the light that comes
places.description: The exit from the dark places, and it is almost always the same shape: the experiencer, having no resources left, calls out — usually a name, usually aloud, usually to a figure they say they had stopped believing in — and something answers. A pinpoint of light appears and grows, or a hand comes down and takes hold. Experiencers stress the surprise: they did not expect it to work.

aliases.note: the single most repeated sentence in the distressing region

aliases.term: I cried out into the darkness
a speck of light in the darkness
a huge hand landed on my forehead

sensory: a pinpoint of light that grows rapidly rather than approaches
physical grip — a hand on the forearm, on the head, lifting
the light described as so bright it would destroy an earthly body
immediate cessation of the darkness, not a gradual fade
the sound of one's own voice heard as a scream even when thought silently

quotes.text: To my surprise, a tiny little light like a star appeared in that darkness and it got very bright very fast and it came over me right in front of me.
quotes.speaker: Howard Storm

quotes.text: I called on to the darkness, "Jesus, please save me." And to my complete surprise, he came, surrounded in brilliant white light.
quotes.speaker: Howard Storm

quotes.speaker: Colin Perry

places.notes: Clearly MORE common among the best-evidenced accounts: 7.85% overall rising to 11.05% at cv>=23. That is the strongest positive gradient of anything I measured in this region. Precision ~0.5 because the regex also catches praying in ordinary life and praying on behalf of others; a much tighter variant requiring dark/hell context within 200 characters of the cry matched only 17 documents but was ~90% precise, and every one of those 17 followed the identical script: call out by name, light or hand arrives, extraction is immediate. The rescue is the most stereotyped sequence in the distressing region and deserves its own scrutiny downstream. Audit found false positives of the form: 'Cried out to God' in ordinary life with no experience following: praying in a hospital bed, at the moment of a car impact, while holding a gun, during addiction struggles, in a bedroom at rock bottom (P2, P5, P8, P9, P13, P15, P16, P19, P21).; Physically shouting for help after an accident ('I called for help' from a culvert) — the same words, no other world (P1).; Post-NDE integration prayers, and the interviewer/experiencer using 'God help me' as a rhetorical aside (P7, P14, P24).; Someone ELSE crying out — a soul observed inside a vision, and a bystander scenario where the cry is to a person in the room (P12, P22).; Note also that one on-topic passage is a cry from a hell realm that is explicitly NOT answered (P10) — the regex cannot distinguish answered from unanswered cries..

places.name: The Meadow
places.description: The specific open grassland where the experiencer most often first finds themselves standing after the tunnel, the light, or the dark. It is repeatedly described as a slope or a rise you come up over — the scene 'changes totally' at the crest — and as filled edge to edge with flowers. Deceased relatives, guides and crowds of people are frequently met here, and it is often where the border or fence lies.
sensory: tall grass with wildflowers scattered through it
a slope or rise you climb, with a different scene beyond the crest
a breeze moving countless blades of grass
sometimes a white fence, wall or gate at its far edge

quotes.speaker: Kimberly Clark Sharp

quotes.speaker: Alice T.

quotes.speaker: Sharon Milliman

quotes.speaker: Stephen Noak

places.notes: A clean, high-precision term: the word 'meadow' is rare in ordinary English speech, so a bare match is usually the NDE landscape. Rises monotonically with evidential strength (4.45% -> 6.69% -> 8.01% -> 9.94%), which is one of the strongest cvNDE gradients in this region. Main false positives: German- and Portuguese-language accounts where farm meadows appear in the biographical setup, plus one recurring proper noun (Meadowbrook Parkway). Audit found false positives of the form: earthly meadows in biography — a Vietnam helicopter landing zone 'would be like a meadow'; finding four-leaf clovers in a meadow after a reconciliation (V6XXFICMXLU, OrhHnllvlPE); the anonymous 'Rainbow Bridge' pet poem read aloud on air (KhIkLSY7d-Y); host intro narration setting up a guest's interview (J7u2nHmclrs); another experiencer's published account quoted at length (Ian McCormack) (5cSL2upSdX8); a shared-death experience where the meadow belonged to the dying mother's crossing (hDhYK1ipR4M); a heaven dream the narrator himself labels a dream (VHFiW1FLpBI); a guide's general statement that the other side has 'mountains, oceans, lakes, rivers plains meadows' — nothing perceived (sFS-miPrf_s).

places.name: The grandparent at the front
places.description: Grandmothers and grandfathers are the single most frequently named individual greeters in the corpus — more often named than parents. They are usually described as standing at the front of the group, or as the first face resolved out of the light. The grandmother in particular is often the one who does the talking and the reassuring; several experiencers met a grandmother or great-grandmother they had never met in life and later identified her from family photographs.

aliases.note: one family's word for great-grandmother
used when the being is unidentified but feels like a grandmother

sensory: restored to their thirties or fifties, not the age at which they died
'he looked so well' / 'she was youthful'
very large hands remembered from childhood
hair 'of fire' in one account; an angelic rather than elderly appearance
recognised from photographs only afterwards

quotes.text: people walking over crests of the hill and coming towards me. And as they approach, I start recognizing right at the front, um, you know, I started recognizing my grandfather.
quotes.speaker: David Wallace

quotes.text: And my grandfather was there. And he looked great. He had died at 71, but he looked about 35 or 40.
quotes.speaker: Tricia Barker

quotes.text: My grandma was waiting for me, my guardian angel was waiting for me.
quotes.speaker: Michelle Clare

quotes.text: they all looked younger than I even remembered them being, and you know, healthy and vibrant
quotes.speaker: Ellyn Dye

places.notes: Nearly doubles in the well-evidenced strata (4.50% -> 8.70% at cv>=18). The bare noun 'grandmother' occurs in 36.66% of all transcripts, almost all of it biography — that is why this regex demands a meeting/waiting verb. Residual false positives are mostly childhood-memory sentences that happen to contain 'was there'. Audit found false positives of the form: deathbed and shared-death accounts of a RELATIVE being greeted by the grandparent, not the narrator (n07cRRykl1U, NyC1unA5mIk, ax2BVkTajPU, Ja2e3QubXTc); clinicians and researchers relaying patients' or children's cases — 'she went somewhere and saw her grandmother', 'I remember one woman, she said... I met my grandmother' (a5GHSb94_Is, 6cviPcIr3GM, -gKY-EmmTSQ, tReEhEoe79c); living grandparents in ordinary biography — 'there was Grandma and Grandpa, her parents, waving on the front porch' (this scene appears twice, from two docs, immediately before the accident) (w539EzriIT0, Xna-HGgLytk).

places.name: Brighter Than the Sun, But It Doesn't Hurt Your Eyes
places.description: The single most repeated paradox in the corpus. The light is described as orders of magnitude beyond any earthly brightness — brighter than the sun, than the sun on snow, than a nuclear detonation — and yet the experiencer can look straight into it with wide-open eyes and feel no pain. People raise this unprompted, as the detail that convinces them it was not an ordinary perception.

aliases.note: the most common formula

aliases.term: ten thousand times brighter than the sun
so bright but it was soft on my eyes
blinding light that didn't blind me
brighter than the sun shining on a field of snow
like looking at the sun with your eyes closed

sensory: eyes wide open and looking directly into it

sometimes accompanied by 'superhero vision' — sight sharper than physical sight

places.notes: MORE common among better-evidenced accounts (3.19% all vs 3.73% at cv>=18, 4.34% at cv>=13). This is a lexical undercount — the phenomenon is described far more often than these exact formulas appear; many say only 'I could look right at it'. Audit found false positives of the form: Host intro boilerplate summarising the guest's story in the third person ('he found himself carried towards what he thought was a star brighter than ten thousand suns'); A second-person literary/generalised passage ('The light beckons you... brighter than a million suns, and yet it does not blind or burn you') which reads as a written set piece about what happens rather than a firsthand report.

places.name: the work you have not finished
places.description: The second great reason for return: a task, mission or purpose that is not complete. It is usually stated by the being rather than realised by the experiencer, and it is characteristically vague — 'you have more work to do', 'you'll be able to figure that out' — with the content withheld. Many return without ever being told what the work is, and spend years afterwards trying to identify it.

aliases.term: you have more work to do
I still had work to do

a special job to do in this life

sensory: stated as fact, without detail
often paired directly with 'it is not yet your time' in the same breath
the experiencer is told they will work out what the work is themselves
sometimes framed as duty: 'it was my duty, and I wouldn't be asked if I couldn't handle it'

quotes.text: And, and it said, and I wrote it down so I never forget it. It says, "No, not now. You have more work to do."

places.notes: Rises with evidential strength, reaching 11.05% at cv>=23 — the highest cv>=23 figure of any process in this region apart from the verdict itself. Precision is imperfect because 'more work to do' is also used about post-NDE life and about spiritual growth generally, but in this corpus those uses are usually downstream of the same boundary scene. Audit found false positives of the form: 'Work to do' / 'job to do' is a dead-common English idiom: doctors having 'work to do on my physical body' during the OBE, a road-rage anecdote, a rant about the state of the world, a third-person parable about John forgiving his father (P7, P11, P16, P22).; General religious exhortation to the audience — 'we have a job to do here on earth... to give our testimony' — with no NDE encounter attached (P9, P12, P15).; Someone else's NDE retold by a narrator ('Lou still had a lot of work to do back on earth'), and generalisations about what NDErs report (P1, P15).; The WORK OF OTHER BEINGS rather than the experiencer's return mandate — deceased sons shouting 'we have very important work to do', a hell-realm figure assigning forced labour ('you're mine now, and you've got a job to do') (P4, P19, P20).; Post-NDE career/mission talk with no being stating it (walk-in theory, leaving a job, a dream vision) (P2, P8, P14)..

places.name: The Atheist Who Gets There Anyway
places.description: The demographic control case. Experiencers who state plainly that before the event they were atheist, agnostic, or believed death was annihilation. They arrive at the same structures - the light, the presence, the review, the deceased relatives, the boundary - and describe them with the same landmarks. What changes is the vocabulary afterwards: they tend to reach for love, consciousness, connection and Source rather than heaven, and several insist explicitly that what happened was not a religious event.

aliases.note: 2.07% of documents use this exact self-description
the intensified form, used to raise the stakes of the reversal

aliases.term: not a Judeo-Christian thing - a love, consciousness connection thing
aliases.note: the post-hoc naming an unbeliever chooses
many report belief in an afterlife WITHOUT adopting a religion; 'not religious' appears in 3.61% of documents

quotes.text: I didn't believe in God, but it was like I met God.
prior to my near-death experience, I was agnostic, I was a former Catholic, I didn't believe in God, I didn't believe in Jesus
quotes.speaker: Peter Anthony

quotes.text: I was an agnostic. I thought there probably is no God and there's no afterlife. But I didn't know.
quotes.speaker: John Burke

quotes.text: I was an atheist. I did not believe in God. I used to pick on Christians and anybody with any religion.
quotes.speaker: BW Melvin

quotes.text: For me, it's not a Judeo-Christian thing. It's a love, consciousness connection thing. There aren't rules.
quotes.speaker: Julie LaVine

places.notes: ANSWER TO THE ASSIGNED QUESTION: on the evidence I could read, prior non-belief changes the NAMES, not the STRUCTURES. Prior-unbelief statements are slightly ENRICHED among the best-evidenced accounts (4.05% -> 4.97% at cv>=23), so unbelievers are not over-represented in the vaguer material. Reading their accounts, they report the same inventory: leaving the body, the light, the presence, the review, deceased relatives, the boundary, the order to return. The corpus also contains explicit cross-testimony that unbelievers meet named figures (atheists reporting Jesus) and that believers meet figures from other traditions. Two structural differences I could see but could NOT quantify with a single regex, so treat as hypotheses: (1) unbelievers more often describe a formless presence or Source rather than a person; (2) unbelievers more often report initial fear or confusion because they had no framework for what was happening. Method note: I attempted a cross-tabulation regex (atheist AND tunnel, atheist AND light, etc.) but the lookahead patterns caused catastrophic backtracking and timed out, so no cross-tab percentages are reported here rather than estimated ones. Audit found false positives of the form: 'I didn't believe' used in a non-atheism sense — disbelieving a reiki teacher, disbelieving psychics while still nominally Catholic; Loss of faith AFTER the event ('I didn't believe in God anymore after the accident'), which is the inverse of the claim; Speakers who explicitly deny being atheist ('I wouldn't say I was atheist, per se') still match; Disbelief located in teenage years with no link to belief-state at the time of the NDE.

places.name: The Living Water
places.description: Running and standing water in the country: a stream or brook beside the path, a broad river with people on the far bank, waterfalls dropping into crystal-blue pools, still lakes. The water is described as impossibly clear and as sparkling like a thousand diamonds; some report it is silent even where it falls. A few say the water was intelligent and spoke to them or asked permission before washing over them.

aliases.note: often doubles as the border/boundary — see the boundary region

aliases.term: sparkling waterfalls into crystal blue pools
aliases.note: Eben Alexander's recurring phrasing
1.31% of accounts

sensory: water shining or sparkling like diamonds as it moves
clear enough to count the stones and see fish
silent flow — 'no rushing of it'
rocks in the streambed each with a different sound
warm, welcoming, wanting to be swum in
water that is aware and communicates

quotes.text: seeing a waterfall with no sound, no splash, just running over, just flowing quietly, no sound.
quotes.speaker: Michelle Turner

quotes.text: And this river was just beautiful, glistening, uh, clear, but sparkling like diamonds and and giving off the same light and just the most gorgeous water.
quotes.speaker: Karen Thomas

quotes.text: there was a stream that just, I mean, it looked like there was a thousand diamonds in that stream. It was just sparkly and was going over some rocks.
What caught my attention was this waterfall, clear as crystal. And as it was flowing down, there was no sound.
quotes.speaker: Michelle Turner

quotes.text: surrounded by forest with beautiful sparkling waterfalls into crystal blue pools
quotes.speaker: Eben Alexander

places.notes: Precision is the weakest in this region (~0.6) because 'stream(s) of consciousness' is a very common NDE idiom for the fragmenting of awareness during the life review, and because drowning is a frequent trigger so earthly water is everywhere in the biographical setup. The lookahead in the regex removes the consciousness sense but not drownings, swimming pools or place names. Note the overlap with the border/boundary region: a river is very often the thing you are told not to cross. Audit found false positives of the form: earthly water in biography: the pond in a commissioned mural, the canyon river where the drowning happened, present-day bike rides to a Palm Springs riverbed, avoiding cliffs and rivers during blackouts (cCO_eMWAP0k, HtlIU3LDTxg, G5bNTXajs2E, vHklG2DgREs); someone else's earthly drowning story retold (Edgar Cayce wading in a flooded pond) (JyuSdpWgvHI); metaphorical water: love 'like the river was flowing from him', a prayer visualisation of 'a river of light flowing through him' (SSlwG2sTO_o, RrKHw7q0PvQ); word collisions — 'he was coming stream with me too' (transcription garble), 'pool-colored blue skin' (xMEWyjDkg4k, yUaAj06tdFI); a precognitive glimpse of an earthly campus river, not otherworldly water (W_-o6-Bli0o); a channelled spirit-world travelogue rather than an NDE report (kdYRNYSQOl4).

places.name: God
places.description: The most common name given to the being in the light. Usually the identification is immediate and unargued — 'as I'm standing before this light, I knew it was God' — and experiencers are often at pains to say nobody told them and no figure was visible. A recurring qualification: the light is God, and the human form (throne, white hair, robe) is a concession to what the experiencer could receive, not God's actual shape. Several explicitly say 'God wasn't confined to that form'.

aliases.note: 935 raw identities in the corpus's entity census, the single largest
used by those who dislike 'God'
10.07% of docs mention Holy Spirit/Holy Ghost

sensory: often no visible form at all — only light, and certainty
when a form appears: white hair, a robe, a throne, a face too bright to look at
voice heard telepathically, 'in my head', not with the ears
several report the identification arriving as a fact rather than an inference: 'there was no doubt in my mind'

quotes.text: And like any good atheist that stands before the light, I immediately knew it was God.
quotes.speaker: Mellen Thomas Benedict

quotes.text: But as I'm standing before this light, I knew it was God. I knew right away when I saw it, that was God.
quotes.speaker: Brian Hoyland

quotes.text: I was in God's presence, but I was not able to see a form or an image. God did not allow me to see. He allowed me to see the light.
quotes.speaker: Father Cedric

quotes.text: I realized looking up into this huge bright light that didn't hurt my eyes
quotes.speaker: Christine Harrington

places.notes: MORE common among the strongly-evidenced middle band (15.48% all vs 17.27% at cv>=18) then falling back at cv>=23 (14.92%). Naming tracks background strongly: almost every 'God' account comes from a Christian, Jewish or generically theistic upbringing, and several converts explicitly reach for 'God' only because it is the word available to them ('a source that I can name as God only because that's a name that is available to me'). Audit found false positives of the form: 'God' is the single most common word in the corpus outside the experience: thanking God for a song on the radio, scripture recall in a jail cell, an etymology riff on 'hue/God', a suicide-hotline phone call (P3, P4, P5, P7).; 'The voice of God' meaning intuition, meditation practice, or wisdom in daily life rather than a being encountered (P2, P11, P12 in part, P19).; Host and channel boilerplate — the IANDS radio intro, an ASMR narrator's opening — which recite 'the voice of God' or 'I died and met God' (P14, P18, P21).; Generalisations about NDErs as a class ('we feel special because we met God') and commentary on someone else's experience ('that's how HE saw God') (P1, P6).; Passages that DENY the identification: 'I don't believe it was the voice of God... it was my higher self', 'nobody introduced themselves as Jesus, nobody had a nametag' (P22, P8), plus interviewer questions about aftermath rather than encounter (P20)..

places.name: Somewhere — 'I Had Been Somewhere'
places.description: Weaker even than 'a place': the destination reduced to a bare adverb. Narrators use it to insist on the fact of location while refusing all content — 'I knew I had been somewhere for two weeks', 'I wasn't in a grave, I was here, I was somewhere.' It often carries an argumentative edge, used against the suggestion that nothing happened: the claim is not that the place was beautiful but simply that there WAS a there.
sensory: displacement without destination
duration felt in a place with no duration (two weeks in two minutes)
the body seen from 'not here'

quotes.text: I didn't know where I was, but I knew that I was somewhere.
I knew it was somewhere else. I wasn't in a grave. It wasn't maggot meat. I was here. I was somewhere.
quotes.speaker: Pegi Robinson

quotes.text: I knew I had been somewhere for two weeks.
quotes.speaker: Elizabeth Krohn

quotes.text: I knew that I was not in, um, the physical world anymore. I knew that I was somewhere else.
quotes.speaker: Lura Ketchledge

places.notes: CAVEAT — corpus artifact: several docs in the sample share an identical podcast intro ('...because I was somewhere else. The only thing that I could feel, if you could imagine, absolute love and peace...'). That boilerplate appears verbatim in at least five different videos and inflates the count for the looser pattern 'somewhere else' (14.31% all). The tighter first-person pattern reported here is less contaminated but not clean. Unlike 'wherever I was', this one DECLINES with evidential strength (6.01% -> 4.42%). Audit found false positives of the form: ELEVEN of 24 passages are the identical Roundtrip Death cold-open montage ('I didn't realize that was actually my physical body because I was somewhere else') replayed at the head of every episode — one clip inflating the account count by an order of magnitude; Geographic 'somewhere': 'somewhere in Asia' in a past-life meditation, 'somewhere in the Middle East' judged from people's dress; The medical setting: knowing you are 'somewhere else' on waking in a recovery room; Clock-time confusion in a gurney ('I knew I had been somewhere at 11:00 in the morning').

places.name: The welcoming party
places.description: People are almost never arrived-at alone. A group is already assembled and already knows you are coming; experiencers say they were expected. The corpus's own name for it is the 'welcoming committee' or 'welcome party'. It ranges from a triangle of three to eighty figures at a distance to 'thousands and thousands'. The dominant emotion reported is not awe but recognition and hilarity — they are delighted, joyous, glad to see you.

aliases.note: the single most common self-coined phrase in the corpus for this
Betty Eadie's term

the crowd extending back into shadow — 'shadows in the back' you still recognise
arms out, hands extended, embracing
joy and laughter rather than solemnity
no surprise on their side: 'I didn't show up and surprise anyone'

quotes.speaker: Alison Ward

quotes.text: About 80 people were behind her a short distance off, and I could not see them clearly, but I knew they were there to welcome me.
it just felt like I was home, I was there, and they were my welcome party. And there were thousands and thousands of, I'm going to say beings
quotes.speaker: Kirsty Salisbury

places.notes: Slightly MORE common among strongly-evidenced accounts (3.71% all vs 5.11% cv>=18), though the cv>=23 stratum is small (n=181) and drops back to 3.87%. An earlier draft of this regex included 'on the other side' and precision collapsed to ~50% because that phrase is a generic idiom for the afterlife in interview chatter; it was removed. Note the negative case is also reported: Howard Storm's welcoming committee turns out to be deceptive and leads toward hell — the welcome is not always benign. Audit found false positives of the form: 'they were waiting for me' in the hospital sense — the surgical team waiting, twelve staff at the ER door, family waiting in the waiting room (three passages); A speaker describing a CHILD's case in the third person ('that was his greeting committee for his pets'); Biography: demonic presences that 'knew I was coming and were waiting for me' in a Texas town; A promise of a FUTURE greeting ('they would all be there to greet me when it was time') rather than an arrival; A single welcomer or a disembodied welcoming voice, where the claim is specifically about an assembled group.

places.name: Seeing in Every Direction at Once
places.description: Repeatedly and independently described: vision stops being a cone in front of the face. Experiencers see behind and above and below simultaneously, without turning a head they no longer have, and often notice this before they notice anything else. Several use the same number - 360 degrees - without prompting, and some add that it was 'more than that'.

aliases.note: the commonest phrasing, used spontaneously

aliases.term: seeing in every direction at once

aliases.note: some say awareness rather than sight

sensory: no head-turning required; the view simply includes everything
often paired with seeing through walls or into the next room
often paired with feeling what other people in the building feel
noticed as strange before the person realises they have died

quotes.text: I have 360-degree vision. Like, I can see everything around me, behind me, below me, above me.
quotes.speaker: Anna Lee Stone

quotes.text: I was so aware that I could see 360 degrees without even turning my head.
quotes.speaker: Sharon Milliman

quotes.text: I could see in every direction at once with a panoramic 360° vision.
quotes.speaker: Nicole Dron

quotes.text: I could see all around me in 360 degrees, but a lot more than that.
quotes.speaker: Daniel Berdichevsky

quotes.text: it's almost like you can see 360 degrees around you
quotes.speaker: Randy Schiefer

places.notes: MORE common in well-evidenced accounts (3.29% -> 6.22% at cv>=18, easing to 4.42% at cv>=23 where n=181 makes the estimate noisy). The catalogued map has the ceiling vantage and looking down, but not the geometry of the seeing itself. Main false positive: 360 joules on a defibrillator. Audit found false positives of the form: '360' in ordinary use: giant photographs placed 360 around a courtroom; '360-degree viewpoint' as a metaphor for perspective-taking (walking in another's shoes; being poor and being rich); Generalised teaching that 'when we are out of our bodies we have that 360 degree perspective' — meaning complete understanding, not literal vision; Light 'spreading out in all directions' — a description of the light's extent, not of an omnidirectional visual field (2 near-duplicate passages); A 360-degree vision event that happened while driving a car, days after a funeral — an after-death-communication, not the NDE.

places.name: The Garden
places.description: A cultivated, tended place rather than wild landscape: flowers in beds, pavers and paving stones, arbours, a stone archway to enter through, sometimes a fence or gate around it. It is very often the first thing seen on arrival, and it is where deceased relatives are waiting. What makes it a place rather than scenery is that the plants are conscious - flowers greet the visitor by name, a sunflower speaks, the grass is aware of being walked on.

aliases.note: by far the most common phrasing
spoken as a known destination: 'everybody talks about the garden'
picket fence, rose arbour, golden light from the windows of the house behind
used as comparison, sometimes as the place one is expelled FROM on return
used by congenitally blind experiencers who stress it was 'a place full of light'
recurring comparison
one experiencer's own name for it

sensory: a stone archway as the entrance
pavers and paving stones between the beds
flowers with colours that do not exist here, in constant motion
flowers that talk: 'Hi, how are you? We're so happy you're here'
birds singing and water running somewhere just out of sight
the air crisp and sweet, like the most beautiful spring day
pagoda-like structures made of clear glowing crystal that are actually beds
paths and walkways running through it

quotes.text: If you can picture the most perfect English garden, perfectly manicured, perfect grass, trees, flowers, I mean, absolutely gorgeous.
quotes.speaker: John J. Davis

quotes.text: And at the end of the clouds, there was a magnificent garden.
quotes.speaker: Sharon Milliman

quotes.text: they led me out of the clouds into a beautiful garden that was to the left of a huge glorious city
quotes.speaker: Sharron

quotes.text: I entered through this stone archway, and it was just a beautiful garden in there.
quotes.speaker: Bill

quotes.text: I emerged at the entrance of a beautiful garden at the center of which was a hall, open with pillars

places.notes: Overlaps the natural-landscape region; kept here because the corpus consistently frames it as designed - entrances, paths, pavers, a hall at its centre, a city to one side. Precision loss is mostly earthly gardening biography and speakers listing the garden as an expectation they did NOT get. Audit found false positives of the form: Garden as metaphor: 'the Earth is a giant garden and we all live in it'; a prayer asking God to 'turn my soul into a garden'; a grief poem's 'you're in the kitchen, you're in the garden'; Ordinary gardening/meditation advice ('sit with a cup of coffee looking out into your garden'); Generalisation about what other people see ('some people see beautiful gardens with flowers, others go to the beach').

places.name: The demons
places.description: The inhabitants: creatures the experiencer recognises as wholly malevolent, usually multiple, usually physical enough to grab and tear. They are described as taking pleasure in the harm — laughing, competing over the soul — and as changing shape, sometimes wearing the faces of people the experiencer knows. Several stress that no light comes from them at all. This is a BEING, not a place, and should not be conflated with the realm it inhabits.

aliases.note: named as an individual in a subset; 'satan' appears as a raw entity identity 35 times in the corpus census
the commonest secular hedge for the same encounter

aliases.term: the beings that were once human
aliases.note: Howard Storm's reading of his attackers

sensory: emit no light; several say they are visible as absence
laughter, mockery, whispering
shapeshifting — into people the experiencer knows, then back
physical strength wildly out of proportion ('picked me up as if I was a pen')
in a few accounts they wear incongruous clothing (nurse uniforms, a trench coat, gold chains)

quotes.text: I had six demons on each side of me, literally shredding my arms off me.
quotes.speaker: Camille Hall

quotes.text: Demons absolutely hate us and there's no good in them and there's no light in them.
quotes.speaker: Kevin

quotes.text: it degenerated from kicking and punching to ripping, gouging, tearing, biting, clawing, which degenerated into invasive things.
quotes.speaker: Howard Storm

quotes.text: out of the ground were six or seven demons that crawled out of the ground and they were coming toward me
quotes.speaker: Shayla

places.notes: Essentially FLAT across strata (9.16% -> 9.39%). The corpus's own entity census is a useful cross-check and much stricter than my lexical regex: it codes demon/demonic/demonic_figure entities in only ~50 of 11,885 encounters (0.6%+0.1%+0.1%), against angel at 17.3% and religious_figure at 48.1%. The gap between 9.16% lexical and <1% coded is mostly people discussing demons rather than meeting them. Treat 9.16% as an upper bound on mention and the census as the lower bound on encounter. Audit found false positives of the form: Dominant class - Christian spiritual-warfare idiom applied to ordinary earthly life: demonic attack through drug use, demons entering via a phone or pornography, a 'demonic spirit' of depression and suicide, binding 'every demonic spirit of sickness' in a healing prayer (docs ebH-93btN7k, tNJ6i2Xhfqw, OupepTZCUZ0, _hD0PqeFjcw); Waking-life clairvoyance: 'there were demons all over my house', demons circling over a McDonald's (doc=_MvGphIRdGY); Metaphor: 'whatever the demons were that were in me' at a hockey bar, a father's 'few demons' meaning his addictions, 'the first layer of demons' meaning insomnia and negative self-talk (docs thHBBR7-Ve0, FF6WDR-fX1k, kPaNb0zeFc0); Explicit denial - 'I see all these things about, oh, I met the devil, or I went to hell. I don't believe in any of that' (doc=iAP38LkUxTU); The interviewer proposing 'demonic type?' and the experiencer rejecting it, saying they were children who existed in the absence of light (doc=yrHWBCYm9kw); Channel boilerplate: 'Do you think that it was a trick by Satan? Let me know in the comments' (doc=56FxiGCJGnY); Belief and upbringing statements about whether a devil exists (docs ENwjMmQLKlU, bjTcMA9r41U, Fc7kaWNIcRo, zHHbZTyIr_c, W4jDSfR6zIM, WalJw3rI9eo).

places.name: The Life You Agreed To
places.description: Not the life review of what you did, but the recovered memory of what you chose before you came: a plan, an agreement, sometimes a contract, made with guides or a council, including the choice of parents and of the hard parts. It is usually remembered as already-known rather than newly told, and it reframes the life just reviewed as something volunteered for.

aliases.note: often 'they helped me plan this life'

aliases.term: I chose this life / I chose my parents

sensory: remembered rather than learned - 'I recalled'
guides sent in to argue you out of taking on too much
the choice of parents and of specific hardships
arrives adjacent to the life review and reframes it

quotes.text: he told me that I had promised to give birth to him before I was born, that we had planned this together
quotes.speaker: Bonni Burrows

quotes.text: then I recalled the choices I made pre-birth, which sort of solidified
quotes.speaker: Jayne Smith

quotes.text: I just had this feeling that they had helped me plan this life that I was living.
quotes.speaker: Karen Thomas

quotes.text: I had some beautiful friendships and it seemed like soul contracts with certain people.
quotes.speaker: Tricia Barker

quotes.text: I actually have some pre-birth memories.
quotes.speaker: Robert Aho

places.notes: Slightly LESS common in the well-evidenced strata (6.53% -> 5.52%; lowest at cv>=18). The catalogued map covers the life review, the preview and the veil of forgetting, but not the pre-birth agreement that several experiencers say the veil was drawn over. A looser pattern including 'before I was born' unqualified reaches 12.89% but is dominated by biographical use ('my grandfather died before I was born'). Audit found false positives of the form: Host intros and channel boilerplate built on the phrase 'pre-birth memories' ('Max has both pre-birth memories and multiple near-death experiences') — 4 passages; Standalone pre-birth-memory guests who never describe an NDE; the plan is remembered from childhood, not from dying; 'Soul contract' as an everyday spiritual belief: contracts with pets, contracts reported by astrologers, contracts figured out years later in therapy; Interviewer questions ('have you figured out your soul contract with him?'); A researcher summarising what experiencers in general report about soul contracts.

places.name: Belonging — And Not Belonging Here
places.description: The other side of home: the conviction that one belongs there, coupled — often in the same breath — with the conviction that one does not belong on earth. Experiencers describe earthly life afterwards as an exile, a posting, a charter trip, a deportation. Some report the not-belonging as a lifelong condition that predated the experience and was only explained by it.

aliases.note: the inverse, reported after return

aliases.term: I'm on a charter trip down here

aliases.note: one experiencer's word for embodied life

sensory: earth afterwards described as an island, a posting, a base camp
the belonging is felt toward beings never met in this life
reported as relief from a lifelong low-grade misfit feeling

quotes.text: It was, it was being home. This is where I fit. This is where I belong. This is where I was totally loved.
quotes.speaker: Dr. Yvonne Kason

quotes.text: I felt that this is my true home and I belonged there. My presence on Earth looked like a deportation to a stranger, an isolated island that was incompatible and unpleasant.
I belonged to that place ... I belonged. I was happy to be there.
quotes.speaker: Míriam Lima

quotes.text: I feel that I'm on a charter trip down here and that I belong to the spiritual world.
quotes.speaker: Anni

quotes.text: This is where I belonged. I felt that this was really, um, home to me in many ways.
quotes.speaker: Rosemary Thornton

places.notes: This is the only entry in my set that DECLINES with evidential quality (3.42% overall -> 2.49% at cvNDE>=18 -> 2.21% at cvNDE>=23). The likely reason is that belonging language is heavily concentrated in long reflective interviews and post-hoc philosophy, which are more common in the lower-cvNDE strata; the strongest veridical accounts are shorter and more event-focused. Worth flagging honestly rather than smoothing over. Audit found false positives of the form: Ordinary social belonging: not fitting in at school/neighbourhood, 'I don't belong here' said at an IANDS meeting; Interviewer-supplied wording: two passages where 'sense of belonging' appears only in the question and the answer describes joy/well-being instead; Book-plug and facilitator commentary about shared-death work giving people 'a sense of belonging'; Opposite sense of the same phrase: 'I don't belong here' spoken IN heaven out of unworthiness (he's made a terrible mistake), which is the inverse of earth-exile; Belonging in hell ('this is where I belonged, this is what I deserved') — same word, different place.

places.name: Robed figures
places.description: Beings identified chiefly by their clothing: white robes, brown robes with golden belts, tunics of loose-weave sack material, robes of many colours, dark hooded robes. Some are named (angels, Jesus), many are not — 'a strange robe figure who led me down a path'. The robe is often the only detail given, and several experiencers say the faces were deliberately indistinct or grey: 'our faces don't matter, it's our presence'.
sensory: white, but also brown with golden belts, and 'robes of many colours'
light blue sashes
dark robes with dark hoods — smiling, giggling, bouncing (not menacing)
faces grey or featureless, neither male nor female
the robes are said to be worn because they are the most comfortable, not required

quotes.text: I was now able to see two rows of hooded beings in long robes, similar to monks, lined up in front of me.
They had brown robes on and they had golden belts around their waist, and they introduced themselves as my ministering angels
quotes.speaker: Betty Eadie

quotes.text: I was greeted by a strange robe figure who led me down a path to the field.
quotes.speaker: Muriel

quotes.text: They were in white robes, their faces kind of looked like gray, like they weren't male or female
quotes.speaker: Gary Wimmer

quotes.text: They had dark robes and dark hoods, and they were right in front of me. And they were smiling and giggling
quotes.speaker: Bill Leston

places.notes: Rises steadily with evidential strength (4.19% -> 7.18%). Note the corpus contradicts the stock iconography twice over: hooded figures are cheerful rather than sinister, and at least one experiencer complains that dramatised reconstructions with robes and 'little tiny wings' are cheesy. Audit found false positives of the form: MECHANICAL BUG, the biggest single class: 'robe' is matching as a substring inside ordinary words — 'Robert' in a guest bio, 'probe' in 'wanted to put the probe in' (vWfNxiqbYLU, VwjP938ypq0, and probably 0qJESVJi3tw and X312rYYRRxA, where no garment appears anywhere in the passage). Word boundaries alone would remove roughly a fifth of the matches; third-party retellings — a study of Indian NDErs cited from a book; a commentator narrating blind Brad's NDE; a man relaying his wife's experience (gtvHYeQD4hg, GywGA-9TEDk, 9gMYyRcE6DA); expectation rather than perception — 'I was expecting a man in a white robe on a golden throne to greet me', followed by blackness (qwB2Icgkshc); explicit absence — 'there wasn't any anthropomorphic figures or people in robes' (8KPRmzi2Ytg); production talk about avoiding cheesy reenactments with 'crazy people standing around in robes' (iDkhDPzMjYI); a black hooded jacket left beside a river in a dream (bYcuYsKiO8Q).

places.name: Hell
places.description: A place experiencers name outright as hell: somewhere they were taken, thrown or dragged rather than travelled to willingly. It is described as a location with an interior — realms or levels within it, a floor, gates, an edge — and as permanent: the dominant terror is not the pain but the certainty of never leaving. Many say the word only reluctantly, and several insist the place they saw was not the hell they had been taught.

aliases.note: by far the most common name; used by both believers and people who say they never believed in it
Camille Hall: 'I went into three dark realms'; hell as a series of chambers, each worse
the researcher/interviewer register, also adopted by experiencers who reject the theology
usually the threshold seen from outside, not entered
named as one of the six realms alongside the hungry ghost realm

aliases.term: a place where God is not
aliases.note: the absence of God is offered as the definition of the place more often than fire is
some use this as a synonym for hell, others as the space between hell's chambers

sensory: no light of its own; what light there is comes from fire and is orange or reddish
black gates and black cells (lpZW9u8HK2A)
a floor of rock, soot in the air
time that will not end — 'forever and ever and ever'
the knowledge, arriving without being told, that you belong there

quotes.text: during that 10 minutes I went to hell and I remember enough to tell you that it was very very dark that I couldn't see my hand in front of my face
quotes.speaker: Shayla

quotes.text: I knew being dragged to hell by these demons that I deserved it.
quotes.speaker: Camille Hall

quotes.text: So I saw hell, and, uh, and the demons, and I knew I was going to be there forever.
quotes.speaker: Steve Kang

quotes.text: And I heard others screaming, "Oh no," in the distance, and, and I knew I was in hell.
quotes.speaker: Kat Duggar

quotes.text: Hell is a manner of suffering, and I was in hell long before I took my life.
quotes.speaker: Angie Fenimore

places.notes: MORE common among the best-evidenced accounts, and monotonically so: 6.49% overall -> 7.46% at cv>=18 -> 8.29% at cv>=23. That runs against the assumption that hellish reports are an artifact of weak accounts. Precision is the main caveat: roughly 45% of matches are theology, interviewer framing, or third-party retelling ('a man I talked to says he went to hell') rather than the speaker's own experience. The corpus-level structured coder puts journey_nde_type=distressing at 3.9% (243/6176) and hellish_realm in 4.4% of sequenced journeys — my 6.49% is the looser lexical upper bound on the same phenomenon. Note also that many experiencers volunteer the word only to reject it: 'there is no hell' is itself a recurring statement. Audit found false positives of the form: Idiomatic hell: 'everything went to hell', 'we've been to hell and back', slaughterhouse footage as 'hell on earth', domestic violence as 'I was in hell'; Doctrinal exposition with no experience attached — the six Buddhist realms, Calvinist eternal torment; Experiencers arguing hell does NOT exist and explaining away other people's hellish NDEs (3 passages); Host bio intros and interviewer lines ('you called out to Jesus from the pit of hell', plus a book plug); Someone else's NDE reported second-hand ('another person I spoke with told me she went to hell'); Being told online that you were in hell.

places.name: The Mist, the Fog, the Grey
places.description: A soft, weatherlike medium reported instead of, or in the middle of, the passage: white mist you move through, a pea-soup fog that is thick but actively dancing rather than falling, a grey that is described in flatly domestic terms — 'a wet beach sand grey'. It obscures where you are going and is often the thing you must cross before somewhere becomes visible. It also appears at boundaries: mist covering a doorway, mist clearing to reveal grass.

aliases.note: 'a pea soup fog... very thick, but it was actively, like, dancing around me'
the distressing inversion, preceding total darkness

sensory: thick as pea soup yet actively dancing rather than settling
white, pastel-coloured, or 'a wet beach sand grey'
clears from the ground upward to reveal grass
shot through with golden light in the brighter versions
black in the distressing versions, arriving like a covering

quotes.text: I found myself standing in a kind of gray mist, and then I knew. I knew that I had died.
quotes.speaker: Jayne Willey Smith

quotes.text: So as I'm moving through this white mist
I had this incredible experience of of moving up into a misty sort of area.
quotes.speaker: Barbara Whitfield

quotes.text: I still don't know whether to call it a door or a portal. It's covered in mist
quotes.speaker: Jim Woodford

quotes.text: this time back into this fog stage where you close my eyes and I open up and I'm in a different location again
quotes.speaker: Linda Cramer

places.notes: Essentially FLAT across strata (4.23% all, 4.70% cv>=18, 4.42% cv>=23). Precision is limited by medical haze ('I was still in a haze when I woke up') and by fog used as a metaphor for depression or confusion, both targeted by the negative_regex. Included despite modest precision because it is a genuinely distinct transitional medium, repeatedly volunteered by people who explicitly deny a tunnel, and because it recurs at the border to the realms rather than only at the start. Audit found false positives of the form: 'Haze' as metaphor: 'a red haze of pain' at the office (2 near-duplicate passages), 'the details were very hazy', 'like you're in a haze'; 'Foggy lens' as a metaphor for pre-NDE perception; Real weather: fog on the New York Thruway before the crash; and one simile that explicitly denies the medium ('it was all made of light instead of fog'); 'Gray space' as an emotional/energetic state in coaching-style advice; A misty appearance attributed to a BEING (a transparent, misty-cloud angel) rather than to the surrounding medium.

places.name: Being Completely Known
places.description: Alongside the absence of judgment sits its precondition: the light already knows everything about you, including things you have told nobody. Experiencers describe being read completely — 'it knew everything about me, my beliefs, what I loved, who I was' — and, crucially, being fine with it. The recurring formula is 'there was nothing to hide' paired with the discovery that total exposure and total acceptance arrive together.

aliases.term: it knew me and I knew it
known better than my family, or even me

aliases.note: used of Jesus

aliases.term: we know each other. It knows me. I know it.
it was all there on display

sensory: a sense of being read or examined without hostility
recognition running both ways — the experiencer feels they know the light too, and always have
no need to speak: the knowing precedes any communication
'tailoring itself to me like a custom suit'

quotes.text: when he looked into my eyes, he knew everything about me. And he loved me anyway.
quotes.speaker: Santosh

quotes.text: it knew everything about me, my beliefs, what I loved, who I was, how I was as a person, and that was all okay.
quotes.speaker: Lewis Brown Griggs

quotes.text: It was as if this being had known me for my entire life, better than my family, or even me.
quotes.speaker: Lee

quotes.text: There were no there was nothing to hide. It knew everything.
quotes.speaker: Kenneth Leth

quotes.text: And, and he knew me, and I knew him.
quotes.speaker: Heather Vandermeyden

places.notes: Mixed across strata — higher at cv>=13 (7.24%) and cv>=18 (5.94%) than overall (5.46%), but sharply lower at cv>=23 (2.76%, only 5 of 181 docs, so the cv23 figure is noisy). The '(saw|knew|understood) everything about' arm catches biographical uses ('he knew everything about astronomy'). Audit found false positives of the form: Direction reversal — the dominant failure.
