Experiencers describe a place where they had never existed and would not exist, where God could not reach because God did not know it was there. It is reported as distinct from the peaceful void: the peaceful void feels full, this one feels cancelled.

aliases.note: the voice in Lorraine Kane's account offering annihilation as the alternative to God

sensory: no sound, no light, no direction, no body
the loss of self as the specific terror, distinct from loss of surroundings
sometimes preceded by a voice asserting that nothing exists
reported as unbearable by some and as the most peaceful state possible by others

quotes.text: It is a bottomless abyss where there's no end to it. It is like a giant vortex of nothingness that if a person would go in there, they'd be super conscious, conscious
quotes.speaker: Mickey Robinson

quotes.text: It felt as if it went forever, and it felt it was nothingness
quotes.speaker: C. Thomas Perry

quotes.text: I felt completely, uh, completely like I never existed
quotes.speaker: Kat Duggar

quotes.text: There is no God, and you're going to go to the ground, and maggots are going to eat your body.
quotes.speaker: Lorraine Kane

places.notes: Roughly FLAT to slightly lower with evidential strength (7.79% -> 6.08% at cv>=23). Precision is the weakest in my set at ~0.35 and I want to be blunt about why: 'nothingness' is used at least as often in a positive, non-dual, Buddhist-adjacent register ('the state of non-self, or the state of nothingness') as it is in a terrified one, and the two are lexically indistinguishable without reading the surrounding paragraph. The distressing sense — annihilation of the self as a horror — is real and vivid but is a minority of these matches. Downstream correction is essential here. Audit found false positives of the form: The claim explicitly excludes the peaceful/full void, but that is what most of the on-topic matches actually describe — 'nothingness, but it was everything all at the same time', 'the nothingness was not empty, it was completely filled with the presence of the living God', 'limbo state of nothingness and just calm, peace, serenity' (P9, P10, P11, P15, P16, P17, P22). Counting those as hits would raise precision to 11/24 = 0.46, but they are a different place sharing a word.; Ordinary idiom: 'I got annihilated by an 18-wheeler', 'I pounded it into oblivion', 'it falls into oblivion' as a figure of speech for being forgotten (P1, P6, P12).; 'Cease to exist' used about the Soviet Union, the human species, the planet, and as generic reassurance that souls are eternal (P13, P19, P20, P21, P23).; Generic speculation about what people fear about death (P5); a simile for being unseen during an OBE, 'as if I had ceased to exist' (P7); a metaphor inside a healing vision, 'vanished into nothingness' (P4); a split-second blackout on collapsing (P14); and a passage that DENIES annihilation, 'I was not annihilated' (P18)..

places.name: Travelling at Impossible Speed
places.description: Whatever the passage is made of, the movement through it is fast beyond reference. People reach for the fastest thing they know: warp nine, the speed of light, a rocket, being flung, a high rate of speed. The speed itself is sometimes the frightening part even when everything else is peaceful, and a few report deceleration at the end as a distinct, noticeable event. Others insist that speed is meaningless there because there was no distance.

aliases.term: at a high rate of speed

aliases.note: Star Trek reference volunteered by several

aliases.term: a tremendously, horrifically rapid rate of speed
like a bullet going through this tunnel

sensory: colours and lights whizzing by and through the traveller
the stomach-drop of a roller coaster
a felt deceleration near the end, before arrival
fear of the speed even inside an otherwise peaceful passage
the paradox that speed felt meaningless where there was no distance

quotes.text: I feel like I'm going through it at warp speed, but it doesn't even make sense because how can I be going fast when it's kind of not physical?
quotes.speaker: Bri Lafferty

quotes.text: And it went at a tremendously, horrifically rapid rate of speed.
quotes.speaker: Vicky Noratuk

quotes.text: I went into a deep dark velvet tunnel at a high rate of speed.
quotes.speaker: Lura Ketchledge

quotes.text: the next thing I felt was being propelled at an incredible speed, a speed that is beyond our comprehension here
quotes.speaker: Alanis Marina

quotes.text: In the next moment, I was floating at full speed through an absolutely dark tunnel, in which there were some gleams
quotes.speaker: Ekaterina A

places.notes: Essentially FLAT to slightly weaker across strata (2.20% all, 1.38% at cv>=18, 2.76% at cv>=23 on only 5 docs) — speed language does not co-vary with evidential quality. I deliberately chose a tight regex: a looser speed pattern reaches 10.9% of docs but its precision collapsed to about 0.4 in sampling, mostly on astronomy digressions about the speed of light and on people typing or driving fast. The tight version at 2.20% is an undercount of a genuinely common feature — treat it as a lower bound. Audit found false positives of the form: Speed of perception rather than speed of travel: life-review scenes 'moving at the speed of light' like a video screen, history absorbed 'at an astonishing speed', observations 'happening at such an incredible rate of speed' (3 passages). Same words, different phenomenon.; Ordinary-life and physical speed: a brain tumour 'growing at a breakneck speed', a plane hitting a tree 'at a tremendous rate of speed'.; Channel boilerplate: a host reading listener comments and quoting a physicist on travelling at the speed of light.; Metaphorical propulsion into a new phase of life: 'suddenly I was propelled at a rapid speed into those experiences'.; Abstract reflection with no described passage: 'I was just picking up on what it's like to travel at the speed of light'..

places.name: The Portal, the Doorway, the Opening
places.description: Not a tunnel but an aperture: something opens and you go through it. It is described as a portal, an opening, an entrance, a door hanging in space, a hole in the sky, or an interdimensional passage with no earthly direction — 'it wasn't up or down'. Some pass through instantly; some stand at the edge and decide; at least one declines and watches it close. Where the tunnel implies travel, the portal implies a single step across.

aliases.note: increasingly the preferred word in more recent accounts
'I still don't know whether to call it a door or a portal'
'amethyst purple, like a channel or a portal with sparkling lights'

sensory: opens and closes — several watch it seal behind them or shut when they refuse
colours: amethyst purple with sparkling lights; golden-white like the sun
covered or filled with mist so you cannot see what you are stepping onto
no orientation: 'it wasn't up or down'
a second, brighter portal sometimes opening beyond the first

quotes.text: finally there was a portal. I didn't see a tunnel, I saw a portal. And I went up to the portal and I could see through the entrance to the portal.
quotes.speaker: Kevin Jeffers

quotes.text: I found myself gliding through a portal, an interdimensional passage that defied Earthly directions.
It was amethyst purple, like a channel or a portal with sparkling lights.
quotes.speaker: Michele A. Livingston

quotes.text: I started to go up into the sky and into this portal, this energy, this vortex, this tunnel of some sort.
quotes.speaker: Philip Siracusa

quotes.text: I mostly remember coming, just coming through this open portal.
quotes.speaker: Catherine

places.notes: One of the few items in this region that is LESS common among strongly-evidenced accounts: 2.36% overall against 1.87% at cv>=13 and 2.21% at cv>=18/23. 'Portal' reads as a more recently acquired, more interpretive word than 'tunnel', and the bare term (8.76% of docs) is heavily used in metaphysical framing rather than in narration of the experience — which is why I constrained it to motion-through phrasing. The door/doorway variant could not be measured cleanly: '(through/into) a door' matches 18.35% of docs but is almost all front doors, hospital doors and knocking. Audit found false positives of the form: Post-NDE psychic/after-effect uses: 'it opened a portal' for mediumship, astral projection, meditation and time-slip experiences (5 passages) - the portal is a metaphor for a new ability, not a perceived aperture.; Haunted-house occult sense: a Ouija board 'opened a portal in the house' that dark entities came through - ordinary life, not the NDE.; Word-sense collisions: 'the portal of the iron lung' (a medical viewing window) and 'I gave an interview to a portal about NDEs' (a news website).; Relayed account: the speaker describing her mother's crossing through an amethyst portal, not her own experience.; Negated / merely-hypothetical references: 'maybe I didn't go through this portal, probably not', 'I think I would have crossed that portal... so I didn't go through the portal'..

places.name: Shadow figures
places.description: Dark human-shaped presences with no features, seen at the edge of the experience: sometimes clustered, sometimes a single tall silhouette. Distinct from demons in that they are usually silent and do not attack — the distress comes from being watched, followed, or clung to. Notably, this figure is NOT always malevolent in the corpus: a substantial minority recognise the silhouette as a deceased relative.

aliases.note: Mellen-Thomas Benedict: sticky, abrasive, holding on

sensory: featureless — no face, or eyes where eyes 'should be'
stickiness or abrasiveness on contact
abnormal height (8-12 feet in several accounts)
coldness radiating from them
movement without walking

quotes.text: I saw a shadow figure, like a silhouette of a man in a trench coat or a day coat, a long day coat. And immediately said, oh, that's, that's my grandpa Joe
quotes.speaker: Zach Tevcar

quotes.text: It was a deep forest of tangled shadows that were grabbing and trying to hold me.
quotes.speaker: Mellen-Thomas Benedict

quotes.text: I saw two very big black deep eyes or where eyes should be
quotes.speaker: Jeff Roods

quotes.text: I was fighting with this dark forces. That was a dark figure.
quotes.speaker: Viktor Horth

places.notes: LESS common in the strongest stratum (2.33% -> 1.66% at cv>=23). Precision for DISTRESSING shadow figures is only ~0.45 and the reason is interesting rather than merely technical: in this corpus a 'shadow figure' is about as likely to be a welcoming dead relative seen against the tunnel light as it is to be a threat — Zach Tavcar (three separate recordings, cv up to 23) recognises his grandfather as 'a shadow figure of a man in a trench coat'. The corpus entity census codes shadow_figure at 1.2% of encounters, which is the better estimate of the neutral category; the distressing subset is smaller still. Audit found false positives of the form: Ordinary-life shadow sightings unconnected to any near-death episode — sleep paralysis from age five, a bedroom entity the husband also sees, a haunted house, a wife glimpsing a figure after a cruise, ongoing post-NDE sightings of three-foot shadow beings (6 passages, the dominant error class); Hooded figures that are luminous, not dark — Christ with wounds, and 'a hooded figure that had only light for a face'; General mediumship commentary about apparitions and 'the shadow people' with no scene attached; Shadow people inside a prophetic vision of earthly crowds — perceived during the experience but not the silhouette at the edge of it.

places.name: you are your own judge
places.description: Where judgement does occur in the review, experiencers overwhelmingly report that they are the ones doing it. The being beside them stays neutral or loving while they themselves recoil, feel shame, and pass sentence. Several say plainly that they were far harsher than anyone else could have been, and one says he judged himself guilty not against other people but against the purity of the love that was holding him. Some are told afterwards that their verdict was their own and not shared.

aliases.term: I was the one doing the judging
the only one judging me is me
the judgment is our judgment, not God holding trial on us
your judgment of it, not ours

sensory: shame and guilt arising in a place where nothing shames you
measuring yourself not against other people but against the love present
the reviewer gently disputing the verdict you have just passed
in one account the elders laughing kindly whenever the experiencer condemned herself

quotes.text: There was no judgment day for me. I judged myself and my shame in comparison to this beneficent, benevolent being of goodness that only wanted love for me.
quotes.speaker: Peter Pagor

quotes.text: I was not judged on the bad and the good, but I, but I judged myself on the bad and the good. And, you know, as individuals, we're harder on ourselves than anybody else could be on us.
quotes.speaker: Scott Drummond

quotes.text: But he wasn't judging me. I was judging me. And, uh, the one thing I saw and felt was if I hurt someone, if my words hurt someone, I felt what they felt.
quotes.speaker: Heidi Barr

quotes.text: I was there with my guide, watching everything that I'd ever done and seeing the ripple effects throughout all the people around me. And I was the one doing the judging.
quotes.speaker: Nancy Rynes

places.notes: Rises steadily with evidential strength (2.12% all to 3.31% at cv>=23), the clearest positive gradient of the judgement cluster. Some false positives are ordinary biographical self-criticism ('I judged myself for that') from depression narratives outside the NDE. Audit found false positives of the form: Ordinary-life self-criticism, before or after the NDE: 'I was judging myself, how I sounded talking about such things', 'I had spent my whole life criticizing myself, judging myself', 'I learned to stop judging other people, then I could stop judging myself' (4 passages).; Explicit negations of self-judgement: 'no thought, no being, no human, not even myself judging myself' and 'I didn't judge myself, and nobody else around me judged me either'.; Post-NDE prayer/meditation realisation rather than the review itself.; Hedged, interviewer-supplied answer: 'they didn't judge me on anything, I could have been judging myself there'..

places.name: the instant
places.description: The temporal signature of the review: it contains a whole life and takes no time. Experiencers describe birth to death presented simultaneously rather than in sequence, and struggle openly with the contradiction - 'it lasted an eternity', 'it was over like that', 'a blink of an eye which seemed like it went on for a long time'. Some describe it as more spatial than sequential, a single room in which every part of a life is visible at once and the connections between them can be seen. Several narrate it linearly only because language forces them to.

aliases.note: Eben Alexander's term for the non-sequential temporal order

sensory: birth, death and everything between present at once
a large disorganised room in which all the parts of a life can be seen connected
an eternity that is also over in a blink
the narrator apologising for telling it in a linear order

quotes.text: The entire review appeared to last for only a split second because all the events of my entire life were shown to me simultaneously
quotes.speaker: Malcolm Miller

quotes.text: I had an instantaneous flash of life review. It felt more spatial than sequential.
when people, for example, describe life reviews, you know, birth, death, everything in between appearing to you simultaneously
I became myself again in all of those circumstances. I relived them instantaneously.
quotes.speaker: Karen Thomas

places.notes: Under-counted: the corpus expresses this constantly with idiosyncratic phrasing ('a moment of no time', 'time meant nothing') that no fixed regex catches. The structured coder marks time_distortion at 58.8% overall, so this lexical measure is a small slice of a very large phenomenon. Audit found false positives of the form: 'Simultaneously' used for perspective simultaneity rather than temporal simultaneity — being in three viewpoints at once, feeling the victim's pain alongside one's own. These are real and vivid but they belong to the 'inside the other person' node, not to the claim that a whole life takes no time (4 passages); Essayistic musing about time, Anita Moorjani and Raymond Moody, with no experience being reported; Ordinary 'split second' usage — taking a split second to answer a being, hedged speculation that 'maybe you have a week's worth of experience in a split second'; A simultaneous panoramic display the experiencer explicitly says was NOT a life review (120 videos of her family's future); A review explicitly described as a sequential black-and-white movie, matched only on a stray 'all at once'.

places.name: The Throne Room
places.description: A chamber containing a seat of authority. Reports split sharply: a minority describe arriving at a real room - steps up to a platform, a huge throne, sometimes two identical white thrones cut from marble, translucent carved artwork like emeralds and diamonds set into the tiles - while a large number invoke the throne only to deny it ('it was not an old man with a beard on a throne judging me'). Both usages are counted here because both are the corpus reasoning about the same structure.

aliases.term: a big chair like a king
aliases.note: a small child's wording, corrected to 'throne' by the adult interviewer
cut from pure white marble, square and angular

sensory: three steps up to a platform, throne on the third step
thrones square and angular, cut from pure white marble
carved translucent artwork in every floor tile, like emeralds and diamonds
a river running out from under the chair, and inside it stars and galaxies instead of water
the viewer shielded from the face of whoever sits there

quotes.text: In what seemed like a nanosecond, I was at the opening of a huge throne room. The doors opened, and I was told to enter.
quotes.speaker: Richard T

quotes.text: what I now know was the throne room that I got to see at this point
quotes.speaker: Joe Joe

quotes.text: There I saw three steps and on the third step I saw there was a huge throne
quotes.speaker: Santosh Acci

quotes.text: I looked up and I saw two men sitting on big white thrones.
quotes.speaker: Kelly DiGiacomo

places.notes: Roughly half the matches are the negation formula ('God was NOT an old man on a throne'), which is itself one of the most stereotyped sentences in the whole corpus. Slightly LESS common among the best-evidenced accounts. Use negative_regex to isolate the affirmative subset. Audit found false positives of the form: Scripture and sermon: Isaiah 6 at the throne, Daniel's Ancient of Days on a throne of fire, Jacob's ladder cosmology, a preacher's set-piece about Jesus getting off the throne and handing over his crown, and a hymn lyric about the river that flows from the throne of God (5 passages); 'Going to the throne room' as a metaphor for praying directly to God ('why not go right to the top'); Interviewer framing ('you were ushered eventually into the throne room of God, so we have a lot to look forward to'); Visions outside the NDE — a church-meeting vision at age 14, a dream of a small throne with Satan on it; Note on scoring: the claim deliberately counts denials ('not an old man on a throne'), so I counted denials as true when an experiencer was reasoning from their own encounter, and false when the denial was mere lifelong belief. Under a stricter reading that admits only perceived thrones, precision falls to 0.46.

places.name: Colors Inside the White
places.description: A recurring surprise: the light looks white, but when experiencers look further into it they find colours — the rainbow spectrum plus colours they say do not exist here and cannot be named. The image reached for again and again is a prism: white light containing all colours, refracting. Several artists in the corpus report being unable to reproduce these colours afterwards.

aliases.term: rays of magnificent colors coming out of it
like the inside of a diamond
millions of blues, millions of greens

sensory: the colours are FELT as much as seen — 'I could feel and sense the rays'
colours outside the human gamut, reported as unnameable
diamond and prism imagery: facets, refraction, sparkle
iridescence that moves, compared to the Aurora Borealis
purples, aquas and magentas named more often than reds

quotes.text: It's like a waterfall of light, and it has 10 zillion colors in it of every hue and tone, and all these colors, and they're all white, and they're all colored all at the same time.
quotes.speaker: Peter Panagore

quotes.text: these other colors started coming out of this light
quotes.speaker: Darrin J. Shinabarger

quotes.text: even though the light seemed to be white, I could feel and sense the rays of magnificent colors coming out of it
quotes.speaker: Janet Tarantino

quotes.text: Everything was white, but I described the experience as being inside a prism.
quotes.speaker: Peter Bard

places.notes: Clearly MORE common among better-evidenced accounts — 2.30% all, 3.31% at cv>=18, 3.87% at cv>=23. Some matches describe colours of the landscape or of beings rather than colours within the light itself. Audit found false positives of the form: The prism used as a teaching metaphor rather than a description — white light refracting into colours as an analogy for individual souls, or for personal healing frequencies. This is the main recurring junk and it reads almost identically to the real thing (3 passages); Rainbow-coloured lights that are not the white light: a chakra column seen during an out-of-body view of one's own body (twice, same account), a refracted rainbow floor; Host boilerplate ('some people go through the tunnel and see rainbows and, I almost said unicorns'); Colour talk about a different object entirely — the planet's coloured vortices seen from outside.

places.name: Being trapped
places.description: The signature inner condition of the region, and the one experiencers say was worse than pain: the certainty that there is no exit and no end. It shows up as physical immobility (muscles clenched, feet fixed, tied down), as spatial enclosure (walls you cannot see closing in), and as temporal enclosure — the arriving knowledge, unspoken and immediate, that this is now permanent.

aliases.term: I would never get out of this place

sensory: muscles clenched, body rigid
feet fixed to a spot, invisible walls at arm's length
cells, gates, ropes, chains in a minority of accounts
the knowledge of permanence arriving without being spoken
time reported as dilating — 'in hell it seemed like it was eternal'

quotes.text: I'm in this like horrible place, and my sense was, is that I was stuck there forever and ever and ever and ever, time without end, with all these other miserable people.
quotes.speaker: Howard Storm

quotes.text: I knew I was never going to get out of this place. I'm going to be here forever and ever and ever.
quotes.speaker: Steve Kang

quotes.text: And I'm just stuck there. It was like my body, my muscles were just, my body was like clenched up.
quotes.speaker: Jordan

quotes.text: it seems like there's walls around you because you can't move your feet, nothing.
quotes.speaker: Gisely

quotes.text: left me on the ground of that place, unable to move
quotes.speaker: Howard Storm

places.notes: LESS common in the better-evidenced strata (2.30% -> 1.38% at cv>=18). Bare /trapped|stuck|couldn't move/ matches 44.53% of the corpus — overwhelmingly people trapped in wreckage, under water, or on a ventilator — so this regex demands otherworld context and still only reaches ~0.5 precision. A separate probe for cells/cages/chains in hellish context reached only 0.83% of docs at roughly 0.2 precision, so I did not promote it to its own place; the vocabulary exists (black gates, black cells, holes in the mountain, a rope burnt to the bone) but is too rare and too lexically fragile to measure cleanly. Audit found false positives of the form: Ordinary-life physical entrapment: pinned under a waterfall, held captive by kidnappers, stuck in the muck under a dock, unable to get up off the bedroom floor (5 passages).; Medical setting: intubated and unable to move hands or feet in ICU; permanent paralysis from a spinal abscess.; Metaphor and general teaching: 'paralyzed by fear', 'we paralyze ourselves with guilt' in a talk about grief.; Biography: a job the speaker felt she could not leave for ten years.; Simile rather than place: 'my life review almost felt like I was stuck in hell... there is no such thing'.; Inverse of the claim: 'I couldn't get out of there fast enough' counted as trapped when the speaker in fact left freely; that passage also runs into channel boilerplate..

places.name: The Hills and the Distant Mountains
places.description: The country has depth: a slope or hillside you climb, and beyond it mountains standing on the horizon. The hill is usually climbed with a guide and the scene changes completely at the crest. The mountains are almost always at a distance and almost never reached — several people are told explicitly that going over the mountains means staying. A few describe ranges vastly larger than any on earth.

aliases.note: the crest where the scenery changes
3.68% of accounts use 'the/a valley'

sensory: a rise you come up over, with an entirely new scene beyond
mountains far off, sometimes snowcapped, often purple or hazy
ranges described as many times larger than Everest
panoramic 360-degree seeing without turning the head
the mountains marked as a point of no return

quotes.text: Over in the far distance, I could see mountains that were 10 times the size of Everest, see buildings that were 10 times the size of what they're now building in Dubai.
quotes.speaker: Linda Cramer

quotes.text: it felt like I was out on a like a meadow on a hillside overlooking distant mountains and a valley
quotes.speaker: Nancy Rynes

quotes.text: you're going to follow this path to the mountains, and you will go over the mountains, and once you're over the mountains, you will stay.
quotes.speaker: Elizabeth Krohn

quotes.text: mountain ranges ten thousand times bigger than, um, Mount Everest
quotes.speaker: Dr. Linda Kramer

quotes.text: I come out onto a mountain ledge, and I'm overlooking the most beautiful, serene, three-tiered mountain meadow, earth-like, but not earth
quotes.speaker: Rodney Rieder

places.notes: Honest caveat: precision is only about 0.55 and this is the ONE feature in my region that DROPS at the highest evidential stratum (3.38% all, 5.01% cv>=13, 4.28% cv>=18, but only 1.10% cv>=23, n=2). Mountains are also a very common element of the earthly biography (hiking, skiing, car accidents on mountain roads, Himalayan travel), which drives most of the false positives. Treat the cv>=23 figure with caution given the small denominator (181 docs). Audit found false positives of the form: A vision seen during automatic writing rather than during an NDE ('while I was writing, I kept seeing this image in my mind's eye of these rolling hills'); Ordinary biography: driving home 'down this beautiful hilly country highway' before the cardiac event; A portal vision during meditation ('I got so excited... it poofed away... that's what my logo is').

places.name: Falling / being taken down
places.description: The transit into the dark places, and the single most consistent kinaesthetic in this whole region. It is almost never voluntary: people are thrown, dropped, sucked, pushed, or the floor simply goes. The speed is emphasised — wind, breathlessness, 'thousands of miles an hour' — and so is the absence of any bottom arriving. Where the classic NDE moves toward light, this movement is unmistakably downward.

aliases.term: the floor dropped out beneath me

aliases.note: Javier Gonzales: 'without my consent I was being pushed down'
Dana's image: 'going round and round and round right into hell'

sensory: wind on the face, breath taken away
extreme speed with no landmarks to measure it against
no impact — the fall is interrupted, not landed
the body position is wrong: head-first, or dragged sideways by others

quotes.text: the bottom dropped out, just like you're in an elevator and the floor opens up and you start falling into total darkness. And the thought came, there is a hell.
quotes.speaker: Kat Dunkle

quotes.text: And then the floor just dropped out beneath me, and I started falling into complete darkness.
quotes.speaker: Kat Duggar

quotes.text: As I literally started free falling into this outer darkness and racing down this uh tunnel
quotes.speaker: Paul O'Hada

quotes.text: Suddenly I fell into this hole without an end and I'm falling fast on that hole.
quotes.speaker: Gisely

quotes.text: I could see myself going on this escalator spiraling down and it was going round and round and round right into hell.
quotes.speaker: Dana

places.notes: Rises steadily with evidential strength: 4.53% -> 5.94% at cv>=18 -> 6.08% at cv>=23. Drowning and vehicle accidents are the chief contaminant (literal falling and literal sinking in water), which the context words only partly exclude. Worth noting that a downward-falling entry is not always distressing: a minority fall into the dark and then find it peaceful (void_darkness>peace_calm is the 6th most common transition in the corpus at 14.3%), so falling predicts the dark region, not distress within it. Audit found false positives of the form: The single biggest contaminant: the blood-pressure free-fall sensation on the gurney — 'imagine jumping out of an airplane without a parachute' while nurses call out 50 over 15. FOUR near-identical passages, all the same story, all the medical setting; 'I fell into a deep depression' / 'a deep hole' / 'a deep peaceful sleep' — biography and idiom (four passages); 'I kind of chose to just freefall' as a life-choice metaphor, and a preacher's 'fallen into the pit of feeling you've gone too far'; Physical collapse on a bathroom floor from hypoxia, and a blow to the temple that 'plunged me into darkness' (loss of consciousness); A host recounting other people's glimpses of a bottomless pit.

places.name: the veil
places.description: A thin, permeable membrane between the two worlds — misting, curtain-like, sometimes literally a curtain hanging the length of a room with movement visible behind it. Unlike the other boundary forms the veil is bidirectional and is often described being passed through on the way in rather than blocked at on the way out. A large share of uses are conceptual ('the veil between worlds is thin') rather than perceptual, and this must be stated plainly.

aliases.term: the veil between heaven and earth

sensory: a misting filling the whole length of a room
movement visible behind it — an elbow, a pant leg, a foot peeking out
thin enough to step through 'like going through someone's room'
described as lifting off the eyes rather than standing in the path

quotes.text: That white light was the veil that kept me from entering heaven or whatever that other side was. I didn't know. But it was a white veil.
quotes.speaker: Melinda

quotes.text: I actually felt like I had entered through a veil, a very thin veil, to get to the place where the angels and my family were.
quotes.speaker: D'vora Power

quotes.text: I see this like misting, like a veil almost, filling the whole length of the room on the other side. I can see movement on the other side.
quotes.speaker: Lynn Monet

quotes.text: My one daughter told me, "Well, Dad, that was the veil of death."
quotes.speaker: Randy Schiefer

quotes.text: there was something like a curtain. And I saw my grandfather on my mom's side peek through
quotes.speaker: Jayme G

places.notes: Honest caveat: this is the weakest member of the region. Roughly half of matched snippets use 'veil' as a metaphor for ordinary human forgetfulness or for the general thinness between worlds, not as a boundary encountered during the experience. It declines with evidential strength (5.07% at cv>=13 down to 3.87% at cv>=23), the opposite pattern from the river and the golden wall — consistent with 'veil' being partly imported vocabulary rather than reported perception. Included because it is unmistakably the corpus's own word for the divide, with 845 documents mentioning it at all. Audit found false positives of the form: the dominant use is idiom, exactly as the claim feared: 'the veil between heaven and earth is thin', 'the veil is thinner for us', 'on that side of the veil', 'those across the veil', 'peer through the veil', 'when the veil will be lifted' (qXpMDacWGe0, tquLbICSQcQ, D4LEsDewoTM, gaKcOv6WZV4, Afr4_LD0Dqo, dqKnO-qxgG0, KxgkceMHyxE, 1N7oh1KLcJ4); doctrine and teaching — 'the veil of forgetfulness that we all go through'; being told during the NDE that a veil separates the planes, with nothing seen (CQpPPZbaNOQ, PBrBoc2C0Sc); post-NDE psychic-openness talk — 'for weeks after this NDE the veil was still very thin with me' (cALgEYwnZYk); spirituality-study biography (b3pLo096qdo); a sound-product pitch about 'traversing the veil' (d39ZxFbYMfc); 'piercing the veil' used as a synonym for dying, no membrane perceived (JyuSdpWgvHI and its duplicate TEdeJcMC_EA); 'veiled' as an adverb for foggy vision, and a life-review projector curtain — the word without the boundary (jCAUIysvTLE, JxbJ9MRAwpY); only 4 distinct docs in 24 actually SEE it: two describe looking down through a cloud that was the veil, one a white veil of light barring entry to the garden, one a thin veil between the OBE and the living.

places.name: the surround
places.description: The other staging, and the one experiencers usually insist is more accurate: the review is not in front of you, it is all around you and you are inside it. Recurring containers are a sphere, a giant bubble, a ball, a dome, a round chamber; recurring adjectives are panoramic, 360-degree, holographic, immersive. Several describe standing inside a hologram that rose out of the centre of a table. People stress they did not have to turn their heads - vision came from every direction at once.

aliases.note: Dannion Brinkley's term, widely echoed

aliases.term: a giant bubble / spherical / inside a ball

aliases.note: Raymond Moody's phrasing, repeated by experiencers

sensory: a sphere the size of a football stadium
a hologram rising in the centre of an oval conference table
no need to turn your head; sight from every direction simultaneously
three-dimensional, forward and backward at the same time
sometimes explicitly not visual at all - 'I wasn't watching it, I was reliving it'

quotes.text: What I found when I went through the life review, there were screens all around me, and they were showing my life and my choices.
quotes.speaker: Claudia Edge

quotes.text: we went into this area that I perceived as being spherical, round, like inside a ball. And we started to relive my life.
quotes.speaker: Dave Bennett

quotes.text: I call it the panoramic life review, and you will see your entire life pass before you in a 360-degree panorama.
quotes.speaker: Dannion Brinkley

quotes.text: now I'm in a giant sphere about the size of a football stadium. And I'm looking all around in 360 degrees. Everywhere are little like motion picture screens of my lives
quotes.speaker: Andy Petro

places.notes: Runs notably richer in the better-evidenced strata (2.67% all vs 4.10% at cv>=13). 'Hologram' outside review context is usually philosophical talk about reality being a hologram, hence the negative_regex. The surround and the-screen overlap in some accounts - people describe curved screens wrapping all the way around, which is the hinge between the two stagings. Audit found false positives of the form: 'surround/surrounding' in ordinary senses: 'eight to ten feet of water surrounding the boat', 'the endless void surrounding me', 'I was surrounded by love', 'surrounded by souls just like yours'; 'Bubble' that is not the review container — a protective bubble of light around the body while the review itself was 'a line of pictures above my head'; Someone else's review seen mediumistically ('when I saw his life review... on this big screen'); A host relaying a third party's hologram-book review (Greg Rickard) rather than his own; 360-degree vision reported after the review, describing the landscape and the city — a real feature, but a different one; Life reviews with no spatial staging at all, matched only on the word 'review' plus a stray 'surrounded'.

places.name: The Trees
places.description: Trees stand at the edges of the meadow, in groves, orchards and forests, and sometimes as a single great tree on a hilltop that the experiencer is drawn toward. Their bark and leaves are lit from inside; the brown of the trunk is described as a colour of brown never seen on earth. Several people report the trees as consciously present — solemn, wise, greeting them, or talking as they pass.

aliases.term: the tree at the top of the hill
aliases.note: a recurring single landmark tree
1.26% of accounts use this exact phrase

aliases.term: leaves that had their own vibration

sensory: bark and leaves lit from within; no shadow under the leaves
brilliant brown with a tint of gold in the trunk
leaves quaking or shaking like aspen in the light
trees perceived as wise, solemn, welcoming, conscious
no dead wood, no decay, buds and blossoms in permanent bloom

quotes.text: I look at a trunk on a tree, it looks dirty to me, but these trees were a brilliant, brilliant brown with a tint of gold on
quotes.speaker: Scott Drummond

quotes.text: I then began to connect, plug into the trees, supreme wisdom and dignity of the trees, the solemnness of the trees.
quotes.speaker: Vinney Tolman

quotes.text: you have to picture the whole tree is like that, and the bark is lit, and everything is almost like lit from within
quotes.speaker: Lesley Lupo

quotes.text: I have traveled to many places here on earth but have yet to find a place where the plants and trees glowed like they did in this place.
I walked down the path toward the woods, these beautiful trees that were totally alive, and they kind of talked to me as I went and welcomed me
quotes.speaker: Ellyn Dye

places.notes: Lower prevalence than grass or flowers and the precision is only moderate — the residual false positives are post-NDE aftereffect passages ('now I can feel the consciousness of trees') which describe a changed relationship to EARTHLY trees rather than the otherworld. A small distressing-NDE variant exists in which the trees are dead, black and scorched at the edge of a crevasse. Audit found false positives of the form: Earth trees seen during the out-of-body phase, not in the other world (two Finland-in-winter passages: 'the trees are supposedly dead, but they were so alive'); After-effect tree consciousness in ordinary life ('I can feel the consciousness of trees... if I put my hand on them, I can communicate with them'); Ordinary-life trees seen with new eyes while walking on earth (two near-duplicate passages, IYhYhyenAWE / AMuNQl3Sxa0); Biography: childhood village with rivers and trees; a Mekong delta treeline from a war memoir.

places.name: The Path
places.description: A way through the country that the experiencer walks, usually behind a guide who says 'follow me' and stays ahead. It runs through the meadow, the garden or the trees, sometimes cobblestone or paved with stone, sometimes gold, sometimes just a track worn through the grass. Where it leads is usually where the choice happens — toward mountains, a river bank, a gate, or a city.

aliases.note: rare — only 0.42% of accounts use 'golden road/path/street'

sensory: the path lined or arched over with trees
cobblestone, flagstone or pavers underfoot
a stream running alongside it
a guide always a little way ahead, saying 'follow me'
light coming up out of the road itself

quotes.text: as I'm walking down the paths, and I'm walking towards this city, by the size of the buildings being this big over in the distance
quotes.speaker: Dr. Linda Kramer

quotes.text: We arrived at the foot of a very large cobblestone path. Ahead, I could see a large city to the left and a beautiful field to the right. A babbling stream ran along the path.
Scene starts to materialize and it's flowers. It's meadows. There's a path. There's rivers.
And I was walking down this path again, knowing that I died
quotes.speaker: Randy Schiefer

quotes.text: with this path going into the park down like that with all these amazing trees lining this path
quotes.speaker: Jody O'Meara

places.notes: Precision ~0.55; 'path' is heavily used metaphorically in these interviews ('my spiritual path', 'the path to healing'), which the negative_regex only partly removes. Prevalence declines with evidential strength. The famous 'streets of gold' is genuinely RARE in this corpus — 0.42% of accounts — far rarer than the plain grass path. Audit found false positives of the form: Dominant junk: ordinary biography 'walking down the path to my car' / 'walking down the road' before the accident — 8 of 24 passages, including three near-duplicate retellings of the same car-crash prologue; Metaphorical paths: 'that path led me to plant medicine', 'the path is unwinding', 'mankind is on a path of destruction'; Real-world trails: a mountaineering route, a jungle clinic path, a watchmaker errand; Secondhand: an angel-escorted 'pathway through the meadows of heaven' narrated about a third party (Jim), and a hospice nurse's story of a dying boy seen walking a path.

places.name: The Door
places.description: A single door, usually oversized, standing where a decision has to be made. It is white, or golden, or glass, or three metres tall, and it is explained to the visitor that passing through it is irreversible. Sometimes there is not one door but thousands - golden doors receding down a corridor without end, each opening onto something different. A few insist it was an entirely ordinary wooden door with light coming through, and that the ordinariness is the point.

aliases.note: 'those doors must have been about 3m tall'
in front of the golden city
down a corridor that never ends

aliases.term: a massive door made out of glass
aliases.note: with glass hinge pins that could not work on earth

sensory: roughly three metres tall and very wide
glass, with glass hinge pins
cloud instead of timber
opening by itself as the guide approaches
you can see light through it but not what is behind it
a row of golden doors receding past the limit of sight

quotes.text: he took me into a hallway with infinite doors, and I walked into one door that was on my right, a gold door.
quotes.speaker: Dr. Amirah Hall

quotes.text: And then there was this big white door.
quotes.speaker: Alysa

quotes.text: there was like thousands of golden doors down this corridor that it's like it would never end
quotes.speaker: Nekesha Burrell

quotes.text: When I get to this door, a huge door, which looked like this church
quotes.speaker: Eliane Costa

quotes.text: I was looking at this massive door, and it was made out of glass.
quotes.speaker: Laurie Ditto

places.notes: Rises steadily with evidential strength (1.72% -> 3.87% at cv>=23). Distinct from the gate: the gate belongs to the city and is public, the door is private and personal, and the irreversibility warning is nearly always attached to the door rather than the gate. Audit found false positives of the form: Idiomatic doors: 'this course opened many doors for me' (PA0_C-Ya238), 'it can open up many many doors of opportunities' (acbEt8BtJKI), 'I knocked on many doors, and no jobs' (TvZHlmMaMwA). Requiring a size/material adjective removes all three.; Earthly doors: the huge white doors of a hospital corridor in a dream about the speaker's dead father (u0Mngi-Bvr4).; Doors seen in mystical or deathbed visions rather than the speaker's own NDE — golden doors opening as a dying woman's aura departs, the same event told twice (1Jumd6LWoCs, gM2YIAFdB0s) — and a recurring bedside vision of a white door/portal outside any near-death event (O3cMj9h3oE4).; One rhetorical reference to 'getting into those gold doors' as a stand-in for salvation rather than a door that was seen (TLeahFEj6iw)..

places.name: The City of Light
places.description: A vast inhabited city seen either from a distance (glowing on the horizon, across a valley, beyond a doorway of cloud) or entered and walked through. People describe wide avenues, towers and buildings so tall they vanish into cloud, and a light that comes from the material of the city itself rather than from any sun. Several say it is 'made of light' though it looks like gold, crystal or white stone. Many arrive at it after the tunnel or after meeting a guide, and it is usually the largest single made thing they see.

aliases.note: the most common phrasing; frequently paired with 'city of God' by the same speaker
used by Dannion Brinkley and repeated by many later experiencers
explicitly tied to Revelation 21 by biblically-framed narrators
plural form used by Monroe-influenced narrators; more than one city
rare non-ornate variant: featureless box-like buildings, no windows or doors

sensory: wide avenues
buildings so tall and shining they look like white gold and are transparent
a glow visible from far off, before the city itself is visible
waterfalls at the edge of the city
no sun anywhere, yet total illumination
sky an intense blue with no light source

quotes.text: I was in a beautiful golden city. Stunningly beautiful, big sky-rise golden buildings with opaque windows as far as you could see up in the sky.
quotes.speaker: Randy Schiefer

quotes.text: I saw this other realm that was like a, a city of light.
quotes.speaker: Aaron Green

quotes.text: a crystal city, celestial city, magnificent place. There, I, I could see wide avenues, and also buildings that were so tall
And beyond it was this beautiful crystal city. I'll never forget it with the waterfalls on the side.
quotes.speaker: Nikesha Burell

quotes.text: And I saw this golden city way in the distance.
quotes.speaker: Reinee Pasarow

places.notes: Strongly enriched among the best-evidenced accounts: 2.56% of all docs but 6.08% at cv>=23 - roughly 2.4x. Most speakers see the city rather than enter it; the commonest verb is 'saw ... in the distance'. A minority explicitly reject it ('I thought heaven was streets of gold and pearly gates - it wasn't like that'), which the regex still catches; those are counted as false positives in the precision estimate above only when the speaker never saw a city at all. Audit found false positives of the form: Revelation 21-22 exposition — the holy city, New Jerusalem, streets of gold, 'the city has no need of sun or moon' — preached or quoted rather than seen (4 passages); Interviewer framing that names the city while asking the question ('I wonder if you could spend a couple of minutes describing the city of Heaven'); Other people's experiences: 'she didn't make it into the city of heaven', and a citation of Seneca Sodi's book '40 Days in Heaven'; Post-NDE research ('I started to Google Golden City') and generalised afterlife teaching about what environments exist there.

places.name: What the Buildings Are Made Of
places.description: A recurring, unusually concrete detail: the material of the built world. Marble, crystal, glass, pure gold, and - most distinctively - 'living stone', a white quartz-like substance with swirling markings that people insist is alive and conscious. Several say the buildings are hewn from blocks of light rather than stone, which is why they have warmth. Furniture inside is the same stuff: marble tables, marble benches, crystal tablets, a glass door with glass hinge pins that could not stand up under earthly physics.

aliases.note: white quartz-like, with visibly moving markings; described as alive and praising God
used where a speaker compares the building to the Parthenon but insists it is not stone

sensory: white quartz with white swirls moving inside it - you can see the life in the stone
marble that is warm rather than cold
crystal with lines of symbols running through it in ultraviolet light
glass hinges that could not bear weight on earth but do there
everything transparent yet still coloured

quotes.text: The other buildings were made out of living stone. It's kind of like white quartz, but you can see the swirling white in the stone.
quotes.speaker: Laurel

quotes.text: these columns, beautiful, tall white marble, maybe 30 feet high
Everything was made of a very clear glowing crystal.
quotes.speaker: Leslie Caradina

quotes.text: it appeared that all the buildings, they appeared to be as if they were made of gold
quotes.speaker: Russell Ricks

places.notes: Rare (1.23%) and flat across strata, with a single cv>=23 hit, so treat the stratum comparison as noise. Included because it is the single most concrete and most cross-culturally repeated physical claim in the built region: the material of heaven is alive. Audit found false positives of the form: Ordinary-life architecture: 'it was marble walls in this bank'; A crystalline structure used as a diagram of life decisions rather than a building ('heaven looked like a snowflake made out of crystal').

places.name: this far and no further
places.description: The commonest form the boundary takes: not an object and not a rule, but a simple inability to proceed. The experiencer is moving freely and then cannot move any more. There is no wall to touch, no gate to open, no one saying no; forward motion just stops being available. People describe it in flat, almost administrative language — 'I couldn't go any further', 'I wasn't allowed', 'this was as far as I could go'.

aliases.term: I wasn't allowed to go further
this is as far as you go

sensory: movement simply ceases to be possible; no impact, no pain
the far side stays fully visible and desirable
sometimes a sense of being 'up against' something soft or water-like
no anger or frustration reported — the limit is accepted as correct

quotes.text: I was aware that somehow there were unseen barriers beyond which I knew I was not permitted to pass.
we had to stop because I felt that I was up against like an invisible barrier of some sort.
quotes.speaker: Randy Schiefer

quotes.text: we came up to an invisible barrier of some sort. And I felt that I couldn't go any further.
quotes.speaker: Randy Schiefer

quotes.text: I couldn't go past that barrier. And if I did, then I wouldn't be coming back.
quotes.speaker: Sharon Milliman

quotes.text: there was this energy wall that kind of stopped me, and I couldn't go any farther.
quotes.speaker: Tricia Barker

places.notes: This is the only rubicon regex that rises monotonically with evidential strength (3.68 -> 4.70 -> 5.25 -> 5.52%), which matters: the better-evidenced accounts report the bare experience of being stopped more often, and the named, furnished versions less often. Precision is dragged down by biographical uses of 'wasn't allowed'; the negative_regex removes the commonest childhood-abuse and hospital-visitor cases. Audit found false positives of the form: 'not allowed' in ordinary life — a restraining order, a teenage girlfriend he 'wasn't allowed to see', a psychologist's account of being sixteen and 'not allowed to pursue it', spirits 'not allowed to come to me' when off duty; 'couldn't get past' as idiom or physical obstruction — firemen and a gurney, a doctor's belly button, a rope jammed on a rock ledge, veterans who 'can't get past things', a host's 'I can't get beyond the fact that...'; The dying body failing physically ('I couldn't get past my knees'), which is the medical setting not a boundary in the realm; Third-party generalisation about NDEs — 'people are only allowed to visit the entrance, they are not allowed to continue in'; Boundaries reported for OTHER souls in a mediumship context, and one meditation vision rather than an NDE.

places.name: The pit / the abyss
places.description: A hole without a bottom, usually below or behind the experiencer, sometimes glimpsed rather than entered. People describe standing at its edge and knowing that if they fall they can never climb back. Where hell is a destination, the pit is a direction: down, and endlessly so. Several describe it as darker than the darkness around it.

aliases.note: Amir: 'I was falling in this black abyss, falling so fast'
Santosh Acharji's own phrase for the drop below the closed gates

aliases.term: a bottomless, endless void beneath me

sensory: no floor, no echo — depth without a bottom
an edge or lip you stand on, often with a wall or closed gate behind you
darker than the surrounding dark
sometimes a single light at the bottom, which turns out to be fire

quotes.text: So I was teetering over the edge of a black pit. And in front of me was a darkness.
quotes.speaker: Rozsa Szamosfalvi

quotes.text: it seemed to be a bottomless, endless abyss, it was a very great darkness
quotes.speaker: Luiz Felipe

quotes.text: I looked down, and what I perceived was a very deep, bottomless black pit.
quotes.speaker: C. Thomas Perry

quotes.text: there was this sense of an absolutely bottomless, endless void beneath me
quotes.speaker: Colin Perry

quotes.text: Only option I have is to, is to dive down on my left into the deep dungeon dark world.
quotes.speaker: Santosh Acharji

places.notes: Slightly MORE common in the better-evidenced strata (3.74% -> 4.42%). Main false positives are idiomatic: 'pit of my stomach', 'pit of despair', 'digging my way out of the pit' as a metaphor for depression — the negative_regex targets these. The pit is frequently paired with a gate or wall: the experiencer cannot go forward into the light and cannot go back, and the only remaining direction is down. Audit found false positives of the form: 'abyss' as pure metaphor: the abyss of grief and bereavement, a black hole of abyss meaning depression, 'the abyss of God's wisdom', 'the abyss of humanity's existence in the Holocaust', a 'weekend abyss' spent nursing a dying partner (six passages); 'chasm' meaning emotional distance from a son, or an 'emotional chasm of stuff' unwound by Jesus; 'abyss' meaning benign cosmic vastness — staring down into galaxies and nebulas with awe and no fear (three near-duplicate passages from the same account); Hosts and interviewers talking about 'the pit of hell' with Bible quotation attached; A speaker retelling another woman's NDE across a chasm.

places.name: Pets and animals
places.description: Dogs above all, then cats and horses. The pet is usually simply present rather than central — 'they were just there in support' — and several experiencers note the animal does not have its earthly body: one describes his childhood dog as a floating sphere of awareness that he merged with. Animals are also reported en masse in the landscape, unafraid and mixed in with children.

aliases.note: one experiencer's description of his dog's form

places.notes: Essentially flat across strata — no evidential enrichment, unlike the human dead. Precision is limited because 'my dog was there' also occurs in ordinary accident narratives (a dog present at the scene, a rescue dog). The corpus's own entity census records only 191 'animal' and 11 'deceased_pet' encounters across 11,885 entity records, consistent with genuine rarity. Audit found false positives of the form: General reassurance with no perception attached: 'our pets are on the other side', 'your dog will be there to pick you up', 'if there are children in heaven, there are animals in heaven' (5 passages) - preaching, not report.; Post-NDE mediumship: pets 'coming through' in readings for clients (2 passages).; Visitation dreams rather than the NDE - the same speaker's childhood dog Shag appears in two packets, both times in a dream years later.; Interviewer / co-host commentary comparing guests' animal encounters.; Explicit negation: 'Did you see any former pets or animals on the other side?' 'No.' followed by a friend's story instead.; Living earthly pets invoked during the NDE as a reason to return ('your dogs need to be fed'), and a doctrinal aside that 'animals are not killed in Heaven'..

places.name: Nothing Here to Compare It To
places.description: A specific and distinct form of the language failure: not that the words are missing but that the referents are. Narrators say there is no earthly equivalent, no frame of reference, nothing on this side that can be held up against it. Where 'indescribable' concedes a failure of vocabulary, this concedes a failure of the world — the listener has never had the raw experience the word would need to point at. It is applied most often to the love, the light and the speed.

aliases.term: nothing here to compare it to

sensory: similes offered and immediately withdrawn
the love measured against parental love and found to exceed it
the speed measured against every earthly speed and found to exceed it

quotes.speaker: Hassan Malik

places.notes: Small but sharply concentrated in the better-evidenced accounts: 1.78% overall but 3.04% at cv>=18, a 1.7x enrichment. Two of the eight sampled snippets (K1TrJKxsZO8 and fCV7ayCLA1A) are near-identical retellings of the same experience by different uploads, so the effective witness count is slightly lower than the doc count. Audit found false positives of the form: 'No comparison' in the ranking/judgment sense — 'there was no judgment, there was no comparison, there was no competition' — 5 of 12 false positives (hDhYK1ipR4M, whDi9xOppRQ, XZ7ztpAloaw, i6KdwZN0f_4, tIkz_plTSbU). This is the opposite claim: not 'nothing on earth is like it' but 'nobody there ranks anybody'.; 'No frame of reference' / 'nothing to compare it to' meaning the experiencer had never heard of NDEs and had no cultural framework afterwards — biography, not the realm (-WjDhktugRU, dpM6AHETrTI, Kqzaowe3T1o, 8eJQg9zfo1w).; Interviewer banter and earthly comparisons: Houston heat 'no comparison' (CbS1au2tx-Y), comparing people's suffering (CHCobOyoPHE), and one passage where the incomparable thing is earthly life itself — sunsets and fireflies (M-DWYU1YJMU)..

places.name: The screaming
places.description: The soundtrack of the dark places, and often the first thing noticed. Experiencers say the screams are not human-sounding — not producible by a vocal cord — and that they come from beyond sight, from people who cannot be seen. Several report they could hear individual voices calling for help, and that hearing another person's torment was as bad as their own. A handful reach for the scriptural formula: weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Camille Hall's own compound

places.notes: Mildly MORE common in the better-evidenced strata (1.98% -> 2.21% at cv>=23). This one required aggressive constraint: an unqualified /scream/ matches 32% of the corpus, almost all of it the resuscitation scene ('I could see people screaming and crying' while watching their own body), so the regex demands hell/darkness/torment context within the sentence. Residual false positives are mostly interviewers and second-hand retellings. Audit found false positives of the form: The experiencer's own screaming rather than the soundtrack of the place: screaming at the beings 'I won't go', waking up screaming from a nightmare, screaming 'let me out of here' at demons, and the figure of speech 'I felt the air scream from my lungs' (5 passages, two of them near-duplicates of one text).; Ordinary-life screaming: the 1989 Santa Cruz earthquake recounted twice, and a school gym crying episode.; Someone else's death: a resuscitated man who sat up shouting 'I'm in hell', and a grandmother screaming that demons were taking her - both relayed second-hand.; Channel narration / AI-style voiceover framing another person's distressing NDE ('a place of fire and screaming').; Theological teaching using the scriptural formula ('weeping and gnashing of teeth') with nothing perceived.; Explicit negation: a cold silent grey place where 'there was no screaming, there was nothing'..

places.name: There Is No Religion Here
places.description: A message reported back from the destination: the denominational labels do not operate there. Delivered in several forms - there is no religion in heaven; God does not care what religion you are; Christ belonged to no religion; all the religions are reaching for the same thing and each has a fragment. Reported by Christians, ex-Christians and unbelievers alike, and often reported as the single most unwelcome thing the experiencer had to bring back.

aliases.note: the sharpest version in the corpus

places.notes: Small but flat across strata (2.61% overall, 2.76% at cv>=23), so it is not an artefact of the weaker accounts. This is the theological counterpart to the alias map: the corpus does not merely use interchangeable names, it reports being TOLD the names are interchangeable. Note the asymmetry in who says it - the strongest versions come from Christian speakers reporting a message that undercuts their own denomination, which is the opposite of the direction expectancy-confabulation would predict. Audit found false positives of the form: The conversational filler 'I don't care what religion you are / what gender you are / what country you're from' — pure inclusivity boilerplate in intros and outros (3 passages); Post-NDE comparative-religion study and book promotion ('I've written over 20 spiritual books about different religions', 'all religions have the same common roots'); Ordinary biography: Catholic upbringing, a priest visiting a dying father in a care home, a New Age spiritual search; A pastor/host summarising what NDErs in general report ('at least according to NDErs, there is no religion in heaven') rather than his own experience; General theological opinion with no anchor to the experience ('all religions are man-made', 'God's religion is love') — plausibly derived from the NDE but never stated as perceived there.

places.name: the rule: if you cross this you cannot come back
places.description: The explicit statement of the condition, delivered as words. A voice, an angel, a guide, a dead relative or Jesus tells the experiencer that passing the marker forfeits return. The wording is remarkably stable across thousands of accounts: 'if you cross this, you can't come back' / 'if you pass through this door, there's no turning back'. The rule is nearly always stated before the choice is offered, never after.

places.notes: One experiencer (t4hCgW5NgQc) spontaneously enumerates the interchangeable forms — stream, wall, portal — which is the strongest internal evidence in the corpus that these are one place with many costumes. Precision is limited by biographical 'if I go out tonight I won't come back' constructions; the negative_regex removes some. The rule is stated by a being roughly as often as it is simply known (see 'the-unspoken-knowing'). Audit found false positives of the form: The dominant miss, and the reason precision is low: the rule is NOT delivered as words in most matches - the experiencer simply knows it. 'I knew if I stepped in that golden sphere, I wouldn't be able to go back', 'I knew that just intuitively', 'I felt like if I went further I wouldn't be able to come back', and most explicitly 'No explanation was necessary for me to understand... that once I crossed the boundary, I could never come back' (7 passages). If the claim were reworded to 'the rule, told or known', precision would be 16/24 = 0.67; as written ('delivered as words... tells the experiencer'), it is 9/24.; Interviewer or host supplies the formula: 'Could that ladder relate to that famous limit that if we go past it we won't come back?' and a channel intro summarising 'both times she saw a limit that if she crossed she wouldn't be able to go back'.; Interviewer generalising about barriers in NDEs at large: 'people see barriers. They know if they cross, they're not going to come back.'; Speculation and denial: 'Some people say if you go too far over there you'll never come back. And I don't think that they would allow that.'; Off-topic biography (a buried infant, a bereavement) and general chat about death not being final..

places.name: Everything Lit From Within
places.description: The physical law of this landscape, stated over and over in the same words: down here the light reflects off things, there the light comes out of them. Grass, leaves, bark, petals, water, rock, and the beings themselves each carry their own light and radiate it outward. Several experiencers say the light IS the aliveness — 'the light within it was what made it alive'.

quotes.speaker: Karen Thomas

places.notes: Prevalence is flat or slightly LOWER among the best-evidenced accounts, which is worth reporting honestly — this is an interpretive formulation people reach for after the fact, and it may be more available to articulate experiencers than to the ones with the strongest veridical claims. Note that the same phrasing is also used of BEINGS (their skin glowing from within), which the regex cannot separate; roughly a third of matches are describing a being rather than the landscape. Audit found false positives of the form: The overwhelming failure is the devotional phrase 'the light within' used about people on earth: 'maybe you could be a light within it' (a church, appearing twice as a near-duplicate), 'connect with their light within', 'they haven't re-remembered that light within them', 'the light within ourselves', 'grow that light within', 'the darker something is, the more pronounced the light within it is' (8 passages). None of these are landscape.; After-effect rather than the place: seeing 'that fragment of light within' other people's eyes back on earth after the NDE.; A spontaneous earthly mystical moment on a subway car where everyone was 'illuminated from the inside... not light shining upon them but light coming from inside of them' - the exact formula, wrong setting.; Psychic vision of pyramids 'glowing from the inside with white light' in a channelling session.; One ambiguous in-NDE line, 'you could see the light within the light', which describes structure inside the light rather than objects carrying their own..

places.name: The Anger and Grief of Coming Back
places.description: The first emotion on regaining the body is very often not gratitude but rage. Experiencers report being furious at the rescuer, the phone call, the paramedic, God, or themselves for the decision to return. Some describe years of clinical depression that they later re-diagnosed as resistance to being back. Small children who could not explain it refused food and refused to be touched.

aliases.term: I was so angry that I came back
why did you bring me back

aliases.note: the diagnosis given to the state
one experiencer's image for re-embodiment

in children: refusal to eat, refusal to be touched, withdrawal
the rescuer or the ringing phone becomes the object of the rage

quotes.speaker: Camryn L.

quotes.speaker: Stephanie Teater

places.notes: Highest in the best-evidenced stratum (1.66% at cvNDE>=23 vs 1.05% overall), though on small numbers. This entry is measured with a proximity regex requiring the anger and the return to sit in the same clause, because bare anger words appear in 21% of transcripts for unrelated biographical reasons. Distinct from the catalogued heaviness-of-re-entry (the physical weight) and refusal-to-return (the decision at the threshold): this is the emotional aftermath of having lost the place. Audit found false positives of the form: anger about something other than the return: a surgical scar and appearance, being late for things, having blamed God; an experiencer explicitly denying it ('a lot of people say they were angry that they had to come back - I didn't have that experience'); a practitioner generalising about how people argue and get angry when told to go back; note: this feature is an aftermath emotion rather than a place, so I scored it as 'the anger/grief is reported as the speaker's own on regaining the body'.

places.name: The Silver Cord
places.description: A minority see a cord, filament or tether still joining them to the body they have just left. It is usually described as silver or luminous, attached at the crown or the torso, and understood without being told to mean that return is still possible. Its absence is reported just as pointedly by those who looked for it and found nothing — for them the missing cord is how they knew they had really died. A few see it frayed or torn.

places.notes: Rare but vivid and flat across cvNDE strata (1.54% all, 1.93% cv>=18, 1.66% cv>=23) — it neither strengthens nor weakens with evidential quality. About a third of matches are commentators discussing the cord as a theory rather than seeing one, and one notable account theorises that the tunnel IS the cord seen from inside. Note the striking cultural asymmetry: people who already knew the term report seeing it; several who did not know it describe a hose or cable and only later learn the name. Audit found false positives of the form: Ecclesiastes 12:6 quoted as doctrine — 'Remember your creator before the silver cord is loose' — in a preaching passage (CFeREug0k1Y), in a list of biblical parallels (ecoG5fo3IWE), and in astral-projection instruction warning the cord can snap (G8tX9pcfxTM).; Interviewer and medium commentary about the cord rather than a sighting: a host summarising what OBE practitioners call it (dXngq55bO80), 'that silver cord hasn't been severed, right?' (ZEYE-gw7ca4), and a host musing that 'hardly anybody' sees it and it might be the vagus nerve (QzBvf9lIfxM).; General teaching about what the cord is and does, addressed to listeners: the umbilical-cord explanation of dying (acbEt8BtJKI), a theory that the tunnel simply is the cord (spjWeT9sNH4), and a model of the moment of death when the cord breaks (j_p8kyiEK9k).; One sighting that occurs in deep meditation rather than a near-death event (n9BjGhrYfNY).; Note also that four of the true positives are the same floating-cord account transcribed across different uploads (q54BP2lR2RI, M5GFp_wVcGw, fRlc2wjzc28, k1nRZ0mQWZQ, plus nNHeb_P4j2M), so the independent-witness count is much lower than the match count..

places.name: The Homesickness
places.description: The chronic, sometimes lifelong condition that follows the return: not grief for a person but homesickness for a place. Experiencers use the ordinary word for the ordinary feeling and mean it literally. Some report it beginning before they were even back in the body. Several were explicitly warned by beings that remembering would cause it. One child experiencer described it as being dropped at a bus stop by God, who then forgot to come back.

aliases.note: the word used unprompted and literally

places.notes: Rises to 1.66% at cvNDE>=18 from 1.33% overall. This is the emotional cost side of the home claim and it is measured with an unusually clean single-word regex — 'homesick' is almost never used biographically in these transcripts. The single cvNDE>=23 hit is a genuine one. Related to but distinct from the catalogued refusal-to-return, which happens at the threshold; this one is the aftermath, and it is what experiencers say ruined or reordered their subsequent lives. Audit found false positives of the form: Ordinary homesickness: moving to Ohio, going away to college at 18, a child put on antidepressants who says 'I wasn't homesick. I was confused and broken'; General theorising rather than own report: 'certain types of depression can be related to a type of homesickness for our true home'; Interviewer and audience questions about minimising clients' homesickness; a practitioner describing experiencers in the third person; Inverted direction: homesickness for EARTH felt while out there ('When the Pacific Ocean appeared in its familiar shape, I felt homesick'); Missing loved ones rather than a place.

places.name: The stench
places.description: A smell reported with unusual specificity and unusual agreement: sulphur, burning flesh, rotting meat, decaying animal — often several at once, and described as thick enough to taste. Multiple experiencers say the smell was the worst part, worse than the sight or the pain, and several report it clinging to them after they returned.

places.notes: MORE common in the better-evidenced strata (1.44% -> 2.21% at cv>=23). This is a genuinely surprising find: NDE accounts are overwhelmingly visual, and smell is barely reported anywhere else in the corpus — but in the distressing region it is reported often, in convergent detail, and treated by the experiencer as the most memorable channel. Chief false positive is the smell of gasoline at accident scenes (two near-identical Jeff Olsen transcripts), covered by the negative_regex. Audit found false positives of the form: Ordinary-life smells: a dying cat, cigarette smoke on returning to the body, a supermarket smell-association story; Alien-abduction and entity sightings outside any NDE: Greys that 'smelled like a cross between sulfur or urine or a dead animal', reptilians with 'almost a stench coming from them'; Third-party material: hypnotherapy clients reporting sulfur, a shamanic medicine journey, a researcher's Bible/brimstone exposition and a Sodom retelling with no smell at all; A post-NDE phantosmia after-effect from nerve damage ('phantom taste and smell'), not the hell smell clinging; One passage with no smell content whatsoever (matched on 'brimstone' inside a denial).

places.name: The lake of fire
places.description: Fire as terrain rather than as event: a lake, a burning valley, a mountainside pocked with holes, all of it alight. What experiencers stress is that the burning does not consume — flesh regrows so it can burn again — and that the flames give no light. It is the most theologically loaded feature in the region and, correspondingly, the one people are most careful to say they did not expect.
