places.notes: MORE common in the better-evidenced strata (2.83% -> 3.59% at cv>=18). Contamination is mainly doctrinal discussion of what hell is or isn't ('I don't believe there's a fiery hell'), which is why precision sits at ~0.7 rather than higher. Notable dissent inside the corpus: several distressing experiencers explicitly report NO fire — Darren Shiner (cv=23) went to a black void that was 'really cold' and says 'I didn't see any fire' — so fire is a feature of some hellish realms, not a defining property of them. Audit found false positives of the form: 'Fire and brimstone' as a label for a preaching style, not a place ('he never talked about the fire and brimstone', 'a fire and brimstone kind of guy') — the single biggest junk class; Doctrine being cited in order to be rejected: ex-pastors quoting 'as the Bible says, in the lake of fire and brimstone', hosts defining hell 'according to the Christian definition'; Explicit denials that fire was seen ('where are the fire and the devils with pitchforks? I didn't see any of that', 'I don't know if I believe in a hell fire burning... that's not what I saw'); Metaphor: 'fire insurance to avoid the pits of hell', 'love the hell out of them'; Word collisions: 'twin flames', 'his eyes of fire', a candle lit against a demon in a dream; Third-party retellings — hosts describing Santos's or Howard Storm's hell, not their own.

places.name: The Halls of Learning
places.description: A building or complex of buildings understood, without being told, to be a university or school. Souls go there between lives to study anything - other planets, other galaxies, the mechanics of a coming lifetime. Some see actual classrooms with chairs and desks and a teacher explaining. One speaker was told he could not go in yet. Another describes rooms that open an aperture in the wall as you approach and close behind you.

aliases.note: usually plural, and usually listed alongside halls of knowledge, healing and music
'almost like, just like school'
the phrase people use when they have no name for it

sensory: no signage - you simply know the building is a place of learning
rooms that form an opening as you approach and seal behind you
colours that are 'alive', not like the purple here
people ecstatic to be going in, like children on the first day
a round room with aisles radiating from all sides and open sky and stars above

quotes.text: I had gone into this hall of learning where the walls go straight up as far as you can see. There are these huge windows, looked like an old library, but very, very clean.
quotes.speaker: Kristen Newman

quotes.text: And I saw this building, this great building, that I was shown to be the university or a place of learning.
quotes.speaker: Vincent Todd Tolman

quotes.text: I then noticed a building, a beautiful building. And I just somehow knew that that building was a university.
quotes.speaker: Vinney Tolman

quotes.text: I'm looking at the halls of knowledge, the halls of learning, the halls of music.
quotes.speaker: John Burke

quotes.text: The hall of knowledge is a wonderful place, where one can listen to spiritual teachers.
quotes.speaker: Bettina-Suvi Rode

places.notes: Main precision loss is the near-universal metaphor 'Earth is a school / a classroom', which is a doctrine drawn FROM the experience rather than a place inside it; the negative_regex targets it. The literal halls (a building you can approach, enter, be refused entry to) are a smaller but robust subset. Mildly enriched with cvNDE (3.38% -> 4.42%). Audit found false positives of the form: By far the dominant junk: the 'Earth is a school' metaphor - 'life and Earth, it's very much like a school', 'this is like a school where we do some homework of evolving our soul', 'Earth is just a place of learning and growth', 'it was a learning ground experience, like a school' (7 passages). The regex cannot tell a building from a simile.; Earthly schools and universities in biography: a school excursion where a teacher rescued the speaker, 'I was a university professor', an esoteric school following a master's teachings, and an English academic who 'teaches at a university there'.; Abstract 'higher place of learning / higher place of education' in a vibration-level teaching, with no structure seen.; Second-hand or generalised: a speaker listing what OTHER NDErs claim ('there were these great halls of learning... I don't have a body. There was no stuff there'), and a channelled description of specialised halls where spirit doctors train.; Explicit non-perception: 'whether it was a school or anything or a classroom' - the speaker says God did not show him..

places.name: The Clouds
places.description: Between the roof and wherever they end up, many experiencers pass through, stand on, or jump between clouds. Some treat the cloud layer as the floor of the next place; others pass through it like a ceiling and come out into space or into a blue that is not our blue. A minority explicitly reject it as cliché, which is itself evidence they were expecting it and did not see it.

aliases.note: looking down through an opening

aliases.term: walking through iridescent bubbles, not clouds
aliases.note: explicit denial of the cliché

sensory: solid enough to stand or jump on
seen from above, like from an aeroplane window
sometimes the boundary where a bubble or capsule stops, 'like it hit a hard barrier'
the sky above them is a blue 'that wasn't our blue'

quotes.text: I started jumping on clouds. I was like, wow, this is so cool. and then jumping from one cloud to another, hugging every cloud
quotes.speaker: Akerke Muratova

quotes.text: I'm up above the clouds. I can see the land masses of the earth as they go away.
quotes.speaker: Wayne Fowler

quotes.text: And then I went to clouds. I started jumping on clouds.
quotes.speaker: Archimura Tova

quotes.text: was this beautiful white staircase. And it just went up into the clouds.
quotes.speaker: Randy Schiefer

places.notes: Slightly MORE common in mid-strength accounts, flat at the top (1.36% -> 1.66%). The catalogued map has the roof/ceiling and the ascent but nothing about what is passed through afterwards. The looser pattern /clouds/ hits 4.24% but is heavily contaminated by metaphor ('heels in the clouds', 'clouds in the sky' teaching analogies) - the tight pattern above is what I measured. Audit found false positives of the form: Medevac airlift: three passages (two speakers) where 'flying through the clouds' turns out to be a real helicopter ride - the giveaway is the big H on the ground; Idiom and metaphor: 'you're still walking on clouds, aren't you?', 'you're not going to just go up into the clouds and ignore everything'; Explicit cliche-denial rather than perception: 'we aren't just sitting on the clouds eating grapes'; Scripture exposition (Jesus 'taken up into the clouds'), childhood imaginings of heaven, and a past-life regression session.

places.name: past lives in the review
places.description: A minority variant in which the review is not confined to this life. Experiencers describe screens that re-scroll to add six earlier lifetimes so that seven are being reviewed at once, or being shown the whole progression of lives and what was learned in each. Some who had no conventional review at all report this instead. Several object to the word 'past', saying the lives are simultaneous or parallel rather than sequential, since time does not run there.

aliases.note: preferred by those who reject sequential time

sensory: the screen re-scrolling backwards past birth
lifetimes seen as bubbles of transparent light arranged in a circle
the progression of what was learned visible across lives
described as silent, like a silent movie

quotes.text: And they gave me this cinema-like an upload into my mind of multiple past life reviews.
quotes.speaker: Chrisand Scott Spacky

quotes.text: I was shown all of my past lives. Um, all of my past lives, kind of like a movie, like a silent movie that I watch.
quotes.speaker: Ellyn Dye

quotes.text: now they have dropped six past lives into the screen, and I'm now reviewing seven lifetimes.
quotes.speaker: Norma Edwards

quotes.text: I saw thousands of lifetimes in a circle around me in bubbles. They were like in bubbles of light, transparent light.
quotes.speaker: Rafael Garcia

places.notes: Gets slightly rarer as evidential strength rises. A meaningful share of matches are past-life regression therapy or general reincarnation belief rather than something seen during the NDE, which is the main precision cost even with the negative regex. Audit found false positives of the form: Ordinary reincarnation talk with no NDE content: children who remember being murdered in a past life, a six-year-old who can fly a plane, a mother's account of her son's memories; Post-NDE healing practice: 'I help them clear past lives', reading whether a client's illness comes from a past life; Past-life memories that arrived AFTER the experience ('I've seen a few of my past lives since this experience', 'I sat on my couch and I saw it'); Researcher and interviewer commentary about how often a 'past life review' occurs in NDE typologies; Explicit denials: 'I didn't have a real past life review', 'some people say they have past life reviews — for me it was more like a glass of water'; 'My past life' used to mean simply this life up to now ('visions of my life, my past life... scenes of my life going before me'); Seeing ANOTHER person's past lives (a bus driver's) rather than one's own review — 2 passages; One textbook-perfect match for the claim (an arena with sections showing several simultaneous lifetimes) that is a retelling of Andy Petro's NDE by someone else.

places.name: The outer darkness
places.description: Darkness that has a quality — thick, pressing, and felt as hostile or occupied rather than merely empty. Experiencers stress that it is unlike any earthly dark: 'blacker than black', a blackness you can feel on the skin, sometimes described as being inside you as well as around you. Some hear voices in it; some feel watched. It is the same darkness others report as peaceful, which is precisely what makes this the most contested region on the map.

aliases.note: explicitly quoted from scripture by many; 0.92% of the corpus uses this exact phrase
Penny Wilson's phrase
Peter Panagore's paradox: dark, yet he can see

sensory: thickness — the dark has texture, weight, or stickiness
cold; several independently pair the black void with freezing (measured separately at 1.78% for cold+dark co-occurrence)
voices heard without bodies ('men screaming out of the darkness')
the feeling of being looked at by something you cannot see
darkness experienced as being inside the self, not only outside

quotes.text: Then I felt this darkness had a spiritual component, a very cold and evil presence. And I thought, where, where am I? I heard men in the darkness saying, shut up.
It's so black there. It's a blackness you can feel. It's like a, a penetrating evil, evil, evil.
quotes.speaker: Camille

quotes.text: You're permeated with darkness. It's not just all around you, it's in you, in your soul and your spirit.
quotes.speaker: Joel Brim

quotes.text: It was like invisible eyes looking at me. It was like a spiritual darkness.
quotes.speaker: Ian

quotes.text: The only way I know how to describe this is complete darkness. It's almost like it was space.
quotes.speaker: Jordan

places.notes: This is the hardest measurement in the region and the number should be read with care. The BROAD darkness/void vocabulary is enormous — void_darkness appears in 57.1% of sequenced journeys, and a plain 'the void / a black void / dark realm' regex matches 17.07% of all documents — but the overwhelming majority of those describe the dark as neutral or actively peaceful (void_darkness>peace_calm is 14.3% of journeys vs void_darkness>fear_distress at 7.0%). The regex here deliberately requires an explicit distress or hostility marker, which is why it lands at 2.20%. Precision is only ~0.45: it still picks up abstract talk about 'darkness and evil in the world' and, worse, sentences that mention fear in order to deny it ('I remember thinking, I'm pretty terrified in the dark... and yet I'm not afraid'). Flat-to-lower across strata, with 1.10% at cv>=23 — of all the places here, this is the one that does NOT strengthen with evidential quality. Audit found false positives of the form: 'Outer darkness' as a scripture tag or doctrinal category with nothing perceived: degrees-of-glory theology (oqzQIHghPpg), 'throw them into the outer darkness where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth' cited over a description of heat and pain (HyTbmpdeQuw), end-times teaching about darkness being confined to the lake of fire (FKOBI1oqfMU).; Earthly darkness and metaphor: 'there was this darkness in his eyes' about an abusive partner (OUyaObD1lgQ), 'my valley of darkness... became a door of hope' (yDfMtakkas0), 'Darkness and evil cannot live in the light of God' as an aphorism (BCzSEtgmTRE).; Book and channel material: a book title, Tightrope of Depression: My Journey from Darkness (7yTJlCHNb44), and a podcast promo montage cutting between clips of different speakers (8YGDBN9X7R8).; Second-hand and commentary: Howard Storm's NDE retold (stcYIqiQvjs); an interviewer's cultural aside plus 'I've interviewed several other near-death experiencers that have gone to that blackness' (-R2iBAH40O8).; Boundary warnings that name the region without entering or describing it — 'one more step, you'll be in outer darkness and you will not come back', the same experiencer twice (4sor4n4MZKA, p9ZggRgHFS8) — plus a void described only as the far end of a tunnel by a being who explained it (y5Nvc1eHywM), and one explicit denial of any malevolence, with a possible medical explanation offered (WpNBRe_QFsI). These four are the most arguable of my rejections..

places.name: This Life Is the Dream
places.description: The inversion. Having named the other place the real one, experiencers demote this one: earthly life is the dream, the shadow, the illusion, the murky film. The claim is almost always made after return and in the past tense of comparison — it is the residue of the visit rather than something perceived during it. Several say the demotion never wore off.

aliases.note: the compressed formula
younger experiencers' framing

sensory: this world described as heavy, slow, 'hip-deep molasses'
emotions here felt as condensed and raging by comparison
the body experienced as a confinement that limits mental bandwidth

quotes.text: It was almost as if my earthly life is the dream state and this heaven that I was standing in was actually my real reality.
quotes.speaker: Crystal McVea

quotes.text: This is the dream. This world, this material world is the murky, kind of dreamlike world.
quotes.speaker: Eben Alexander

quotes.text: This life feels like a dream. Feels like I'm walking in a dream because I'm confined in this body with limited mental ability, and I long to go back home
quotes.speaker: David Bennett

quotes.text: This is the dream. Heaven and all the things that are spiritual is the real thing.
he says that it's like a shadow, this life is a shadow compared to that life.
quotes.speaker: Camille Hall

places.notes: Deliberately measured separately from more-real-than-real, and it is far rarer (1.30% vs 7.48%). The asymmetry is the finding: many people will say the other place was more real; comparatively few take the further step of calling THIS one a dream. The zero at cvNDE>=23 (0/181) is a small-denominator effect but worth flagging — the strongest veridical cases lean toward sober medical description rather than metaphysical inversion. Audit found false positives of the form: Interviewer-side material: a host reading an audience comment about illusion, a host asking 'would you say this world is not real?', a host aside plus book plug; Literal dreams: a precognitive dream about motorcyclists, a dream of an aunt on a spiral staircase; Generic new-age or mediumistic illusion talk with no anchor to the experience ('because I see beyond the real truth, because this is illusional'); Integration doubt rather than the inversion ('you ask yourself, what is reality? Where is the illusion?'); Adjacent framings that are not the inversion: everything is 'a perception', 'this hologram' used in passing.

places.name: The Golden Light
places.description: A distinct and consistently reported colour variant. Where most describe white, a substantial minority insist on gold or amber — often as a warmth-bearing colour rather than a hue, and often at the centre or edge of a white light. Several describe standing in 'a place of golden light', gold streaming off in icicle-like points, or a golden glow taken on by their own body.

aliases.term: the most beautiful color of gold as can be imagined

sensory: gold streaming outward 'in streams in all directions, just like pinnacles, icicles'
warm rather than bright — the colour is doing the work of the warmth
gold at the edges with white at the centre, or the reverse
the experiencer's own body takes on the golden glow
one account: 'a golden sparkle in the air' as the whole of the visible apparition

quotes.text: I was surprised to see myself encompassed within a beautiful yellow-gold light, very intense and very soothing.
quotes.speaker: Dea M

quotes.text: I was instantly in the place of golden light and pure love.
quotes.speaker: Timothy V

quotes.text: my consciousness is seeing this golden light, white in the center, just unbelievably beautiful
quotes.speaker: Tony Woodey

quotes.text: The light was of the most beautiful color of gold as can be imagined.
quotes.speaker: Nancy Evans Bush

places.notes: LESS common among better-evidenced accounts (6.27% all, 4.83% at cv>=18, 3.87% at cv>=23). Some matches describe golden features of the wider realm (a golden city wall, gold-clad beings) rather than the light itself. Audit found false positives of the form: gold as the colour of scenery rather than of the light: gold-edged tree trunks, gold undersides of leaves, gold-tipped grass (3 passages, 2 of them the same duplicated account); a waking vision seen 'in my mind's eye' while writing at a desk, with a gold glow over green hills - not an NDE (2 copies of the same account).

places.name: Being seized and dragged
places.description: Hands, claws or bodies that take hold of the experiencer and pull them downward. Reported with striking physical detail — the thickness of the fingers, a nail that is a claw, hands on both arms, a grip that tears skin — and always against the person's will. In some accounts the grip is a swarm; in others one enormous hand. It is the mechanism by which people arrive in the dark places rather than fall into them.

aliases.term: shadows grabbing and trying to hold me

sensory: grip strength described in physical measurements (finger thickness, nail as claw)
skin and tendon damage that heals instantly so it can recur
being held on both sides simultaneously by many hands
stickiness — the shadows that will not let go
the experiencer fighting back and losing

quotes.text: being pulled back by what felt like a hundred hands scraping and clawing over every inch of my body
because I had demons on each side, six demons on each side grabbing me.
quotes.speaker: Camille

quotes.text: I heard demons yelling 'hell,' and they were dragging my soul down to hell.
quotes.speaker: Jay

quotes.text: the fingers are like this thick, and the nail, it was a claw.
quotes.speaker: Dominic Morrow

quotes.text: his nails or his claws, whatever it may be, I can feel it hitting my spine
quotes.speaker: Chris

places.notes: MORE common in the better-evidenced strata (2.17% -> 2.76% at cv>=23). The false positives are almost entirely literal and physical: drowning victims clawing at ice, rescuers grabbing an arm, a car dragging a body — the negative_regex targets these. An unconstrained /grabbed me|pulled me|dragging me/ matches 12.90% of the corpus and is essentially useless; the demon/dark/claw proximity requirement is what makes this measurable at all. Audit found false positives of the form: Metaphorical clawing: 'clawing my way through life', 'clawing my way back to this world', 'obstacles pulling me down into the abyss' before a suicide attempt (3 passages).; Benign or neutral pulls with no grip: pulled upward toward the light, pulled forward into the glimmer, a guide leading 'like a parent pulling you... not forcefully', sucked into a black hole like a vacuum cleaner (4 passages).; Creature descriptions with talons but no seizing - two passages inventory the beings' fur, fangs and yellow eyes without any hold being taken.; Word collisions: palace stones 'that looked like lion's claws', 'they tied me down with red claws' (prayer ties in a healing ceremony), a teaching about which animal species have claws.; Own body / medical: the experiencer's own hands turning to claws as he morphs; clawing and fighting to breathe during resuscitation.; Ordinary life: heavy winter clothes 'pulling me down into the water', a truck of soldiers pulling up, plus interview boilerplate..

places.name: The Staircase
places.description: Steps that must be climbed. Two distinct forms: a brilliant white staircase rising out of the ground into the sky with no visible top, which the dying person crawls toward hoping to be found; and a long flight of stone steps leading up to the entrance of a great building, worn hollow in the centre by everyone who has walked them before. The second form is often accompanied by other spirits going up and coming down.

aliases.note: going up as far as the eye can see, into the clouds
several speakers use the phrase self-consciously, calling it 'the proverbial'
ancient, mossy, cold, slippery, worn down in the middle
with huge steps, no visible end
the approach to the columned hall

sensory: steps so worn in the centre that you know how many have come before
cold, moist stone with moss on it
steps bigger than a human stride
the top of the stair disappearing into cloud
other spirits ascending and descending on the same flight

quotes.text: I looked over and I saw this big beautiful staircase going up into the sky. I said, "If I can get to that staircase, maybe somebody will find me."
quotes.speaker: Randy Schiefer

quotes.text: this beautiful staircase going up into the sky.
quotes.speaker: Randy Schiefer

quotes.text: I was in a stone stairway, a very old stone stairway
quotes.speaker: Robin Aisha Landsong

quotes.text: vibrantly white with many steps leading up to it and huge columns in front.
quotes.speaker: null

quotes.text: it had the huge white columns in front and a and a huge number of stairs, just so many stairs
quotes.speaker: Karen Thomas

places.notes: Very strong cvNDE enrichment: 1.67% overall, 8.84% at cv>=23 - a 5.3x rise, the steepest gradient of any place in this region. Some of that comes from the same high-scoring narrators who describe the columned hall (the stairs are its approach), so the two should be treated as partially the same finding. Audit found false positives of the form: Book titles: 'Stairway to Heaven' discussed as a published book (c7qstScs3eI, _jDrbRk96l8) and 'Crystal Stairway to Heaven' haggled over on air with editing costs (Rkho24Vkve4).; Ordinary domestic and hospital stairs: the long staircase at home after discharge (3BjfBiLXQcA), steep steps the paramedics couldn't get a gurney up (wZFbkcngdDM), and a passage that matched only on 'no footsteps in the fresh snowfall' (E016R6wu-Y8).; Metaphor and denial: 'like walking up a spiral staircase' as a figure for spiritual progress (EGrpt5KgwH4), and 'There is no stairway to Heaven. There's nothing. It's darkness' (DOYgrnM1iKs).; The hell-pit accounts where 'spiral staircase' is a simile for the shape of a pit lined with cells, not steps to be climbed (sjvD1FvIhdo, dwCEPYFD67s — same experiencer twice).; Second-hand and dream stairs: another child's tornado NDE with stairs to heaven (3oEi1487nAU), a dream of Machu Picchu steps (nHe0gyl3uiE), a dream of a hospital marble staircase (u0Mngi-Bvr4)..

places.name: The Landscape That Sings
places.description: The country is heard as much as seen. Experiencers describe every element having its own vibration, note or sound — the leaves one pitch, the trunk another, the grass another, the water another, the rocks another, even the colours — and all of it combining into what one person calls 'big music'. It is often the first thing noticed after the visual shock, and several people say the landscape is praising or worshipping.

aliases.note: one experiencer's own coinage, used repeatedly

aliases.term: each blade of grass has a vibration
each colour has its own vibrational sound

sensory: distinct pitches for leaves, trunk, grass, water, rock, colour
sound perceived as visible — one experiencer sees it rise as a pink haze
harmony rather than noise; nothing discordant
the sound felt through the feet as well as heard
flowers singing high or low notes according to their colour

quotes.text: The trees had a sound; the leaves on the trees had their own sound; the grass had a sound; the rocks had a sound; the water had yet another sound
The leaves on the trees have a vibration. Each blade of grass has a vibration.
quotes.speaker: Dianne Sherman

quotes.text: the trees have a sound, the leaves have a different sound, the grass has a different sound, the water has a different sound
quotes.speaker: Sharon Millerman

quotes.text: like the leaves have a vibration. The trunk of the tree has a different vibration.
And the blades of grass and everything were swaying in rhythm of the vibrations that it was sending out.
quotes.speaker: Russell Ricks

places.notes: Declines across cvNDE strata (2.83% -> 1.66%), and the vocabulary overlaps heavily with New Age 'raise your vibration' talk in the aftereffect sections of interviews, which is the main precision risk. Distinct from celestial music (9.7% of sequenced accounts in the structured report) in that the source here is the landscape itself rather than choirs or unseen instruments. Audit found false positives of the form: Overwhelming junk: the free-floating new-age/physics slogan 'everything is vibration' / 'everything is frequency' used in ordinary conversation — bioresonance and Rife machines, quantum-physics asides, 'everything is mathematics' interviews, capitalism 'keeping everything in that vibration', book promotion about 'vibrational alignment', coaching advice about raising your vibration. Roughly 14 of 24 passages are this one pattern and none of them describe a landscape; Personal vibration: the experiencer's own body shaking at a high vibration, or 'my vibration changed' as an aftereffect; Post-NDE perception of ordinary objects (a chair, a cat) having energy; A third-person narrative of an unborn baby sensing vibrations.

places.name: the ripple
places.description: The chain of consequence made visible. In these accounts the review does not stop at what you did and how it felt to the other person - it follows what that person then did to a third person, and outward from there, sometimes described as running out to infinity. Experiencers see kindness compounding and hurt propagating, and several say this was the most morally shocking part of the experience: not the acts themselves but their unbounded onward travel. The corpus's own word for it is almost always 'ripple'.

aliases.note: overwhelmingly the dominant phrasing

aliases.term: they carried that hurt on to other people
you were the creator of that

sensory: consequences followed out to infinity, not stopping at the first person
seeing a hurt person go on to hurt someone else, and that person another
a kind act 'like a ripple that changed universes'
concentric circles spreading outward

quotes.text: I was shown my life in a three-dimensional panoramic view, meaning that I saw everything forward and backward. And every single ripple effect of my every thought, action, out to infinity
quotes.speaker: Chrystal Rae

quotes.text: It was just an amazing ability to see the ripple effect of how you interact with other people and that it's how we're all connected
quotes.speaker: Karen Thomas

quotes.text: everything that if you did that affected and rippled out to someone else, you were the creator of that, and so you experienced your creation.

places.notes: The unconstrained phrase 'ripple effect' matches 4.57% of the corpus but is mostly post-NDE moral advice; requiring life-review proximity cuts it to 1.10% with much better precision. This is under-counted, since many describe the same mechanic as 'chains' or 'how it went on and on' without the word ripple. Audit found false positives of the form: Second-hand summary of what NDErs in general see: 'a lot of NDEers will talk about, in their life review, they saw...', 'anybody's had a life review knows', a practitioner describing 'a person' experiencing it; Citing a named other experiencer's review (Mary Neal seeing the ripple 16, 25, 30 times down the road); Channel intro boilerplate ('In her life review, Nikesha Burell was shown three specific scenes'); Hypothetical speculation ('if Hitler had a life review... how that's rippled'); Channelled teaching about a future collective 'living life review' for humanity rather than the speaker's own.

places.name: The Golden Road / Streets of Gold
places.description: The paved surfaces of the built world: streets of gold, golden roads, cobbled roads with guttering, a path of light laid across water toward the sun. Some walk on gold and say everything underfoot was gold; one describes cobbled pathways followed for what she estimates as thousands of kilometres, through valleys and past lakes, into a city. A large share of mentions are people naming 'streets of gold' as the cliche they expected and did not receive.

aliases.note: the single most quoted expectation about heaven in the corpus
'crystal cities and golden roads with diamonds reflecting the universe'
laid across the ocean toward the setting sun
with guttering, 'like we have here'

sensory: gold underfoot and gold in every direction at once
cobbles with guttering at the kerb
diamonds set into the surface reflecting the universe back
a path of light on water that you travel along at enormous speed
roads with no cars on them

quotes.text: To this day, I can still envision the golden streets, but even more so how they felt beneath my bare feet.
that's when I walked in, steeped into this golden streets. Everything was gold.
quotes.speaker: Karina Ferrigno Martinez

quotes.text: It's understand it as crystal cities and golden roads and with diamonds reflecting the universe off there.
quotes.speaker: Bill Tortorella

quotes.text: There was golden houses and golden streets and it was just pretty everywhere.
quotes.speaker: Shacolby

quotes.text: there were roads, cobbled roads with guttering like we have here.
quotes.speaker: Lynda Kramer

places.notes: Precision ~0.5 and the number falls at the top stratum (one hit at cv>=23). Roughly half of all 'streets of gold' mentions in the corpus are explicit denials: 'I saw nothing like that', 'no streets paved with gold', 'no gold streets, nothing like that'. That negative pattern is itself the finding - the golden street is the corpus's canonical example of an expectation the experience does not honour. Audit found false positives of the form: 'path of light' as a moral/spiritual metaphor ('the opportunity to follow the path of light, but it depended on us'); 'path of light' meaning the illuminated trajectory of the tunnel ascent, not a road; earthly paved surfaces: a marked highway before the crash, the unpaved muddy streets of his family's poor district, the cobbled streets of the speaker's own city seen through time; a garden of glowing paths explicitly framed as a dream; the anti-mention: 'it's not one of those things where you cross over and some people say, oh, I saw golden streets' - a denial the regex counts as a hit.

places.name: The Mansion / My Father's House
places.description: A dwelling: a house, a mansion, a home that is recognisably yours. Some are shown a specific house on a bluff or a cottage with a rose arbour and told, or decide, that it is theirs. Others enter a white mansion whose corridor holds thousands of golden doors, each room a different world. The Johannine 'in my Father's house are many rooms' is quoted constantly, but usually to explain something the speaker saw, not to substitute for it - the rooms are read as levels or realms, not bedrooms.

aliases.note: quoted from John 14:2, glossed as many levels or many worlds

aliases.term: in my Father's house are many rooms

aliases.note: described as entry points to more of the beyond, thresholds that are alive
'there were houses, but we don't need houses because we don't sleep'
recognition of a dwelling as one's own
golden light streaming from the windows at dusk; God is inside

sensory: a round room with gold candles on the walls and robin's-egg-blue walls with gold trim
a corridor of golden doors that never ends
stone walls with an ocean below and rose gardens behind
golden light streaming from the windows at late dusk
the mansion is not big enough to contain God - the point of showing it

quotes.text: I was looking on this huge white mansion. And as soon as I was to think, I was inside the doors. And inside the doors, I could see like infinite doorways, golden doors
quotes.speaker: Nekesha Burrell

quotes.speaker: Nekesha Burrell

places.notes: Only one hit at cv>=23, so the apparent collapse in the top stratum is not reliable. A recurring rhetorical move worth noting: several speakers are shown a mansion specifically so that a guide can ask 'can you contain God in that mansion?' and then dissolve it into trees, clouds and earths - the building exists to be outgrown. Audit found false positives of the form: Bare John 14 quotation used homiletically or as theology, with nothing seen: a pastor quoting it at funerals (xQCSh0wcOGo), an interviewer citing it to frame a book question (Nfnsd_yvCa0, 3rTk7Xmffi0), 'there are many mansions in my father's house. So there are many places' (02lXN7FqiOE), 'Prepared a mansion for all of us' (Kh5vu-3RQgc), Paul's 'house in heaven' meaning the resurrection body (_TsOqTRUL3c). This is the single largest junk class.; Literal earthly father's house: living at dad's while studying (S3e7nba_ffI), hearing footsteps at night in Russia (69UKHPIDgc0), and the prodigal son parable (cnKhuI7kahQ).; The mansion mentioned only to be declined or dismissed inside the NDE — 'I can go see my mansion later' (7nmCYK0L1BU), 'people talk about a mansion. I don't care about that' (QHNW29X-nrE) — and one explicit denial: it 'looked nothing like the mansions in the sky I had learned about in childhood' (3rAYA_P1pXQ).; Second-hand or generalised dwellings: a dream in which the speaker's mother says she lives in a castle (_jDrbRk96l8), a seven-level cosmology asserting 'at least there are houses there' (j_p8kyiEK9k), and a lecture on building astral houses by thought (0oQKp4266YQ)..

places.name: The Temple / Cathedral
places.description: A place of worship in the otherworld, distinct from the library and the school. Descriptions cluster into two shapes: a cathedral with spires going up thousands of feet, pews and a long central corridor scaled far beyond human size; and a crystal temple of light that radiates more brightly than the sun and appears as you approach. A third variant, the healing temple, is where the imprints and traumas carried in the soul are dissolved.

aliases.note: used even by non-religious speakers as a size-and-shape comparison

used by one speaker to say she got only as far as heaven's entryway

places.notes: Weakest precision in this region (~0.5): 'temple' is heavily polluted by the anatomical temple, earthly Buddhist and Hindu temples visited in biography, and the Pauline 'your body is a temple'. Also the only structure here that is LESS common among the best-evidenced accounts (3.32% at cv>=13 falling to 2.21% at cv>=23), which is worth flagging - explicitly religious architecture may be more expectation-shaped than the generic columned hall. Audit found false positives of the form: 'Chapel' is almost entirely earthly and accounts for most of the junk: hospital chapels during surgery, a school chapel, a convent chapel, a childhood parish chapel, a chapel in the speaker's own backyard, a chemo-unit chapel; Earthly cathedrals as history or parable: the Anasazi-vs-Europe conversation with a park ranger, the three-stonemasons parable, 'this is why you have the cathedrals' cosmology; Physical religious sites visited after the event (a Fatima shrine, Rennes-le-Chateau grotto, Lily Dale's healing temple); Channel boilerplate ('you are indeed a pastor of a great church there in Minnesota') and an interviewer asking about a chapel in a dream; One genuine NDE chapel that is nonetheless an earthly building (a Glastonbury chapel seen out-of-body), not an otherworld temple.

places.name: The Room
places.description: A bounded interior with no discernible architecture: you know you are in a room because there is an inside, but the walls may be cloud, atmosphere, or nothing at all. Most often white or brilliantly bright; sometimes round, with aisles radiating from all sides and open sky and stars overhead. It has no reference points, so people cannot say whether it is small or vast. This is frequently where a being of light appears, or where a life review is presented.

aliases.note: the commonest form; often the whole of what was seen

aliases.term: a room without walls - the walls were made out of the atmosphere

aliases.note: aisles from all sides; sky and stars visible above

sensory: no reference points at all - 'I don't know if it was an igloo or an airplane hangar'
walls of cloud, or of atmosphere
an architect's table with a huge open book in it

quotes.speaker: Briana Lafy

quotes.speaker: Brian Hoyland

places.notes: Rises steadily with cvNDE (3.29% -> 5.52%). The 'white room' is the minimal built structure in the corpus - the least furnished thing that still counts as being somewhere rather than nowhere, and it sits right at the boundary with the void/darkness region. Audit found false positives of the form: the circulating 'if you're white and you're in a white room, how would you know you're white?' teaching analogy about why souls incarnate - 5 passages, none of them a perceived place; a sleeping visitation dream in a white room with a table and chair, and a deliberate out-of-body practice session, neither during an NDE; the interviewer offering 'a white room or white light' as a menu option; the experiencer answers 'the nucleus of the white light', not a room; an experiencer explicitly rejecting the word ('I was in this white space. It's not a white room').

places.name: how did you love
places.description: What the review turns out to be measuring. Not achievement, not belief, not money, not career - experiencers say over and over that what registered were acts of kindness, often trivial ones they had entirely forgotten, and the love given and received. Several report that the review skipped everything they had been proud of and lingered on a kind word to a stranger. One says her review consisted only of moments of intense shared love and nothing else. The measure is repeatedly phrased as a single question: how did you love?

aliases.term: what did you do for others?
what you bring back is your heart

sensory: small forgotten kindnesses shown as 'the most magnificent thing I had done'
achievements offered up ('I'm an Eagle Scout') and dismissed

quotes.speaker: Nicole Dron

quotes.text: It's a life review of how much you loved people. What was the love impact that you had on people on this earth?
quotes.speaker: Jason Janas

places.notes: Honest precision warning: about half of the matches are the experiencer stating the lesson in the interview rather than describing the measure being applied during the review. That is still evidence about the content of the belief, but it is not the same as a described scene. 'Acts of kindness' also appears in ordinary post-NDE advice-giving. Audit found false positives of the form: 'It's all about love' as podcast filler — it appears in host outros, sign-offs, channel plugs and general life advice in at least ten of the twenty-four passages, almost never attached to a review; Sermon and scripture exposition (Paul on freedom and love, Jesus on the cup of cold water and visiting prisoners); 'Random acts of kindness' in ordinary life: paying for the car behind at Burger King, teenagers inventing cancer tests, a medium's third-eye errands; Second-hand reports — a family member recounting that the experiencer 'came back saying it's all about love and relationships'; Explicitly flagged speculation ('this is just my take on it, coming back from the NDE') and generic post-NDE value shifts.

places.name: Earth as the Trip, Not the Home
places.description: The framing that makes the home claim coherent: earthly life is temporary and instrumental — a school, a classroom, a base camp, a passage, a trip you took on purpose. Several experiencers report being explicitly corrected on this point by a being: it is a classroom, not a courtroom. The framing is presented as taught information rather than as personal opinion.

aliases.note: recurring near-verbatim formula

aliases.term: life here is just a passage
spiritual beings having a human experience
aliases.note: the most-quoted formula in the corpus

sensory: presented as instruction received, often from a named guide
the correction 'classroom not courtroom' delivered as a relief from expected judgement
earth viewed from outside as small, temporary, and purposeful

life on Earth is just a classroom. We come here so we can learn, and that's it.

quotes.speaker: Vincent Tolman

quotes.text: This is temporary. That's all it is.
quotes.speaker: Becki Hawkins

places.notes: This is the entry that climbs most steeply with evidential quality: 1.13% overall, 2.07% at cvNDE>=18, 2.76% at cvNDE>=23 — more than doubling. It is the cosmological complement to the-home: if that place is home, this one has to be explained, and the corpus's own explanation is school, passage, or trip. Note that the 'classroom not courtroom' phrasing clusters in accounts connected to one experiencer (Vincent/Vinney Tolman) appearing under multiple video ids, so the true independent-witness count is lower than the document count suggests. Audit found false positives of the form: Personal opinion rather than taught information, which is the distinction the claim itself rests on: 'I believe that Earth is really a great big classroom', 'I'm a firm believer that we come to this life to learn'; Produced channel narration quoting Vincent Tolman almost verbatim in two separate documents, including a section heading 'Earth School & Your Mission'; Doctrinal 'we believe' framing, scriptural teaching about the first and second death, and new-age ascension teaching ('we are moving to a more advanced school for souls'); Word overlap on 'trip' and 'passing through': a literal trip with a partner, and passing through blue scenery during the NDE journey itself.

places.name: the council
places.description: A seated group - most often twelve, sometimes three, sometimes an unnumbered circle - who receive the newly arrived and go through their life with them. They sit in a circle or around an oval table, wear white or golden robes, and speak in one voice. Experiencers call them the council, the council of light, the council of twelve, the elders, or simply 'my council'. Their tone is consistently reported as loving and non-punitive; several describe being laughed with rather than at.

aliases.term: a council of high spiritual beings

merged duplicate

places.notes: Parent left null because the council appears in two distinct settings: presiding at the life review, and pre-birth life planning ('we sit with a council of 12 and they help us write what we need to master'). It is one of the few items in this region that gets LESS common as evidential strength rises (1.59% all vs 1.10% at cv>=23), which is worth flagging - the numbered-council motif is heavily New Age inflected. Remaining false positives are church councils and civic councils not caught by the negative regex. Audit found false positives of the form: Ongoing channelled contact with a 'council' outside any NDE: beings arriving while eating Cheerios, automatic-writing sessions (two passages, same speaker), thirteen nights of visits from twelve elders at a ranch (two passages), a spirit team of wisdom keepers; Host intros and channel boilerplate: 'was introduced to the Council of Light where he experienced a life review', 'she met a council of vibrational beings'; Interviewer speculation ('I think that's because a lot of times in near-death experiences people see the council of 12 elders') and third-party accounts (Aaron Green's pre-birth plan, a channeler's 'council of 12 angels'); Bare label with no scene: 'whether you want to call him Council of 11 or whatever you want to'.

places.name: The Waiting Room Where the Family Sits
places.description: Out of the body, a large number of experiencers do not stay at the ceiling: they go looking for their family and find them in the hospital waiting room, the corridor, or the relatives' room. They report what was said, who bought a candy bar, who was praying, what people were wearing. Because these details are checkable, this is the room that most often becomes the verified detail of the case.

aliases.term: the relatives' room / the little room outside the operating room

aliases.note: many name the people rather than the room

sensory: hands passing through a relative who is standing there
hearing conversations and jokes verbatim
seeing people praying, holding hands, pacing
arriving simply by thinking of the person

quotes.text: I went into the waiting room, where I saw my stepdad get a candy bar. He was like a health nut, so I thought that's odd.
quotes.speaker: Tricia Barker

quotes.text: I saw them sitting in a little waiting room outside the operating room, holding each other's hands, hoping and praying that I was going to make it
quotes.speaker: Christine Stein

quotes.speaker: Paulo Victor

places.notes: The single steepest cvNDE gradient I found: 1.28% overall but 6.63% at cvNDE>=23, a 5.2x enrichment - unsurprising, since this room is where the corroborating evidence lives. Entirely absent from the catalogued map, which covers the ceiling vantage and passing through the roof but never the tour of the rest of the building. The bare pattern /waiting room/ hits 4.74% overall and 16.02% at cv>=23, but includes the family's own later account, so I used the OBE-constrained pattern. Audit found false positives of the form: 'Waiting room' as an otherworldly place, not the hospital one: 'heaven's waiting room', a light-filled waiting room, a receiving area for the newly dead, a glass waiting room floating in space; The experiencer or a relative physically sitting in a hospital waiting room in ordinary time - oncology appointments, four hours bleeding before surgery, a deathbed vigil; Second-hand comfort rather than perception: 'Knowing that our friends were in the waiting room and praying for us meant so much to me' (two near-duplicate passages); A revival scene where the experiencer physically walks to the waiting room after coming round.

places.name: The Great White Building with Columns
places.description: A specific, repeatedly described edifice: an enormous glowing white or pearlescent building fronted by tall columns, approached up a long flight of stairs, with a huge doorway at the top. Spirit-beings in white robes are milling around outside, going in and coming out. Speakers who have no vocabulary for it reach for 'Greek or Roman temple'. Inside, it usually opens into the library or hall of records - the columns and the books belong to the same structure.

aliases.term: like a Greek or Roman temple
aliases.note: the single most common comparison; the speakers stress they are only borrowing the shape

aliases.term: the Parthenon, but hewn from blocks of light

places.notes: The most strongly cv-enriched item in this region: 0.71% overall but 3.31% at cv>=23, a 4.7x enrichment. Part of that is one experiencer (Karen Thomas) retelling the same NDE in several interviews, all of which score high, so the enrichment is inflated; but independent accounts (pjxqvZQNFWY / u-_bkoxO0uM, uGMtd3YN3B0, g2QgPL2Q06w) describe the same columned white hall with steps. Audit found false positives of the form: a motivational parable about an architect visiting workmen at a Roman temple; biography: a year of travel visiting Greek and Roman temples in Turkey, Syria and Jordan; a speaker describing the 'Greek column places' of learning he chose not to visit and only knows from other people's accounts; a teaching that Earth's Greek buildings and pyramids exist on the other side first, attached to a visit to a medieval castle; note: about a quarter of the true positives are the same columned-library account re-uploaded across channels.

places.name: Strangers you already know
places.description: A distinct and very consistently worded experience: the experiencer meets beings they have certainly never met in this life, and knows them anyway — 'I knew them, but I didn't know where I knew them from'. The knowing is described as older than the lifetime ('we had known each other for eons'), and the inability to place them is reported as mildly frustrating rather than frightening. This is the strongest formal argument the corpus itself makes against the 'expectation fulfilment' explanation.

I felt like I knew her, though we'd never met
I knew each and every one of them intimately
I didn't know them in this lifetime

no names attached to the recognition

quotes.speaker: Phillip

places.notes: Rare but the wording is remarkably stereotyped, which is why precision is high despite the small n. Doubles at cv>=18 (0.65% -> 1.38%). Note two of the 40 matching documents are near-duplicate uploads of the same narrator (Sharon Milliman), so the true independent count is slightly lower. Audit found false positives of the form: Ordinary-life recognition: a hospice nurse feeling she 'knew' a patient she'd never met; two living people in an NDE support group who felt they 'knew each other but didn't know why' (docs HwmnyYSXE44, Bvc3Y5SqpOk).; A family apparition seen in waking life rather than in an NDE - the sister who 'felt like we knew her, but we didn't know from where' was seen in the house, not on the other side (doc xZ_ID_3zt78).; Inverted phenomenon: an OBE-er looking down at her own LIVING husband and failing to place him ('I knew I knew him, but I didn't know who he was') - the same wording, the opposite experience (doc D3Ql06RhYlI).; A psychedelic ceremony in which the recognised beings turned out to be the physically present trip sitters (doc Dpbf1fK5J04)..

places.name: the river and the far bank
places.description: Water dividing the experiencer from the dead. The river is consistently small — twenty to thirty feet across, shallow, sparkling, 'not a very wide river' — and consistently uncrossable. On the far bank stand relatives, ancestors and crowds of souls, close enough to recognise faces and feel their love. Several accounts describe stepping-stones or a shallow ford that make the impossibility of crossing all the stranger.

aliases.note: several experiencers reach for the hymn 'Shall We Gather at the River'

places.notes: The strongest evidential gradient of any place in this region: 1.15% overall, 1.99% at cv>=13, 2.76% at cv>=18, 4.97% at cv>=23 — a 4.3x enrichment among the best-evidenced accounts. Whatever else is true, the river-with-relatives-on-the-far-bank is not an artefact of weakly-evidenced storytelling. Precision is limited by real rivers in accident narratives (drownings, rafting); the negative_regex removes some but not all. Audit found false positives of the form: metaphorical rivers: a 'river of all knowing' (the Akashic records, 2 copies), a raging river used as a simile for incoming love; earthly rivers in biography (the Mohawk River in childhood) and a Nile/Egypt past-scene with reeds and a boat; a river used as the exit portal back to the body, with no far bank and no dead; a creek with a footbridge toward a golden castle - water, but not the uncrossable divide; a commentator cataloguing river-crossing as a common NDE trope, and an audience member's question about the river; note: 6 of the 14 true positives are the same two accounts duplicated across channels.

places.name: The Healing Place
places.description: A building or chamber where souls are repaired. Descriptions include pools of living water that people are lowered into, a curved room with a defined curvature that guides call a healing chamber, and 'a spiritual hospital' where those who died traumatically or by suicide are brought gently to awareness of what has happened. The work done there is described as being at the atomic or energetic level - stitching, repairing, flushing damage out with light.

places.notes: Genuinely rare (1.07%) and flat to slightly declining across strata. Precision ~0.5 because 'place of healing' is also common as a metaphor for a therapeutic setting in the speaker's earthly life. Kept because when it is literal it is unusually specific and physically detailed. Audit found false positives of the form: earthly 'healing centers': the speaker's own practice, yoga therapy in Thailand, retreats and workshops, a repurposed building in Colorado, a bio blurb (5 passages); Egyptian healing temples at Saqqara recalled as history/past-life, not the NDE; a vision of future Earth in which surviving homes become healing centers; a medium watching angels heal a dying woman at her bedside, plus speculation about 'the healing centers in the spirit world'; 'looking into the healing room' as a metaphor for treating cancer patients.

places.name: The Switch — Arriving With No Passage At All
places.description: For some there is no travel of any kind. One moment they are in bed, on a bike, at a party, on the operating table; the next moment they are somewhere else entirely, with, as one puts it, no sense of transition. They reach for the same handful of images: a switch flipped, an instantaneous shift in consciousness, 'boom, there I am'. This is the cleanest statement in the corpus that the journey is not necessarily a journey.

aliases.term: like somebody turned a switch on and you moved
one moment I was... and the next moment I was...
aliases.note: the corpus's dominant syntax for this

aliases.term: a smooth transition into the other side
I just turned and stepped down

no sense of transition at all — the seam is simply absent
the same construction used for the return: 'boom, I was back in my body'
sometimes accompanied by an accompanying feeling of relief rather than motion

quotes.text: I didn't go through a tunnel. I didn't any of that kind of thing. It was an instantaneous shift in consciousness. Boom, there I am.
quotes.speaker: Tony Woody

quotes.text: Like somebody turned a switch on and you moved.
quotes.speaker: Ray Ferstein

places.notes: MORE common among the best-evidenced accounts (0.92% all vs 1.66% at cv>=23), though the absolute numbers are tiny (3 docs at cv>=23). This is a severe undercount of a common phenomenon: I tightened the regex hard because a looser version (4.16%, including bare 'boom' and 'in the blink of an eye') fired mostly on the RETURN transition and on the speed of the life review, not on outbound translocation. What survives is the specific 'one moment X, the next moment Y' construction, which is highly diagnostic. Conceptually this is the positive form of the-tunnel-that-wasnt. Audit found false positives of the form: a literal switch on a portable ventilator, in one widely re-uploaded account (3 passages); 'a flick of a switch' as a metaphor for how easily he could have died had he chosen to stay (2 passages); 'from one moment to the next' in ordinary life: deciding to send an email, the onset of a haemorrhage, the moment after an electrocution; a host reciting what NDErs generally say about having 'no sense of transition'; note: I counted the return leg (light to body with no passage) as in-scope, since the claim's own wording is drawn from such a passage.

places.name: The Bridge
places.description: A crossing over water. Small, often stone or wooden, sometimes described as ornamental rather than structural - 'like a garden ornament'. What happens on it matters more than what it is made of: people are seen walking across, and the moment they reach the far side they stop walking and simply float away. Several experiencers get to the point where the bridge begins and are turned back there, making it the exact place where the decision to return is taken.

places.notes: Flat across strata. Precision losses are the medical 'bridge' device, the metaphorical bridge between beliefs, and the bridge of the nose. Distinct from the wall/fence barrier: the bridge is a boundary you are permitted to approach and even step onto, which is why it shows up in return-decision narratives rather than in 'I was stopped' narratives. Audit found false positives of the form: The bridge as a metaphor for dying, from an 80-year-old interviewee - 'I recognize the bridge... and I go to the other side' - appearing twice as duplicate uploads (docs OizX472ycCw, coSo-eQS1jI).; Ordinary-world bridges: fleeing a pursuer over a street bridge at 6am, a retreat walk over a bridge to a waterfall, and a cobblestone bridge in an 1800s past-life memory (docs OLGWAewZDp0, Hsr31XRRqSI, tlQGWtu9emM).; A prayer visualisation - 'I pictured a golden healing, like a bridge' - imagined deliberately, not perceived (doc HfEcEjYuT9k).; Generalisation about what most NDErs report ('they couldn't cross a bridge, they couldn't cross a creek') and a third-person retelling of someone else's footbridge NDE (docs BXtPCN_At9Q, P1MVSAwKZ8Y). The second one is painfully on-claim but it is 'she', not 'I'.; Also note: the two strongest matches are the same experiencer (hhADKDdhTTk, IZWbojibwyA), so the surviving evidence is two distinct accounts, not three..

places.name: The One Who Wears the Face You Would Know
places.description: Experiencers repeatedly volunteer their own theory of why the same destination has so many names: the light, the energy, the presence takes whatever shape the arriving person can bear. A Christian meets Jesus, a Buddhist meets Buddha, a Hindu meets Shiva or Krishna, a Muslim meets Allah, and several say this is deliberate comfort, not deception. Some experiencers report meeting a figure from a tradition that was NOT their own, which they treat as evidence the naming is not simple projection.

aliases.note: the commonest phrasing

to make you comfortable in the transition

places.notes: This is the single most important finding for alias-mapping: the corpus theorises about its own naming variation, and it does so MORE among the best-evidenced accounts (1.55% overall, 3.31% at cv>=23 - a doubling). Cross-tradition mismatches are reported in both directions: a Hindu-raised man seeing Archangel Michael, a non-Hindu seeing Shiva, atheists seeing Jesus, a Hindu woman seeing Jesus. Caveat: many of these passages are spoken by researchers, mediums and pastors summarising other people's accounts rather than by the experiencer about their own NDE - roughly a quarter of matches. Where an experiencer offers it about their own experience, it is almost always offered defensively ('I know how this sounds'). Audit found false positives of the form: This node is mostly a discourse, not a place. The single biggest class (about 6 passages) is the theory stated in the abstract about people in general, with no encounter attached: 'one person will say I saw Buddha, the other Krishna, the other Jesus' (Tqa05mlAjEE), 'Christians will say it was Jesus. Buddhists will say it was Buddha' (x3voOKz5YJA), 'the love of heaven will appear to you in the form that you recognize' (cElqN6A0ll0), 'people in other cultures see Krishna... an NDE is a little bit culturally colored' (WFFHntnF52o), 'other people based off of their belief system see what it is they believe in' (QvJUaJ669wM), 'Some people that were Jewish saw Jesus' (nsc0Z2N-HJE). Under the stated rule these are speculation about what happens generally; if the map wants the theory itself as the node, precision rises to about 0.5, and that is the honest headline: the regex measures NDE comparative-religion talk-show discourse, not a perceived figure.; Interviewer framing and channel boilerplate: a host posing the many-faces theory to a guest who rejects it (9m77ID3wC6s), an episode teaser (oJABwVFUKrc), a Christian testimony preamble (w_WtY63NnoM).; Passages that matched only on a religion word: complaints about atheist and Jewish friends (EzAqXCw1inc), 'the Buddhist smile that you might see on Buddha' describing the speaker's own face (feep8OaA8xc), demons and generational curses (k6kLAU6cP-I), body-heating and dormant knowledge (XliDnmcoND0), word-frequency energy talk (rL3KRwPz4TA), ego and the light (ckN-AJxfpi0), general encouragement to listeners (I3U3frTbE94), and a past-life review in which the speaker was a Buddhist (I9NyXh0mMfI).; Second-hand cases: Jewish children who see Jesus, reported about others (vko4tnKFRA8), and 'a young man... Aaron Green' style referrals..

places.name: the invisible barrier
places.description: A boundary with no visible substance that nonetheless stops the body absolutely. Experiencers reach for physical analogies they immediately reject: like glass, like water, like a dome, like a wall of energy. It is transparent in both directions — the dead can be seen and sometimes heard on the far side — and touching it, or being touched through it, is often forbidden.

aliases.note: one family's name for exactly this barrier

sensory: transparent, seen only by its effect

the light of the far side can be seen through it but not entered
sometimes described as soft or cloud-like on impact rather than hard

quotes.speaker: Elisabeth Tauss

places.notes: Flat at 0.97% through cv>=18 then doubling at cv>=23 (2.21%), though the cv>=23 stratum is only 181 documents so that jump is 4 docs and should not be over-read. This is the form of the boundary most often reported by people who also report seeing deceased relatives standing just beyond it. Audit found false positives of the form: the phrase 'energy field' in new-age teaching and healing patter - lightening your energy field, clearing it with tones, Archangel Michael vacuuming it (6 passages, the single dominant junk source); 'an invisible wall went up between me and them' as a social metaphor after the NDE; a physical barrier in the accident scene (trapped under a car); an interviewee relaying another person's NDE barrier; a visible golden city wall, which is a wall but not the invisible one; a meditation/surrender threshold rather than a boundary in the other world.

places.name: the fence
places.description: A low, unimposing, entirely domestic barrier standing between the experiencer and a meadow, garden or gathering of people. Wooden, white, ornate, chest-high, or barbed wire. It is never described as defensive or menacing; several people note it is far too low to keep anyone out, which is precisely what makes its authority strange. In some accounts the ground beyond the fence is visible and sharp; in others it is deliberately blurred.
sensory: chest-high, 'not real high', clearly climbable
ordinary wood or wire — nothing celestial about the material
the view beyond is fuzzy and blurry in the barbed-wire accounts, crystal clear in the garden accounts
people on the far side are talking, laughing, unhurried

quotes.speaker: Alba Monn

places.notes: The fence rises with evidential strength (1.04 -> 1.21 -> 1.80% at cv>=18), one of the few boundary objects that does. The barbed-wire variant is one experiencer (Bri Lafferty) told across four separate videos, so document counts overstate distinct people; the wooden/white-fence-in-a-meadow variant is genuinely multi-source. Precision is limited by literal childhood fences in biographical passages. Audit found false positives of the form: 'the picket fence' as shorthand for a conventional suburban life - house, marriage, two kids (2 passages); earthly fences: the South Africa/Zimbabwe border fence, a backyard fence a bird lands on, wooden gates during home renovations, a whitewater rapid named the Picket Fence, a gang called the white fence; fence as a metaphor for mental limits ('there's no fence around heaven', 'our little fence building and logic building'); an earthly barbed-wire fence invoked only as a contrast to how run-down this world looks next to the new one; incidental fenced yards in an otherworld village that are scenery rather than the boundary.

places.name: The Wall / Fence / Barrier
places.description: A built or quasi-built limit that cannot be crossed. It appears as a white fence in the distance across a meadow, a low wooden fence approached step by step, a picket fence, or - most often - an invisible barrier with no material at all which nevertheless stops both the visitor and the dead who are waiting on the other side. Everyone understands the same rule without being told: cross it and there is no return.

aliases.note: the commonest form; nobody can come through it in either direction
seen at a distance across a meadow, with low shrubbery beyond
understood afterwards as the symbol of passing over for good
something is behind it, and you cannot go behind it

aliases.term: the barrier I could not get past

sensory: the fence is always in the distance, never close up
the barrier has no substance and no visible edge
the dead cannot come through it either - they stop at it too
a foot lifted for one more step, and then you are back in your body
beyond it: low shrubbery, trees, 'it looked like Kentucky'

quotes.text: I understood without being told that if I crossed that line or passed through it, there would be no coming back.
quotes.speaker: Cherylyn

quotes.text: It was like there was like some kind of invisible barrier that I couldn't cross and she couldn't cross.
quotes.speaker: Annie Rea

quotes.speaker: Kimberly Clark Sharp

quotes.text: As I took some further steps towards this fence, this wooden fence
quotes.speaker: Alba Monn

places.notes: Deliberately narrow regex - the unconstrained forms of 'wall' and 'fence' match 25% of the corpus and are almost entirely earthly. At this tightness it is genuinely rare (0.53%) but doubles by cv>=23. Overlaps the border/boundary region; included here only for the constructed forms (fence, wall, gate-as-limit), not the river or line-of-light forms. Audit found false positives of the form: 'Picket fence' as the standard American metaphor for conventional life - 'the picket fence, the marriage, the two kids', 'the house and the picket fence' (docs RvTt0Qyt-4Q, xtCpWPldQIE). This is the one recurring junk type; three of seven FPs.; Literal ordinary-world walls and fences: a hospital operating-room glass wall, a wooden fence in an apartment complex, and a rapid on the Rogue River nicknamed 'the picket fence' (docs lMEQ4Oe18FU, qt8LlDTFIk8, uHjUZNJ76dc).; A transparent wall used as a viewing window inside a craft, not a limit (doc Md2PdURAXGI).; An interview passage in which the experiencer explicitly DENIES having any sense of a limit or line (doc -wXVPKwR-OM)..

places.name: The others who are suffering
places.description: Seeing other people in torment: crowds in the fire, bodies in holes trying to climb out and being pushed back, faces bobbing in the lake. Experiencers consistently report that witnessing this was as distressing as anything done to them, and several recognise individuals they knew in life. The crowd is dense — 'thousands' is the recurring word.

aliases.term: people in the lake of fire

sensory: density — thousands, as far as the eye can see

recognition of specific individuals from the experiencer's life
in the grey place the equivalent crowd is silent and does not look up

quotes.speaker: Bryan W. Melvin

quotes.speaker: Mario

places.notes: Erratic across strata — 1.10% overall, dipping to 0.69% at cv>=18 then jumping to 2.21% at cv>=23, which on n=181 is only 4 documents, so that spike is not meaningful. Report as rare and roughly flat. The tighter regex (requiring torture/torment/burning rather than merely screaming) cut the match set from 349 docs to 68 and lifted precision from about 0.25 to about 0.70; the discarded matches were almost entirely people watching their own resuscitation. Audit found false positives of the form: 'on fire for God' as an idiom for religious enthusiasm (3 passages); 'tormented' used of ordinary life: abusive relationships, being an empath, clients with tormented souls; host intros and book plugs summarising a guest's hell NDE in the third person; political/theological argument about whether people deserve to be tortured in hell; visions of Earth burning in end-times prophecy, or God showing 'people being tortured' worldwide - not the afterlife multitude; the experiencer's own torment by entities rather than witnessing a crowd of others.

places.name: the unspoken knowing of the limit
places.description: The boundary arrives as certainty rather than as information. No one speaks, nothing is written, often nothing is even visible, and yet the experiencer knows with total confidence that a specific further step ends the return. Several people explicitly contrast this with being told: 'I was never asked if I could go. I was never told I couldn't go. I just knew.' This is reported as the same order of certainty as knowing one's own name.
sensory: certainty without a source — 'it just hit me'
no words, no voice, no visible sign
coexists with intense desire to cross anyway
described as more reliable than earthly knowledge

quotes.text: but there was an energetic threshold, I knew if I stepped over that, I wouldn't be going back.
quotes.speaker: Sara Jayne

quotes.text: I understood without being told that if I crossed that line, or passed through it (if it was opened), there would be no coming back.

quotes.text: I was never asked if I could go. I was never told I couldn't go. I just knew I couldn't go with them.
quotes.speaker: Brianna Laferty

quotes.speaker: Kevin Milsom

places.notes: This is a deliberately high-precision, low-recall regex: 12 of 12 sampled snippets were genuine. The measured 0.37% is a floor, not a prevalence — the same phenomenon appears unregexable in a much larger share of accounts, where people just say 'I couldn't go any further' with no explanation (see 'this-far-and-no-further', 3.68%). Zero hits at cv>=23 is a small-denominator artefact (181 docs), not evidence of absence. Audit found false positives of the form: None. Every one of the 23 passages is a first-person report of knowing, without being told, that a specific further step ends the return - across water, a tree, a gate, clouds, a door, a threshold, a line, a light.; The only impurities are cosmetic: two passages run into channel boilerplate after the sentence (docs AEgxTodIs3o, YOi92hxfJgA) and three are the same 'behind this gate' testimony re-uploaded (docs WzyaTY1Wt5U, Y0McKoG83Ds, oRF8Y6GeJ4Q). Neither affects the judgement.; Caveat for the map, not the regex: duplicate uploads mean 23 matches are roughly 19 distinct accounts..

places.name: the questions
places.description: In a distinct minority of accounts the review is not silent. A voice - usually identified as God, sometimes simply 'a voice' - asks a small fixed set of questions, most commonly two or three, and waits. The recurring question across unrelated accounts is remarkably stable: 'What have you done with your life?' Experiencers describe answering with their credentials and having the answer rejected, then discovering that in that realm you cannot think one thing and say another, because the questioner already knows.

aliases.term: what have you done with your life?
what have you done for others?
how do you think you've done? what could you do better?

sensory: the question repeated verbatim after an evasive answer
the voice penetrating 'my very being' rather than being heard
the impossibility of hypocrisy - the questioner already knows what you think
the questions asked while the images are still running

quotes.text: Following several minutes of silence, an unknown voice inquired, "What have you done with your life?" Sadly, I heard myself say, "Nothing. I have wasted the entire 47 years."
quotes.speaker: not provided

quotes.text: this wonderful voice, with the voice that I now recognize as the voice of God, issued three questions.

quotes.text: And he threw a question, "What had I done with my life?" And I thought, "Well, I'm an Eagle Scout."
quotes.speaker: Andy

quotes.text: a voice asked me, "What have you done for others? What have you done to help yourself? And have you always believed in Me?"
quotes.speaker: Eugene Braxton

places.notes: Rare but strikingly consistent across unconnected accounts, which is why it is included despite the low count. The 'three questions' phrasing occasionally matches interview logistics ('I have three questions for you'), the main false positive. Note the interrogative review is the exception, not the rule - the no-judgement accounts vastly outnumber it. Audit found false positives of the form: the bare phrase 'three questions' in ordinary contexts: the interviewer's own questions, a daily self-improvement ritual, a rune-casting party, a medium's client Q&A; self-directed existential questions in the void ('I asked myself three questions: who am I, where did I come from') - the claim requires a voice asking the experiencer; researcher/host narration listing the questions other NDErs report, or introducing a guest's account in the third person; sermon speculation about what Jesus will ask you when you die; questions the experiencer asked the being, i.e. the reverse direction; note: 4 of the 8 true positives are the same Eagle Scout account re-uploaded on different channels, so distinct-account support is much thinner than the count suggests.

places.name: Remembering Who You Really Are
places.description: A specific event inside the experience: an amnesia lifts and the person remembers their own identity — not their biography but what they were before the biography. Several describe it as the veil of forgetting being drawn back, and report astonishment that such a thing could have been forgotten at all. The mirror-image report is equally common: on return, they forget again, and know that they have forgotten.

aliases.note: the inverse, describing incarnation

aliases.term: the veil of forgetting had been lifted
I remembered that I was source
I've known all this, but why did I forget it?

aliases.note: one experiencer's later framing of the same moment

sensory: reported as a lifting or drawing-back, not as being told
arrives with the memory of choosing this life
the forgetting is described as structural, a condition of being born, not a personal failure
on return the knowledge drains away and the loss is felt as it happens

quotes.text: I remembered why I came here. I remembered who I am. I remembered what's happening.
quotes.speaker: Dianne Sherman

quotes.text: I literally remembered who I was. And as if the veil of forgetting had been lifted, and I remembered that I was source.
quotes.speaker: Lelañea Fulton

quotes.speaker: Nanci Danison

quotes.text: Why did I forget all this?
quotes.speaker: Kenneth Leth

places.notes: Deliberately narrow. A looser regex catching 'I remembered everything' reaches 8.4% but is dominated by people remembering the accident, so I discarded it. What is left (1.25%) is the soul-identity sense only, and it holds up at cvNDE>=18 (1.24%). This is the recognition of self that parallels the-recognition's recognition of place; it is adjacent to but distinct from the already-catalogued veil-of-forgetting, which names the barrier rather than the moment it lifts. Audit found false positives of the form: The sermon form dominates: 'we have forgotten who we are' as general teaching about humanity - at least eight passages, none reporting an event inside an experience; Interviewer questions built on that phrase ('you said that we've forgotten who we are. Do you feel like that is by design?'); Biography: a medium who 'forgot who I was and what my life purpose was' growing up; post-discharge memory confusion explicitly NOT identity loss; Recognition of something else - an angel, a dragon - phrased as 'it was like I had always known this presence'; Ego-dissolution in a dream ('so profound that I forgot who I was') and a translation artefact ('I forgot say that I'm from Gaucha').

places.name: Buddha, Krishna, the Great Spirit
places.description: Rare but real: the being in the light identified by a name outside the Christian frame. Buddha is the most frequent — sometimes recognised years later from a picture on a wall — followed by Krishna, the Great Spirit, and Allah/Yahweh. Two features stand out. First, the recognition is usually retrospective: 'the man in my near-death experience was Buddha' comes long after the event. Second, at least one shared-death account has different people in the same event seeing different figures.

aliases.note: 23 raw identities in the entity census
15 raw identities
reported as the Hindu reading of the same figure
offered in the corpus as an example of culturally-fitted recognition
the corpus's own summary of the whole problem

sensory: young, thin, bald, long brown robes, bare feet (Buddha)
a raft, a river bank
laughing face appearing in grass (the 'Happy Buddha')
in one shared account, three people in the same event met three different figures — a guide, a deceased father, and Buddha

quotes.text: As Christ was gracing me, the light transformed, and within it, I saw the Buddha as a living lotus, the center unfolding endlessly.
quotes.speaker: Mellen-Thomas Benedict

quotes.speaker: Ellen Whealton

quotes.speaker: Pam Reynolds
